lead: Two stories about who receives God’s gift. In the First Reading, an enemy general with a skin disease is healed in the Jordan, once he stops demanding a cure fit for his rank. In the Gospel, Jesus reminds his own townspeople of that same general, and they try to kill him for it. Between the two the Psalm sings of a soul that thirsts for the living God. Thirst is the one qualification. The key words are wash, clean and accepted.

r.h: Go, wash in the Jordan
set: Elisha worked in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, when Israel and Aram (Syria, with its capital at Damascus) were often at war. The first verse holds a surprise: it was “the Lord” who had given victory to Aram. The God of Israel is at work in the career of Israel’s enemy before that enemy has ever heard of him.

Naaman has rank, wealth and the favor of his king, and he has a disease that none of it can touch. The Hebrew word translated “leprosy” covers a range of skin conditions, and not only what we now call Hansen’s disease. The reading ends in the middle of v. 15, with Naaman’s confession of faith.
str: vv. 1–3: the great man and the captive girl who knows where help is.
vv. 4–7: the wrong road: king writes to king, and the king of Israel panics.
vv. 8–10: Elisha sends a message and does not come out.
vv. 11–12: Naaman’s anger: too plain, and the wrong river.
vv. 13–14: his servants reason with him; he goes down and is healed.
v. 15: he returns and confesses the one God.
kw: A general word for serious skin diseases. Here it stands for what lies beyond all human power: the king of Israel himself says that only God could cure it (5:7).

The story begins with a “little girl”, a captive who serves in Naaman’s house (5:2), and it ends with the proud commander’s flesh made like that of a “little boy” (5:14). The two Hebrew phrases match. He is healed by becoming small.
The word comes four times (5:10, 12, 13, 14). Naaman comes asking for a cure; what he receives is called cleansing, and a word of worship comes with it.
vv: If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria!
She has been carried off from her home and she has no name in the story. She could have enjoyed her master’s misfortune. Her one sentence starts the healing of a Gentile commander.
I thought that for me he would surely come out,
“For me.” Naaman has already written the script: a prophet at the door, a solemn prayer, a wave of the hand. What offends him is that God’s way asks nothing grand of him.
So he went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.

The Greek Old Testament translates “immersed himself” with the verb ebaptisato, the word that gives us baptism. Seven is the number of completeness: he obeys fully, and the waters heal because of the word he obeys.
Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel;
This is the real goal of the story. He came for his skin and he goes home with faith. In the verses that follow he will say that he will sacrifice to no other god (5:17).
ch: St Ambrose, instructing the newly baptized in his work On the Mysteries, uses Naaman to teach that the water of the font does not heal by itself, and that it is the grace of Christ that heals (in substance). Lent is the season of preparing for that font and of renewing our baptism, and the story speaks to both. Each of us at some point has to go down, drop the script and do the plain thing God asks: go to Confession, make the apology, kneel down to pray.

r.h: No prophet is accepted in his hometown
set: We are in the synagogue at Nazareth, on the Sabbath. Jesus has read from Isaiah 61, announced that the Scripture is fulfilled, and at first “all spoke well of him” (4:22). Then they ask for the wonders he worked at Capernaum (4:23). Mark and Matthew tell of the visit to Nazareth later on. Luke places it at the opening of the ministry, and many scholars think he does so on purpose, as a preview of all that will follow in his Gospel and in Acts.

Jesus is a Jew in his own synagogue, arguing from the Scriptures of Israel. The anger is that of one village on one day, as Luke tells it, and it is no ground for any blame of the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Elijah and Elisha, whom Jesus names, are Israel’s own prophets.
str: v. 24: the proverb.
vv. 25–26: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.
v. 27: Elisha and Naaman.
vv. 28–29: rage, and the brow of the hill.
v. 30: he goes on his way.
kw: A small word with a sting. A few verses earlier Jesus read of “the year of the Lord’s favor” (4:19), using the same Greek word. The year is dektos and the prophet who brings it is not.
A Phoenician region beyond Israel’s borders. Elijah was sent there in a famine, to a foreign widow (1 Kings 17:9), who fed him and whose son he raised.
The verb at the end of v. 30. Luke uses it again and again for the journey that leads to Jerusalem: “I must be on my way” (13:33).
vv: Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in the prophet’s hometown.
The people want the benefits without the prophet. Being close to Jesus, in a family or a parish or a Christian culture, carries its own danger: we may think we already know him.
There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

Jesus is not saying that God had abandoned Israel. He is answering a claim on his gifts, and in the very next verses he heals many in Capernaum (4:31–41). God’s gift is a gift, and no one has it by right, whether by nation or by neighborhood.
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.

Luke does not explain how. The hill at Nazareth is not the hour. The rejection and the walking on both point ahead to Jerusalem, where he will again be taken outside the city, and where his way will not end in death.
ch: The Catechism says that the Kingdom was first announced to the children of Israel and is intended for people of all nations (CCC 543). This Gospel holds both halves of that sentence. For us who are Gentiles by descent, it is a matter for gratitude: we are the household of the widow of Zarephath and the company of Naaman. And it is a warning against thinking that we have earned the place.

qa: Why does Jesus seem to provoke his own people?

The people of Nazareth have asked for signs, and he answers with a word that tests what they are asking for. A prophet tells the truth to those he loves, as Elijah and Elisha did. Luke shows that Jesus knew where this would lead, and he went on all the same. The sharpness serves love, and the rest of the Gospel shows him healing, teaching and weeping over his own people (19:41).
study: Where am I like Naaman, wanting God to deal with me in a way that suits my position? What plain thing is God asking of me that I keep putting off?
Who is the “little girl” in my life, the person I overlook, through whom God may be pointing me to help?

lead: Today’s readings look at mercy from both sides. In the First Reading, a young man in a furnace has nothing left to offer God but a broken heart, and he offers it. In the Gospel, a servant forgiven a debt beyond counting takes a colleague by the throat over a small one. The Psalm prays between them: “Remember your mercies, O Lord.” We ask for mercy as Azariah does. Then we have to give it. The key words are contrite, debt and heart.

r.h: With a contrite heart
set: King Nebuchadnezzar has set up a golden statue and has had three young Jews thrown into a furnace for refusing to worship it. At this point the Aramaic text of Daniel moves straight on to the king’s amazement. The Greek text includes a long passage here, with the prayer of Azariah and the song of the three young men. The Catholic Church receives this passage as Scripture. Some Bibles print it separately among the Additions to Daniel.

The story is set during the Babylonian exile. Many scholars think the Book of Daniel took its final form in the persecution under Antiochus IV, about 167–164 BC, and that this prayer may have spoken directly to those days. In either age, the prayer belongs to a people who have lost what they counted on.
str: v. 25: Azariah stands in the fire and prays.
vv. 34–36: an appeal to God’s own promise: the covenant, Abraham, Isaac, Israel.
vv. 37–38: what has been lost: ruler, prophet, offering, a place of worship.
vv. 39–40: the one thing left to offer.
vv. 41–43: following with all the heart, and asking to be delivered.
kw: The Greek says literally “a crushed soul”. The picture is of something ground down, and it is the same idea as Psalm 51:17: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.”
A spirit brought low. It is more than a feeling of being unworthy. It is the plain truth of someone who no longer has anything to bargain with.
The word comes three times in these verses (3:35, 38, 42). Azariah has no merit to plead, so he pleads God’s mercy and God’s name.
vv: Do not withdraw your mercy from us, for the sake of Abraham your beloved and for the sake of your servant Isaac and Israel your holy one,
He does not say, “We have been faithful, standing here in the fire,” though he might have. He leans on what God promised.
In our day we have no ruler, or prophet, or leader, no burnt offering, or sacrifice, or oblation, or incense, no place to make an offering before you and to find mercy.
The list strips everything away. All the ways by which Israel used to come before God are gone. For those whose parish, health or family has been taken from them, this verse gives words.
Yet with a contrite heart and a humble spirit may we be accepted,
This is the turning point. Everything else has been taken, and the heart is still there to be given.
for no shame will come to those who trust in you.
He says this from inside the furnace, before any rescue.
ch: The Church has placed this prayer at the heart of the Mass. After the gifts are set on the altar, the priest prays quietly, in words drawn from these verses: “With humble spirit and contrite heart may we be accepted by you, O Lord.” Azariah had no altar. We have one, and the words still apply: the one sacrifice of Christ is offered there, and we are asked to bring our own broken hearts to be joined to it. The Catechism teaches that outward sacrifice, to be genuine, must express the spiritual sacrifice of the heart, and it quotes Psalm 51 (CCC 2100).

r.h: Forgive from your heart
set: Chapter 18 is the fourth of the great discourses in Matthew, on life together in the community of disciples. It has spoken of the little ones, the lost sheep, and how to correct a brother who sins. Now Peter asks how far this goes. His offer of seven times is generous, and he may expect to be praised.

Some background is needed for the sums. A denarius was a laborer’s pay for a day (20:2), and a talent was about six thousand denarii. So ten thousand talents comes to some sixty million days’ wages, while a hundred denarii is about a hundred days’ wages. The first debt is six hundred thousand times the second. The figure is meant to be absurd: no servant could ever owe that or repay it.
str: vv. 21–22: Peter’s question and the answer that ends all counting.
vv. 23–27: the huge debt and the king’s mercy.
vv. 28–30: the small debt and the servant’s violence.
vv. 31–34: the king hears and judges.
v. 35: the lesson: “from your heart”.
kw: The Greek can mean seventy-seven times or seventy times seven. The NRSV gives the first and notes the second. The POC’s “seven seventy” stays close to the Greek. The phrase recalls Lamech’s boast of vengeance, “seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4:24). Jesus turns the old rule of endless revenge into endless forgiveness.
A strong word for a mercy felt in the depths of one’s being. In the Gospels it is used of Jesus himself and of the figures in his parables who act as God acts.
Matthew uses this family of words in the Lord’s Prayer: “forgive us our debts” (6:12). Sin is here pictured as something owed. The parable is a commentary on that line of the prayer.
vv: Not seven times, but, I tell you, seventy-seven times.
Anyone who is still counting has not yet forgiven. Jesus does not supply a higher number to keep track of. He ends the keeping of accounts.
And out of pity for him, the lord of that slave released him and forgave him the debt.
The servant asked only for time. The king gives him far more than he asked: the whole debt is gone.
Should you not have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?
This is the center of the parable. He demanded the small debt so harshly only because he had forgotten the large one. Mercy received is meant to flow on.
So my heavenly Father will also do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother or sister from your heart.
Forgiveness has a place, and it is the heart. Lips alone will not do. The severity of the end is the language of parable, a warning that a closed heart cannot go on receiving what it refuses to give.
ch: The Catechism is unusually direct here. It calls it daunting that the outpouring of God’s mercy “cannot penetrate our hearts as long as we have not forgiven those who have trespassed against us” (CCC 2840). It also says, with great tenderness, that it is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offense, but that the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies the memory, transforming the hurt into intercession (CCC 2843). There is no limit or measure to this forgiveness (CCC 2845).

qa: Does forgiving mean I must forget, or stay close to someone who harms me?

No. The Catechism says plainly that we cannot command ourselves to stop feeling or to forget (CCC 2843). To forgive is to give up revenge and the wish for harm, to hand the debt over to God, and to begin to pray for the person. It does not pretend that wrong was not wrong. It does not require anyone to stay in danger, and it does not cancel the claims of justice. Often it comes slowly, and the first step is simply to ask God for the willingness.
study: Azariah offers God his contrite heart because he has nothing else. What in my life this Lent has been taken away from me that I could offer to God in this way?
Whose debt am I still carrying? What is one thing I can do this week to begin handing it over, even if it is only a prayer for that person by name?

lead: Moses tells Israel that God’s law is its wisdom and its glory. Jesus says he has come not to abolish that law but to fulfill it. The Psalm sings the same thing: God has made his word known to Jacob and his statutes to Israel. Lent is a good time to learn that God’s commandments are a gift to those he loves. The key words are statutes, near and fulfill.

r.h: What other nation has a god so near?
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses’ farewell, spoken on the far side of the Jordan “in the land of Moab” (1:5), before the people enter the land he will not enter. Chapter 4 closes his first speech. The verses left out of the reading (4:2–4) recall the sin at Baal-peor. Many scholars think the book reached its final shape over a long time, perhaps as late as the exile, and so these words would also have reached a people who had lost the land.
The argument is striking. Israel was a small people among great empires, and Moses tells them that they have what the empires lack: a God who is near, and a law that is just.
str: v. 1: “give heed”: keep the law and live.
vv. 5–6: the law is your wisdom in the eyes of the nations.
vv. 7–8: two questions: what other nation has a god so near, or a law so just?
v. 9: take care to remember, and pass it on to the children.
kw: A standing pair in Deuteronomy, meaning the whole body of God’s instruction for life in the land.

What makes Israel great in v. 7 is not its size but God’s nearness, “whenever we call to him”. Deuteronomy will later say the same of the word: “the word is very near to you” (30:14), and St Paul takes that up in Romans 10:8.
“This entire law” in v. 8. The Hebrew means instruction, such as a parent gives to a child. It is much wider than a code of penalties.
vv: give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live
The commandments lead to life. God’s law is not a test set up to catch people out.
You must observe them diligently, for this will show your wisdom and discernment to the peoples,
Israel’s way of living is to be a witness. The nations are to look and say, “a wise and discerning people”. The same is asked of Christian homes among their neighbors.
For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?
Prayer is treated here as Israel’s greatest privilege. The Psalms, the Temple and every cry to God rest on this.
make them known to your children and your children’s children
Forgetting is the great danger in Deuteronomy. Memory is kept alive when it is handed on at home.
ch: St Paul lists the giving of the law among the abiding gifts of Israel (Romans 9:4), and he says that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The Church reads this text with gratitude, as something received from the Jewish people. She adds that in Jesus Christ this nearness of God has taken flesh (John 1:14). The Catechism calls the Old Law the first stage of revealed law, holy, spiritual and good (CCC 1962–1963). It also teaches that parents have the first responsibility for the education of their children (CCC 2223), which is what v. 9 asks of them.

r.h: I have come not to abolish but to fulfill
set: These verses are part of the Sermon on the Mount. They come just after the Beatitudes and the sayings on salt and light, and just before “You have heard that it was said … but I say to you” (5:21–48). Before Jesus deepens the commandments, he makes clear that he is not setting them aside. Many scholars think Matthew writes for a community largely of Jewish Christians, for whom this question mattered a great deal.
str: v. 17: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill.
v. 18: not the smallest part will pass away.
v. 19: least and great in the Kingdom: doing and teaching.
kw: Literally to take down or dismantle, the verb used of the stones of the Temple being “thrown down” (24:2). Jesus has not come to pull the law down.

To fill up, to bring to fullness. It is one of Matthew’s favorite words (1:22; 2:15). Jesus fulfills the law and the prophets by keeping them, by teaching their deepest meaning, and by living out in his own death and resurrection what they were reaching for.

The iota is the smallest letter in Greek, and it stands here for the small Hebrew yod. The keraia, a “little horn”, is a tiny stroke on a letter. The POC’s “വള്ളിയോ പുള്ളിയോ” is a happy Malayalam equivalent.
vv: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
“Do not think” suggests that some did think so. “I have come” is the voice of someone with a mission from God. Jesus takes up a position toward the law that only its Giver could take.
until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.
Strong language for the lasting worth of God’s word. “Until all is accomplished” points toward what Jesus himself will do.
but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
Doing comes first, and then teaching. It is a word for every priest, catechist and parent, and it goes with the warning at the end of the Sermon (7:21).
ch: The Catechism devotes a section to Jesus and the Law. It quotes these verses (CCC 577) and says that Jesus fulfilled the Law by keeping it in its all-embracing detail (CCC 578). It teaches that the Law of the Gospel “fulfills”, refines, surpasses and leads the Old Law to its perfection (CCC 1967). Jesus is a Jew who loves the Torah, and the Christian who despises the Old Testament has not understood him.

qa: If not one stroke of the law will pass away, why do Catholics not keep the food laws or circumcision?

The early Church faced this very question at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15), and Mark’s Gospel records the insight about foods (Mark 7:19). St Thomas Aquinas taught a distinction that became standard: moral, ceremonial and judicial precepts (Summa Theologiae I–II, q. 99). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binds us. The ceremonial laws reach their goal in Christ, in whom Gentiles are welcomed without becoming Jews first. None of this slights Jewish people who keep those laws in faithfulness to God. The Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121).
study: Do I think of God’s commandments as a burden laid on me or as a mark of his nearness? Which one do I find hardest to see as a gift?
What in the faith did I learn from my family, and what am I now handing on to the next generation, in words and in the way I live?

lead: Today’s readings are about a refusal to listen. Jeremiah is told that the people will not hear him, and he is told to speak all the same. In the Gospel, people see a mute man speak and some of them explain it away. The Psalm gives the whole matter one word: “today”. If today you hear his voice, harden not your hearts. The key words are obey, finger and stronger.

r.h: This is the nation that did not obey
set: Chapter 7 opens with Jeremiah’s great Temple sermon, also told in chapter 26, which dates it to the beginning of the reign of King Jehoiakim, about 609 BC. The people trust in the Temple as if it guaranteed their safety (7:4). A little more than twenty years later Jerusalem will fall.

These verses come from a section on what God really asked of his people (7:21–28). Jeremiah speaks as one of his own people, and he grieves over them (9:1). These hard words were preserved by Israel itself, as Scripture, and they must never be turned into a weapon against the Jewish people. The Church hears them as said to herself, and to each of us.
str: v. 23: what God asked: “Obey my voice”.
v. 24: the response: their own counsels, and walking backward.
vv. 25–26: God kept sending prophets, and they kept refusing.
v. 27: Jeremiah is told in advance that they will not listen.
v. 28: the verdict.
kw: In Hebrew the same verb means to hear and to obey. To hear God’s voice without doing what it says is not really to have heard it.
The Hebrew says literally “rising early and sending”, and it is used several times in Jeremiah. God is pictured getting up at dawn, day after day, to send another prophet.
“Truth has perished” in v. 28. The word means reliability and faithfulness, of the kind one can lean on. It is lost from the lips first, and then from the life.
vv: Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people;
This is the covenant in a sentence, and it is put in terms of a relationship: your God, my people.
and looked backward rather than forward.
Sin here does not stand still. It takes us the wrong way along the road.
So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you.
A hard call for a preacher. Success is not promised, and faithfulness is what is asked. Every priest, catechist and parent has known such a day.
This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the Lord their God, and did not accept discipline;
“Discipline” (mûsār) means the training a parent gives. Even the verdict speaks of what God wanted to do for them.
ch: The Catechism says that to obey in faith, from the Latin ob-audire, is to hear or listen, and to submit freely to the word that has been heard (CCC 144). The Psalm of this day, Psalm 95, is also the psalm with which the Church traditionally opens her daily prayer, and the Letter to the Hebrews applies its “today” to Christians (Hebrews 3:7–4:11). St Benedict’s Rule begins with the word “Listen”, and its Prologue quotes this same psalm. In Lent we are given the same call to listen, every morning.

r.h: By the finger of God
set: Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem that began in 9:51. Just before this he has taught about prayer, and he has promised that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask (11:13). Now he casts out a demon, and the crowd divides. Luke says only “some of them”. Mark names scribes from Jerusalem (3:22), and Matthew names Pharisees (12:24). In Luke the crowd is amazed, and the charge is made by a few among them.
No one here denies that something has happened. The man who could not speak now speaks. The only question is by what power it was done.
str: v. 14: the healing and the amazement.
vv. 15–16: two reactions: an accusation and a demand for a sign.
vv. 17–19: three replies: a divided kingdom, Satan divided, your own exorcists.
v. 20: the real meaning: the Kingdom has come.
vv. 21–22: the strong man and the stronger one.
v. 23: there is no neutral ground.
kw: Here the prince of the demons. The name seems to go back to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron in 2 Kings 1:2, and to a title of Baal. Its exact meaning is uncertain.

Pharaoh’s magicians say, “This is the finger of God!” (Exodus 8:19), and the tablets of the covenant are “written with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). Matthew has “the Spirit of God” here (12:28). The POC’s “ദൈവകരം” (hand of God) gives the sense.
The same word John the Baptist uses of the one who is coming: “more powerful than I” (3:16). Luke’s reader knows who the stronger one is.
vv: Now if I cast out the demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your exorcists cast them out?
The Greek says “your sons”, which the POC keeps; the NRSV makes the meaning clear. Jesus grants that God acts through others among his own people. He is arguing with them on common ground.
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come to you.

This is the center of the passage. The God who freed Israel from Egypt is at work again, and the verb says it has already arrived. What people are looking at is not one more wonder but the beginning of God’s reign.
But when one stronger than he attacks him and overpowers him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his plunder.
Jesus does not bargain with the strong man. Those whom he frees are the plunder, and Christ’s victory will be won finally on the Cross.
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
The image is of a shepherd gathering a flock. To stand by and do nothing is itself a way of letting the sheep scatter.
ch: The Catechism quotes the parallel saying in Matthew: the coming of God’s kingdom means the defeat of Satan’s (CCC 550). It connects “the finger of God” with the Holy Spirit and notes that the hymn Veni Creator Spiritus calls the Spirit the “finger of the Father’s right hand” (CCC 700). The Church also teaches that the power of Satan is not infinite (CCC 395). In the rite of baptism a prayer of exorcism is said over the candidate (CCC 1237). Lent’s purpose, for those preparing for baptism and for the rest of us, is to let the stronger one take back what the strong man has held.

qa: Here Jesus says, “Whoever is not with me is against me”. But in Luke 9:50 he says, “Whoever is not against you is for you”. Which is it?

Both, because they are said about different questions. In Luke 9 the disciples want to stop a man who is casting out demons in Jesus’ name, and Jesus tells them not to be jealous of the good done by those outside their circle. Here the issue is one’s stance toward Jesus himself. So we should be generous in judging others and honest in judging ourselves. No one can be neutral toward Christ.
study: When have I heard God’s voice clearly and chosen not to listen? What would it mean today to “incline my ear”?
What is the mute place in my life, the thing I cannot speak of, even to God, that needs the stronger one to set it right?

lead: Today we hear one of the tenderest chapters in the prophets, and the question at the heart of the whole Law. Hosea gives Israel the very words to say on the way home, and God answers, “I will love them freely.” In the Gospel, a scribe asks what matters most, and Jesus and he agree. The Psalm stands between them: “Hear my voice.” God’s love comes first, and our love answers it. The key words are return, hear and love.

r.h: I will love them freely
set: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel (he often calls it Ephraim) in the eighth century BC, in the last anxious decades before Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722/721 BC. His book accuses Israel of unfaithfulness in the language of a broken marriage, and it also contains some of the most loving words in Scripture (11:8–9).
This last chapter closes the book with a promise. It is worth knowing that some Bibles and lectionaries count these verses as 14:2–10, following the Hebrew numbering. The words are the same.
str: vv. 1–3: the call to return, and the words of the prayer to pray.
v. 4: God’s answer: healing and love.
vv. 5–7: pictures of a land in bloom: dew, lily, olive, vine.
v. 8: Ephraim and the idols; God as an evergreen tree.
v. 9: a closing word of wisdom for the reader.
kw: The great word of the prophets for conversion. It means to turn around and go back. Hosea plays on it: God will heal their məšûbâ, their “turning away” (NRSV “disloyalty”), a word from the same root (14:4). The turning back heals the turning away.

In the Law this word means a freewill offering, something given not because it is owed but because the giver wishes to give it. God’s love is such an offering. Nobody is paying for it. The POC says “സ്നേഹം ചൊരിയും”, “I will pour out love”.
In a dry land where summer rain does not fall, dew keeps the plants alive. It comes quietly and overnight. God’s love is compared to this.
vv: Take words with you and return to the Lord; say to him, “Take away all guilt; accept that which is good, and we will offer the fruit of our lips.

God even supplies the words of repentance. That Hebrew phrase is difficult: the traditional text reads “bulls of our lips”, while the Greek reads “fruit of our lips”, and the NRSV and POC follow that sense. Either way, the prayer of the lips is offered as a true gift to God. The Letter to the Hebrews takes up the phrase for the praise offered through Christ (Hebrews 13:15), praise that flows from his sacrifice.
Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses;

Here are the false securities of that time: a great power, a strong army and, in the following words, idols made by human hands. To turn to God means to name and give up what we have trusted in instead.
I will heal their disloyalty; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.
Notice what comes first. God does not say, “I will love them when they have changed.” He says that he will heal them. Conversion itself is his gift.
I am like an evergreen cypress; your faithfulness comes from me.

God likens himself to a tree, a rare image in Scripture, and one all the more striking because trees were often linked to false worship in Hosea’s day (4:13). “Your faithfulness” is the NRSV’s reading of the Hebrew “your fruit”, which the POC keeps (ഫലം). Even our good fruit grows from him.
ch: The Catechism says that God’s only reason for choosing Israel was his “sheer gratuitous love”, and that this love is compared to a father’s and a bridegroom’s (CCC 218–219). It also teaches that conversion is first a work of the grace of God who makes our hearts return to him (CCC 1432). That is the theology of Hosea 14 in a sentence. It explains why the Church has us begin Lent, and every Confession, by trusting that God has moved first.

r.h: You are not far from the kingdom
set: Jesus is in the Temple in Jerusalem, in the last days before his Passion. He has been questioned by one group after another, and the Sadducees have just asked him about the resurrection (12:18–27). Now one of the scribes, an expert in the Law, approaches him with a sincere question. Matthew and Luke present a similar question as a test (Matthew 22:35; Luke 10:25). Only in Mark does the scribe reply and receive this word of praise.

Jesus answers from the Torah itself. His first commandment is the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5), which devout Jews prayed then, and still pray today, each morning and evening. His second comes from Leviticus 19:18. In this scene a Jewish teacher and a scribe agree on what the Law is about, and it is a scene to treasure.
str: v. 28: the scribe’s question: which is first?
vv. 29–31: Jesus’ answer: two commandments that belong together.
vv. 32–33: the scribe agrees and adds his own conclusion.
v. 34: “not far from the kingdom of God”.
kw: The first word of Israel’s daily prayer. Only Mark includes this opening line in the reply. Before “you shall love” comes “hear”: love begins by listening to the God who has spoken.
This is a command about the whole person. Deuteronomy lists heart, soul and might. Mark’s Jesus has four terms, adding “mind”. Nothing in us is left out.
Literally “having a mind”. The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Jesus recognizes real understanding in this scribe, and he says so.
vv: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one;
The love commandment rests on who God is. Because he is the one God, he cannot be given a share of the heart while something else takes the rest.
The second is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.
He was asked for one and he gives two, and then he speaks of them together. The love of God is proved in love of neighbor (1 John 4:20).
this is much more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.

He says this in the Temple itself, where such offerings were being made. Like Hosea and Samuel before him (Hosea 6:6; 1 Samuel 15:22), he sets out the order of things. He is not rejecting worship. Within days Jesus will give himself up as the offering in which love of God and of neighbor are one.
When Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”
A warm word and an open one. The man is near. What remains is the one who is speaking to him. He stands at the threshold, and Mark leaves him there for us to think about.
ch: The Catechism quotes this reply of Jesus when it opens its teaching on love of neighbor (CCC 2196) and when it teaches about the one God (CCC 228). Pope Benedict XVI begins Deus Caritas Est with these same texts, noting that Jesus united into a single precept the commandment of love of God and the commandment of love of neighbor (no. 1). The Church reads the Ten Commandments in that light: the first three concern love of God, and the other seven love of neighbor.

qa: How can love be commanded? Surely one cannot order a feeling.

Pope Benedict XVI answers this directly: love can be “commanded” because it has first been given (Deus Caritas Est 14). The biblical word points to more than emotion. To love with heart, soul, mind and strength includes choosing, serving and being faithful, also on days when feelings are dry. And today’s First Reading shows the order of things: God says “I will love them” before anything is asked of us.
study: Hosea tells Israel to “take words” with it. What words do I need to take to God in Confession this Lent? What is my Assyria, the thing I lean on in place of him?
Is there a part of me (heart, mind, strength, or time) that I keep back from God? Who is the neighbor I find it hardest to love, and what could I do for that person today?

lead: Today’s readings ask what kind of religion God wants. Hosea hears a beautiful song of repentance and answers that their love vanishes like the morning dew. In Jesus’ parable, two men go up to pray, and the one with nothing to show goes home justified. Psalm 51 is the prayer of the second man. God is not against sacrifice or fasting. What he wants is the heart behind them. The key words are steadfast love, know and justified.

r.h: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice
set: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BC. Many scholars connect this passage with the war of about 733 BC, when Israel and Judah fought one another and Assyria stepped in, which would explain why both Ephraim and Judah are named here. Just before the reading, God compares himself to a lion that tears its prey (5:14), and that is why the people speak of being “torn”.

The reading is a dialogue. The people sing a hymn of return (6:1–3), and God answers it (6:4–6). Many commentators think the song is too easy: it speaks of God’s return as sure as the dawn, but it does not name any sin. God’s answer suggests that he has heard such songs before.
str: vv. 1–3: the people’s song: let us return; he will heal; he will come like the rain.
v. 4: God’s question: what shall I do with you?
v. 5: the prophets’ word has cut deep.
v. 6: what God really desires.
kw: A central word of the Old Testament, meaning loyal, committed love within a covenant. It is what God shows to Israel and what he hopes to see in return, toward him and among his people.
In Hosea to know God is not to have information about him. It is the knowledge of a close relationship, which shows itself in faithfulness and justice (compare 4:1–2).

In the land of Israel a morning cloud or dew may look like a promise of rain and be gone by mid-morning. The people said that God would come like the spring rains, and he replies that their love is like the morning mist.
vv: Come, let us return to the Lord; for it is he who has torn, and he will heal us;
True words. The danger is that repentance can become a mood or a phrase that costs nothing.
After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up,

In its setting, this hopes for a nation’s quick recovery. Many of the Fathers read in it a foreshadowing of Christ’s resurrection, and many scholars think it may lie behind St Paul’s “on the third day in accordance with the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).
What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud,
We hear the grief of a parent here, more than the anger of a judge. The word for love in this verse is the same ḥesed as in v. 6.
For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

The second half of the verse explains the first: “rather than”. In Hebrew idiom, “this and not that” can mean “this more than that”. God gave Israel the sacrifices; he does not condemn them here. He refuses them when they are empty. Jesus quotes this verse twice, as “mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).
ch: The Catechism teaches that outward sacrifice must express the spiritual sacrifice of the heart, that the prophets denounced offerings that did not come from the heart or were not joined to love of neighbor, and that Jesus recalls these words of Hosea (CCC 2100). The Mass is no empty ritual of the kind Hosea feared: there Christ’s own self-offering, the perfect love of the Son for the Father, is made present, and we are drawn into it. What remains for us is to come with our hearts, and to carry that love out through the church door.

r.h: God, be merciful to me, a sinner
set: This parable is found only in Luke, and it comes just after the parable of the widow and the judge (18:1–8), also on prayer. Luke tells us who it is for: “some who trusted in themselves”. He does not say that they were Pharisees. A Pharisee is simply one of the characters.

To hear it as the first listeners did, we must remember how each man was regarded. Pharisees were a respected lay movement devoted to holiness in everyday life. Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling powers, often made a profit from it, and were widely despised. No one listening would have expected this ending. The parable is no portrait of Pharisees in general, or of Judaism, and Jesus shared much with them (CCC 575). It is aimed at something that can grow in any believer.
str: v. 9: the audience: those who trust in themselves and despise others.
v. 10: two men, one Temple.
vv. 11–12: the Pharisee’s prayer.
v. 13: the tax collector’s prayer.
v. 14: the verdict and the rule.
kw: To treat someone as nothing. Luke places this word in the first verse, and it is the key to the parable. Trust in oneself and contempt for others tend to come together.

This is more than “have pity”. The verb belongs to the language of atonement, and is related to hilastērion, the “mercy seat” of Hebrews 9:5. In the Temple, where sacrifices of atonement were offered, this man asks for exactly that.
Made right with God. It is a passive form: God does this, and the man does not do it to himself. St Paul will build much on this word, and here Jesus uses it in a story.
vv: God, I thank you that I am not like other people:

It begins well, with thanks. But the rest is about himself, and he never asks God for anything. The Greek may also be read as “he prayed these things to himself”, or as the NRSV’s “standing by himself”. Either reading makes its point.
I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of all my income.

This is more than the Law asks. The Law commanded one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29), and later Jewish sources mention Mondays and Thursdays for such voluntary fasts. His practice is real and good, and he is not called a liar.
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even look up to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
Everything in his body says what his lips say. In Greek he says “the sinner”, as if there were no other in the world. He does not compare himself with anyone.
I tell you, this man went down to his home justified rather than the other;

Luke does not say that he left his trade or made amends; that is told of another tax collector, in the next chapter (19:8). Here the point is who was received by God, and how. Jesus has said the closing line before, at a dinner table (14:11).
ch: The Catechism calls humility the foundation of prayer and quotes St Augustine, “Man is a beggar before God” (CCC 2559). It names this parable among the three great parables of prayer in Luke, the one about the humility of the heart that prays (CCC 2613), and it says that asking forgiveness is the first movement of petition, as in the tax collector’s words (CCC 2631). The Eastern Churches’ Jesus Prayer grows from this verse. In the Latin Mass, we make the same gesture at the Confiteor, striking the breast at the words “through my fault”.

qa: Does this parable mean that fasting and tithing do not matter? Is it wrong to thank God for what I am doing well?

No. Jesus does not criticize the Pharisee’s fast or his gift, and the Church calls us to fasting and almsgiving in this very season. It is right to thank God for any good in our lives, since it comes from his grace. What goes wrong here is the comparison. Good works done by God’s grace are precious to him. When they are turned into a stick to beat our neighbor with, the heart has gone astray. One test: does my Lent make me gentler with others?
study: When is my repentance like the morning cloud, sincere for an hour and gone by noon? What would make it last this Lent?
Do I find myself praying with one eye on someone else? Can I stay for five minutes today with no other words than “God, be merciful to me, a sinner”?

lead: This is Laetare Sunday, named for the first word of the Latin entrance antiphon, “Rejoice, Jerusalem” (Isaiah 66:10). We are past the midpoint of Lent and Easter is three weeks away. Rose vestments may be worn, and the mood lifts a little. But the Church has not chosen light readings for her day of joy. The joy is that of people who know how far they had fallen and who have heard that God loved them anyway.

The readings tell the same story at three levels. The Chronicler tells it of a nation: unfaithfulness, destruction, exile, and then a pagan king says, “Let him go up.” Psalm 137 is the song of those sitting by the rivers of Babylon. St Paul tells it of each believer: “dead through our trespasses”, and made alive by grace. And John tells it of the whole world: “God so loved the world.” In each case the turn comes from God alone. The key words are compassion, grace and lifted up.

r.h: Let him go up
set: The Books of Chronicles were written after the exile, probably in the fourth century BC according to many scholars. They retell the history of the kings with the Temple at the center, for a small community trying to understand what had happened to it and what its future might be. This last chapter hurries through the final kings of Judah to the end.

The Babylonians took Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple in 587/586 BC. Cyrus of Persia, having conquered Babylon in 539 BC, allowed the exiles to return, about 538 BC. In the usual Jewish order of the books, Chronicles stands last in the Hebrew Bible, so that the whole of Scripture there ends on this note of going up to Jerusalem. The Lectionary omits vv. 17–18, which describe the slaughter.
str: v. 14: the sin: leaders and people together pollute the Temple.
vv. 15–16: God keeps sending messengers; they keep mocking.
vv. 19–21: the destruction, the exile and the land’s long sabbath.
vv. 22–23: Cyrus and the edict.
kw: To spare, to feel for someone. God sent the prophets “because he had compassion” (36:15). The Chronicler also uses the word in v. 17, left out of our reading, where the conqueror “had no compassion”. It is God’s compassion that has the last word.
Literally “no healing”. The Chronicler is saying that a people can go on refusing the physician until nothing more can be done from the human side. The next thing that happens must come from God.
The land “made up for its sabbaths” (36:21), recalling the warning of Leviticus 26:34. Even the desolation has a strange mercy in it: the land rests.

The last word of the passage in Hebrew. ‘Ālâ is the verb for going up to Jerusalem on pilgrimage. The story of the fall ends with an invitation to climb. The POC orders the clauses differently, but the sense is the same.
vv: The Lord, the God of their ancestors, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place;
“Persistently” renders the Hebrew “rising early and sending”, the idiom we know from Jeremiah. Long before the disaster, the prophets were the form God’s compassion took.
but they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words, and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord against his people became so great that there was no remedy.
Three verbs of contempt. The “wrath” of God in Scripture is not a loss of temper; it is the way his love looks when it meets stubborn refusal.
All the days that it lay desolate it kept sabbath, to fulfill seventy years.

The seventy years come from Jeremiah (25:11; 29:10). From the fall of the city to Cyrus’s edict is about fifty years; seventy is a full, round number, the span of a human life, and here it marks the time God set.
the Lord stirred up the spirit of King Cyrus of Persia

The surprise of the chapter. The instrument of return is a foreign king who does not worship Israel’s God as Israel does. Isaiah even calls him God’s “anointed” (Isaiah 45:1). God is not bound to the channels we expect.
Whoever is among you of all his people, may the Lord his God be with him! Let him go up.
The same edict opens the Book of Ezra (Ezra 1:1–3). It ends here on an open door. The rest is left to those who will rise and go.
ch: The Catechism reads the exile in this way: unfaithfulness to the covenant ends in death, and the exile looks like the failure of God’s promises but is in fact the mysterious faithfulness of the Savior God and the beginning of the promised restoration (CCC 710). In Lent the Church hears in this her own story and that of every sinner. No one is too far gone for God to send a word of return. Those who have made a long way home in the confessional know what this chapter feels like.

r.h: By grace you have been saved
set: The letter presents itself as written by Paul from prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Many scholars think that a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, because of its style and its developed thought about the Church. Others hold that Paul himself wrote it. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case, and its teaching is what matters here.

The first verses of the chapter paint a dark picture: “you were dead through the trespasses and sins” (2:1). The reading starts at the turning point, with two of the most important words in the letter: “But God”.
str: vv. 4–5: But God: rich in mercy, he made us alive with Christ.
v. 6: raised with him and seated with him.
v. 7: the purpose: to show the riches of his grace.
vv. 8–9: by grace, through faith, a gift.
v. 10: created for good works.
kw: Paul’s language of wealth keeps returning in this letter (“immeasurable riches”, 2:7). St John Paul II took the title of his encyclical on mercy from these words, Dives in Misericordia (1980).
God’s favor, given without any claim on our part. The Catechism defines grace as the undeserved help God gives us to respond to his call (CCC 1996).

A perfect participle in Greek: a past act whose effect continues. Paul elsewhere also speaks of salvation as something still ahead (Romans 5:9). We have been saved, and we go forward in hope of final salvation, without presuming on it (CCC 2005).
The word comes from poieō, to make, and our word “poem” comes from the same family. We are God’s handiwork.
vv: But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ
God loved us while we were dead, so it was not our movement toward him that began it. A dead man cannot do anything to deserve life.
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,

Three Greek verbs in a row begin with syn-, “with”: made alive with, raised with, seated with. The Catechism uses this verse to say that the baptized already truly share in the heavenly life of the risen Christ (CCC 1003).
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God

“This” in Greek is neuter, and most interpreters take it to mean the whole event of being saved by grace through faith. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, says that even faith is not from ourselves, since we could not have believed unless God had called us (in substance).
not the result of works, so that no one may boast.
Nothing that comes before justification earns it. The Council of Trent says the same (Session 6, chapter 8).
For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.

This verse must never be left out. Grace does not end with faith. We were remade so that we might do good. The works themselves are prepared by God, and the Greek says we are to “walk” in them. By his grace they are truly ours.
ch: The Catechism teaches that no one can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification (CCC 2010), that there is no strict right to any merit before God (CCC 2007), and yet that God has freely chosen to associate us with the work of his grace, so that the merit of good works is to be attributed first to his grace and then to the believer (CCC 2008). As one of the Mass prefaces of the Saints says to God, in crowning their merits you crown your own gifts. In the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation said together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work, and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God (no. 15).

r.h: God so loved the world
set: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader, has come to Jesus by night (3:1–2) and has been told that he must be born from above. He will appear twice more, speaking up for Jesus (7:50) and bringing spices for his burial (19:39). In the course of the chapter the dialogue fades out, and Jesus’ words become a meditation. Scholars differ over where Jesus’ speech ends and the Evangelist’s reflection begins. The NRSV keeps it all in Jesus’ mouth, through v. 21.

The reference is to Numbers 21:4–9. In the desert, the people complained and were bitten by poisonous serpents. God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, “and everyone who is bitten shall look at it and live” (21:8). The Book of Wisdom explains it carefully: the one who turned toward it “was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all” (Wisdom 16:7). Later, when people made the serpent an object of worship, King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4).
str: vv. 14–15: as the serpent was lifted up, so the Son of Man.
v. 16: the source of it all: God’s love.
v. 17: the purpose: to save and not to condemn.
v. 18: believing and not believing.
vv. 19–21: light and darkness: the judgment we bring on ourselves.
kw: A word with two meanings at once: raised on a cross, and exalted in glory. John uses it three times in this way (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–34), and he tells us that the phrase speaks of “the kind of death he was to die” (12:33).

The one and only of his kind. John uses it of the Word (1:14, 18), and it stands behind the Creed’s “only begotten Son”. The POC has ഏകജാതൻ. Many readers also hear Abraham’s “your only son” behind this verse (Genesis 22:2).
In John, the world is often what opposes God and does not know him (1:10). That makes v. 16 all the more surprising: it is this world, in all its refusal, that God loves.

From a verb meaning to separate or decide. In John the judgment begins when people encounter the light. They show by their response where they stand. John also keeps the judgment of the last day (5:28–29).
vv: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,

The “must” is the Greek dei, the word for what God’s plan requires. St Augustine draws out the comparison: the biting serpents are our sins, and the serpent lifted up is the Lord’s death on the Cross. To look at it in faith is to be healed of what has been killing us (Tractates on John 12, in substance).
For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.
The Gospel in one sentence. The Cross begins here, in the Father’s love, and it is not a way of changing God’s mind about us. “Gave” includes both the sending and the handing over.
Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
Those who think of Christ first as a stern judge should read this verse slowly. He will judge, as the Creed says, but this was not the purpose of his coming.
And this is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.

This is a verdict we give ourselves. People who have done wrong may avoid the light of the confessional for years, for this very reason: not because God has shut the door, but because of what the light will show.
But those who do what is true come to the light,
Literally “do the truth”, a Semitic way of speaking. For John, truth is more than something to know. It is something one does. This is why Lent is not only a time for thinking.
ch: The Catechism quotes John 3:16 when it asks why the Word became flesh (CCC 458). On this passage it also says that the Son did not come to judge but to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life one already judges oneself (CCC 679). It sees in the bronze serpent an image God himself allowed, one pointing toward salvation through the incarnate Word (CCC 2130). The Church reads a part of this Gospel on 14 September, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. The sign of healing lifted up over a wounded people hangs in our churches.

qa: The First Reading says that God’s wrath destroyed Jerusalem. Are disasters today God’s punishment?

We should be slow to say so. The Chronicler reads the fall of Jerusalem through the eyes of prophetic faith, and his purpose is to call for repentance and hope. Jesus himself refused to treat those who suffered a disaster as worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5), and he said of a man born blind that neither he nor his parents had sinned (John 9:3). We may not read God’s judgment into another person’s suffering. We may ask him what he wishes to teach us in our own.
St Paul says “not the result of works”. Do Catholics believe that we are saved by works?

No. The Council of Trent taught that nothing before justification, neither faith nor works, merits the grace of justification (Session 6, chapter 8). But the same grace truly changes us and makes us capable of good. So the Church also teaches, with Ephesians 2:10 and James 2:24, that good works done in grace are pleasing to God and have merit, which is itself his gift (CCC 2008–2011). Paul speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). We are saved by grace, and that grace bears fruit in works.
“Those who do not believe are condemned already.” What about those who never heard of Christ?

John is writing about those who meet the light and turn from it. The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will as they know it through their conscience, may also attain eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). That does not lessen the Church’s duty to proclaim the Gospel. It does forbid us to pronounce on anyone’s final state.
rite: On this Sunday, parishes with adults preparing for baptism at Easter celebrate the second Scrutiny, and for that Mass the Year A readings (the man born blind, John 9) may be used. Elsewhere the Year B readings are heard, as here. In the Latin tradition this is the Sunday of rose vestments and flowers on the altar, a brief relaxing of the Lenten rule. It is also a good day to look at how one’s Lent has gone so far, and to begin again. Three weeks remain. Many parishes offer a Lenten service of Confession about now, and the Gospel gives its reason: come to the light.
study: The Chronicler says God’s compassion kept sending messengers. Who has God sent to me, more than once? How have I received them?
Read Ephesians 2:4–10 and put your own name where you see “us” and “you”. What changes for you when you think of your life as God’s handiwork, with good works prepared for you to walk in?
Take time before a crucifix this week and simply look at it, as the bitten people looked at the serpent. What is the poison you bring to him?
Which part of my life am I keeping out of the light? What would it take to bring it to the Sacrament of Reconciliation before Easter?

lead: From this Monday until Holy Week the weekday Gospels at Mass are taken mostly from St John, and the first scene is a father begging for his dying son. Isaiah promises a Jerusalem where no more weeping is heard and no child dies young. John shows that promise beginning in one house in Capernaum, through a word heard at a distance and believed. Psalm 30 gives the response of someone brought back from the edge of the grave: “You have turned my mourning into dancing.” The halfway point of Lent has passed, and the Church now looks toward what God will make new.

r.h: New heavens and a new earth
set: Many scholars think that the last chapters of Isaiah (56–66) speak to the community that came home from exile in Babylon, in the late sixth century BC or after. The return had been announced in glorious words, but the reality was poor: a ruined city, hard harvests, quarrels among the people. Into this disappointment God says that he has not finished. What he is about to do will be as great as creation itself.
str: v. 17: God announces a new creation; the former troubles will not even come to mind.
v. 18: the people are told to rejoice in what God is making.
v. 19: God himself rejoices, and weeping ends.
v. 20: no early death; a hundred years will count as youth.
v. 21: people will live in the houses they build and eat what they plant.
kw: The verb of Genesis 1:1, used only with God as subject. It comes three times in vv. 17–18. Going home from exile is only the beginning: God is doing again what only God can do.
In v. 18 these two verbs are a command to the people. In v. 19 the same two verbs come back with God as subject: “I will rejoice … and delight”. God's own joy is the source of theirs.
vv: For I am about to create new heavens and a new earth; the former things shall not be remembered or come to mind.
The Hebrew form suggests something already under way: God is at work now. 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 take up these very words for the world to come.
I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and delight in my people; no more shall the sound of weeping be heard in it, or the cry of distress.

Revelation 21:4 carries this further: “Death will be no more”. Isaiah's picture, as v. 20 shows, still has old age and dying in it, though long delayed. The promise grows clearer as revelation goes on, until the Resurrection of Christ shows its full measure.
They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

This reverses the curse of Deuteronomy 28:30, where a person builds a house and does not live in it, plants a vineyard and does not enjoy its fruit. God's new world is pictured in very ordinary terms: a home, a harvest, a family that lives to see its grandchildren. Salvation does not despise daily life.
ch: The Catechism takes up the language of “new heavens and a new earth” for the final renewal of all things (CCC 1042–1050). It says that creation itself will be transformed, and that this hope does not weaken our care for the present world but gives it strength (Gaudium et Spes 39; CCC 1049). In Lent the Church hears this page as a reminder of where her penance is leading: to Easter, and through Easter to a world without tears.

r.h: Your son will live
set: Jesus has just spent two days among the Samaritans (4:40) and now goes back to Galilee. He comes again to Cana, where he changed water into wine (2:1–11). The man who comes to him is a royal official, probably in the service of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, who was popularly called a king (Mark 6:14). Capernaum lies down by the lake, some hours away on foot, so the man has walked far and asks Jesus to “come down”.

The remark in v. 44 about a prophet in his own country has puzzled commentators, because the Galileans then welcome him. John may be hinting that their welcome is shallow, since it rests on what they saw at the festival (v. 45; compare 2:23–25). Those who think so read “his own country” as Galilee; others take it as Judea. The question remains open.
str: vv. 43–45: back to Galilee and the Galileans' welcome.
vv. 46–47: the official and his request.
vv. 48–49: Jesus' hard word, and the father's repeated plea.
v. 50: the word, and the man's faith in it.
vv. 51–53: the news on the road; the hour is compared; the whole household believes.
v. 54: John numbers it the second sign.
kw: John's word for Jesus' miracles. A sign points beyond itself to who Jesus is. Here it shows that his word gives life, and that distance is no obstacle to it.

The Greek at vv. 50 and 53 is literally “your son lives”, in the present tense, and v. 51 repeats the verb. The English “will live” is right as a promise, but the Greek shows the word taking effect as it is spoken.
A person from the ruler's circle, a man used to giving orders. Here he has no power at all over what matters most, and he begs.
vv: Then Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”

In Greek the “you” here is plural, so the words reach beyond this man to the crowd that wants a show. The father does not argue. He only repeats what he needs, and this humble persistence is the beginning of his faith.
Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and started on his way.

He had asked Jesus to come; he receives only a sentence. He walks home with nothing to hold except the word. This is the faith of every Christian who has not seen, and John will end his Gospel by blessing it (20:29).
So he himself believed, along with his whole household.
He already believed in v. 50, and now he believes again, more fully. Faith here is a road with stages: from need, to trust in a word, to belief in the person, and from one man to a whole family.
ch: The Catechism says that the signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him and invite belief in him (CCC 548). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, notes that Jesus refused to go in person to this official's son, yet offered to go to the centurion's servant (Matthew 8:7): he did not honour rank (in substance). The same word still reaches us at a distance from Galilee: in the Scripture read at Mass and in the sacraments, Christ is present and speaking.

qa: Is this the same story as the centurion's servant in Matthew 8 and Luke 7?

The stories are similar: a man of some standing, a sick boy at Capernaum, a healing at a distance. Many scholars think that they may come from one memory told in different ways; others treat them as two events, and there are real differences. The Church has not decided this, and nothing in the faith depends on it. Each Gospel uses the story for its own lesson, and in John the lesson is faith in Jesus' word.
study: The official had to walk home with only a word. When has God asked me to go on without seeing the result of my prayer?
Isaiah pictures God's new world as houses, vineyards and long lives. Where in my ordinary life can I already help someone to have a home, a meal or less reason to weep?

lead: Today both readings are about water, and both reach toward Baptism as Easter draws near. Ezekiel sees a stream from under the Temple door grow into a river that brings even the Dead Sea to life. John sets Jesus beside a pool where a man has lain for thirty-eight years with no one to help him. Psalm 46 sings of “a river whose streams make glad the city of God”. The sick man never gets into the water at all: the life that Ezekiel saw flowing now stands in front of him and speaks.

r.h: Wherever the river goes
set: Ezekiel, a priest, was taken to Babylon with the exiles of 597 BC, and there he learned of the destruction of the Temple (587/586 BC). His last great vision (chapters 40–48) is dated in the twenty-fifth year of the exile (40:1), about 573 BC. A heavenly guide leads him through a restored Temple, and the glory of God, which he had seen depart (chapters 10–11), returns (43:1–5). Now comes the fruit of that return.

The geography gives the vision its force. East of Jerusalem the land falls away through bare desert to the Dead Sea, the lowest and saltiest water in the land, where fish cannot live. The vision sends a river straight through it.
str: vv. 1–2: water comes from under the threshold of the Temple, flowing east.
vv. 3–5: four measurings: ankle, knee, waist, and a river that cannot be crossed.
vv. 6–7: trees on both banks.
vv. 8–9: the river enters the sea of stagnant waters and everything lives.
v. 12: trees with monthly fruit and healing leaves.
kw: The word usually means a wadi, a desert watercourse that runs only after rain and then dries up. This one grows greater the further it goes, with no tributary to feed it. Its only source is God's house.

Behind the English “will become fresh” (vv. 8–9) stands the Hebrew verb “to be healed”: the waters of the sea are healed. A related word closes the reading, leaves “for healing” (v. 12). The prophet sees creation itself as sick and cured.
vv: there, water was flowing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east

It begins as a trickle under a door. A Temple needs a great deal of water for its sacrifices, but this water is not brought in; it comes out from the place where God dwells. Compare Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8.
Again he measured one thousand, and it was a river that I could not cross,
A thousand cubits is roughly half a kilometre. At each stage the prophet goes deeper, until he can no longer stand. God's gift is not something a person can stay in control of.
Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live,
The words recall creation, when God filled the waters with swarming creatures (Genesis 1:20–21). The dead place becomes as full of life as the first days.
Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing.

Revelation 22:1–2 takes up this picture for the heavenly city: a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and leaves “for the healing of the nations”. The reason is given in the same verse: the water flows from the sanctuary.
ch: In the Roman Rite this vision is heard every Eastertide in the chant Vidi aquam, “I saw water flowing from the Temple”, sung at the sprinkling at Sunday Mass. So the Church reads Ezekiel in the light of Easter: the true Temple is the body of Christ (John 2:21), from whose opened side came blood and water (John 19:34). Jesus says that rivers of living water will flow, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:38–39). Those preparing for Baptism hear this page as a promise about themselves.

r.h: Do you want to be made well?
set: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for an unnamed festival. Near the Sheep Gate, north of the Temple, is a pool with five porticoes. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool with colonnades close to the present Church of St Anne, which fits John's description well. The sick waited there because they believed that the stirring of the water brought healing.

A note on the text. The ancient copies spell the name in several ways (Beth-zatha, Bethesda, Bethsaida). The explanation that an angel stirred the water (the end of v. 3 and v. 4 in older translations) is missing from the earliest manuscripts, and most modern editions leave it out, as the NRSV does and as the POC's verses do. It is probably an early note that explained v. 7.
str: vv. 1–3: the feast, the pool, the crowd of sick.
vv. 5–7: the man and his answer.
vv. 8–9a: the word and the cure.
vv. 9b–13: it is a sabbath: the authorities question the man.
vv. 14–15: Jesus finds him in the Temple.
v. 16: the opposition begins.
kw: The word comes five times in this reading (vv. 6, 9, 11, 14, 15). It means sound in every way, and the story asks how far this man's wholeness will go.
The same verb is used for rising from the dead. On the next page Jesus says that the Father “raises the dead” and the Son likewise gives life (5:21).

Jesus, the sick man and the crowd are all Jews. In passages like this John uses the phrase for the religious authorities in Jerusalem who oppose Jesus, as the Church teaches us to read it (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). It says nothing against the Jewish people, then or now.
vv: When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be made well?”

Jesus takes the first step: nobody asks him for anything. The question is not as strange as it sounds. After thirty-eight years a man's whole life may be built around his illness, and healing would mean a new life.
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up;
He does not say yes. He tells the story of his loneliness, “I have no one”. He can imagine healing only through the pool, and only with someone's help. Jesus will give it without either.
Jesus said to him, “Stand up, take your mat and walk.”

Three commands, with no water, no touch and no request for faith. The mat that carried him he now carries. Carrying a burden on the sabbath was forbidden on the authority of Jeremiah 17:21–22, which is why the question arises at once in v. 10.
See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you.
Jesus goes looking for him a second time. The cure of the body is not the end of what he came to give. On what is “worse”, see the question below.
ch: St John Chrysostom and St Ambrose saw this pool as a figure of Baptism: there one person was healed and only now and then, while in the font all are healed, and Christ himself is the one who was missing beside that water (in substance). The Catechism says that Christ's compassion for the sick, and his many healings, are a sign that God has visited his people, and that he goes on touching us in the sacraments to heal us (CCC 1503–1504). Where the first reading shows the water, the Gospel shows the one who gives it.

qa: Is Jesus saying that the man's illness was a punishment for sin?

No. In John 9:3 Jesus rejects that reasoning directly about a man born blind. Here he does not say what caused the illness. He warns that there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat, and that is to lose God through sin. Illness must never be used as an accusation against the person who suffers.
study: Jesus asks, “Do you want to be made well?” Is there something in my life, a habit or a hurt, that I have grown so used to that I am not sure I want it healed?
“I have no one.” Who lies near me, in my parish or my family, who could say those words? What is one thing I can do for that person this week?

lead: Today two great statements about God stand side by side. In Isaiah, Zion thinks she has been forgotten, and God answers with the most tender image in the Old Testament: a mother and her nursing child. In John, Jesus answers those who object to his healing on the sabbath by speaking of his oneness with the Father, who gives life and judges. Psalm 145 joins them: “The Lord is gracious and merciful.” The God who cannot forget his people is the God who, in his Son, calls the dead out of their graves.

r.h: I will not forget you
set: Isaiah 40–55 is often called the Book of Consolation, and it speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon, before Cyrus let them go home (539 BC). Chapter 49 opens with the second of the Servant Songs (vv. 1–6), in which God's servant is called from the womb and made a light to the nations. Today's reading comes straight after that song and describes what the servant's mission will bring: a new exodus, with a road through the mountains and God himself as shepherd.
str: v. 8: God answers and gives the servant as a covenant to the people.
v. 9a: prisoners are called out of the dark.
vv. 9b–11: the journey home, with food, water and a road.
v. 12: they come from far places.
v. 13: heaven and earth are called to sing.
vv. 14–15: Zion's complaint, and God's answer.
kw: The same phrase appears in 42:6. It is striking: the servant does not only make or announce a covenant, he is given as one. The Church hears in this the person of Christ, in whom God and his people are joined.

This verb is close to reḥem, “womb”. It comes three times in the reading: God “has pity” (v. 10), God “will have compassion” (v. 13), and the mother “show no compassion” (v. 15). God's mercy is described with a word that comes from a mother's body.
vv: In a time of favor I have answered you, on a day of salvation I have helped you;

St Paul quotes this line in the Greek form and adds: “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The Church reads that passage on Ash Wednesday, and the same word is still being said to us here in the middle of Lent.
But Zion said, “The Lord has forsaken me, my Lord has forgotten me.”
The Bible does not hide this complaint. Zion is the ruined city, personified as a woman left alone. God lets her say it and does not rebuke her; he answers her.
Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.

It is hard to imagine a stronger human love, and yet God admits that even this can fail. The next verse, just outside the reading, adds that God has inscribed Zion on the palms of his hands. Whoever feels forgotten by God has this verse to pray.
ch: The Catechism draws on this kind of passage when it says that God's love for his people is stronger than a mother's love for her children (CCC 219), and that his parental tenderness can also be expressed by the image of motherhood, for God “is neither man nor woman: he is God” (CCC 239). Jesus teaches us to call him Father, and the Church keeps that name, as Scripture does; Pope John Paul I recalled Isaiah's words on this at the Angelus of 10 September 1978. Revelation 7:16–17 takes up v. 10 for the saints in heaven: they will not hunger or thirst, for the Lamb will guide them to springs of the water of life. The promise made to exiles is fulfilled beyond what they could picture, and it holds without being taken away from Israel, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

r.h: As the Father, so the Son
set: This is the continuation of Tuesday's healing at the pool. Jesus is accused of working on the sabbath, and his reply goes to the heart of who he is. Jewish teachers of the time also discussed how God could rest on the sabbath when births and deaths go on and the world is kept in being; many scholars think that this is the background. God does not stop giving life or judging, and these are the two works that Jesus now claims as his own.

John writes that “the Jews” sought to kill him (v. 18). As on Tuesday, he means the authorities who were opposing Jesus, not the Jewish people; this is what the Church teaches (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: vv. 17–18: “My Father is still working”; the charge.
vv. 19–23: the Son does what the Father does: gives life, judges, receives honour.
vv. 24–25: the one who hears has passed from death to life, even now.
vv. 26–27: the Son has life in himself and authority to judge.
vv. 28–29: the last resurrection.
v. 30: his judgment is just, because he seeks the Father's will.
kw: The verb of v. 17. The Father has never stopped working, and the Son works with him. Later Jesus will speak of finishing that work (17:4; 19:30).

This word can mean a verdict, or a separation. In John a person's response to Jesus is already a kind of judgment: those who hear and believe do not come under it (v. 24). Yet there is also a last judgment (v. 29). Both are true.
“The hour is coming, and is now here” (v. 25). Eternal life begins now, by faith, and will be complete on the last day. Christians live between the two.
vv: But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, and I also am working.”

He says “my Father”, and the listeners rightly understand that he is claiming more than a pious person would (v. 18). John states it plainly: Jesus was “making himself equal to God”. The evangelist's point is that the claim is true.
Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing;
This does not mean that he is less than the Father. He has his whole being from the Father and never acts apart from him; see the question below.
Very truly, I tell you, anyone who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come under judgment, but has passed from death to life.
Notice the past tense: “has passed”. For the one who believes, the great crossing has already started. This is a gift of grace, to be lived and guarded in love, and it gives a firm hope (CCC 2005).
those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation.

The Catechism cites this verse when it teaches that the resurrection of all the dead comes before the Last Judgment (CCC 1038). The two statements of vv. 24 and 29 belong together: the faith that receives life is a faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6), and those good deeds are themselves the fruit of grace.
