ch: The Church confesses that the Son is “consubstantial with the Father” (Nicaea; CCC 465), and this chapter is one of the Gospel's foundations for that faith. Christ's right to judge comes from his having “acquired” it by his Cross (CCC 679, citing John 5:22). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, distinguishes two resurrections: the raising of the soul now by faith (v. 25) and the raising of the body at the end (vv. 28–29) (in substance). The Catechism adds that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and that he gives its authentic meaning (CCC 2173).

qa: If “the Son can do nothing on his own”, is he less than the Father?

No. The Arians in the fourth century used verses like this one, and the Fathers answered them. St Augustine explains that the Son does nothing of himself because he is not from himself: he is God from God (in substance). The verse speaks of the order of origin and of a perfect unity of action, not of a lesser power. In the same passage Jesus says that whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise (v. 19), and that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father (v. 23). As man, too, he willingly submits his human will to the Father's (v. 30).
study: When have I, like Zion, said “The Lord has forgotten me”? What would it change to pray Isaiah 49:15 slowly at that place in my life?
Jesus says that the one who believes “has passed from death to life”. What in my daily living shows that I am already living this new life?

lead: Moses stands at the centre of both readings today, in two different roles. In Exodus he pleads for his people after the golden calf, and he wins. In John, Jesus calls him as a witness: the Scriptures themselves testify on my behalf, and Moses “wrote about me”. Psalm 106 remembers the same scene and says that Moses “stood in the breach”. The great intercessor of the Old Testament prepares us for the one who, in these last weeks of Lent, goes up to the Cross to intercede for all.

r.h: Moses stood in the breach
set: Israel has heard the commandments and accepted the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 19–24). Moses has been on the mountain for forty days (24:18), and the people, tired of waiting, press Aaron to make them something they can see. The golden calf is not simply a turn to a foreign god: many scholars think that the people took it as an image or a throne of the God who brought them out, since Aaron proclaims “a festival to the Lord” (32:5). But the commandment against images has just been given, so the covenant is broken almost as soon as it is made.

Nearly the same words, “Here are your gods, O Israel”, are said in 1 Kings 12:28 about the calves King Jeroboam set up at Bethel and Dan, and many scholars think that the two stories have been told with an eye on each other.
str: vv. 7–8: God tells Moses what has happened below.
vv. 9–10: God's verdict and his offer to begin again with Moses.
vv. 11–13: Moses' prayer, with three arguments.
v. 14: God relents.
kw: An image from farm life: an ox that stiffens its neck against the yoke and will not be led. Here it is the people who have just made an image of a young bull.
Literally “leave me be”. It is a strange thing for God to say. Many commentators hear in it an invitation: God speaks as though Moses could hold him back, and so opens the place for his prayer.
to change one's mind, to relent
The verb of vv. 12 and 14. It carries a sense of being moved or sorry. See the question below.
vv: The Lord said to Moses, “Go down at once! Your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have acted perversely;
God says “your people”, and Moses will reply “your people” (v. 11). Each hands them to the other. Moses' answer is the sharper: they are yours, Lord, because you brought them out.
Now let me alone, so that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them; and of you I will make a great nation.
This is the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2) offered to Moses alone. It is a real temptation: his own name in place of theirs. He refuses it without even mentioning it, and argues only for them.
Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants,

Moses has no argument from the people's goodness. He appeals to what God has done (v. 11), to God's name among the nations (v. 12) and to God's own oath (v. 13). This is the pattern of all intercession: we plead on the ground of who God is.
And the Lord changed his mind about the disaster that he planned to bring on his people.
Moses' prayer is heard. The sin still has its consequences, as the rest of the chapter shows, but the people live.
ch: The Catechism presents this moment as the great example of Moses' prayer: he does not pray for himself, but after the people's apostasy he “stands in the breach” before God to save them (Psalm 106:23; CCC 2577). His arguments, it says, will inspire the boldness of the great intercessors of the Jewish people and of the Church. St Paul tells Christians that these things “occurred as examples for us” (1 Corinthians 10:6). So we do not read this page as a story about other people's sin. Every Christian can recognize the calf, the god we make because the true God seems too slow, and every Christian has an advocate greater than Moses (1 John 2:1).

r.h: Moses wrote about me
set: The discourse of John 5 now reaches its last part. Jewish law requires two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), so Jesus calls his: John the Baptist, the works he does, the Father himself, and the Scriptures. Here “testimony” is the key word, used as in a courtroom. Before the reader's eyes the accused becomes the one who is calling evidence.

When Jesus speaks in harsh terms here, he is speaking to those who oppose him in that dispute. Elsewhere John says that some in authority believed in him (12:42). Christians must not turn these words into a charge against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
str: vv. 31–32: one witness is not enough, and there is “another”.
vv. 33–35: John the Baptist, a burning lamp.
v. 36: the works.
vv. 37–38: the Father.
vv. 39–40: the Scriptures.
vv. 41–44: why they do not believe: glory from one another.
vv. 45–47: Moses as the accuser.
kw: This noun and its verb run through the whole reading, and the word later gives us “martyr”. Faith in John means accepting a testimony and then bearing it.
In v. 44 it means reputation, the esteem of others, and also the true weight of God's presence. The root of unbelief, says Jesus, is not lack of evidence but the desire to be praised by one another.

The Greek form can be read as a statement (“you search”) or a command (“search!”). The NRSV and the POC both read it as a statement, and most modern scholars agree. Either way, the Scriptures point to him.
vv: The works that the Father has given me to complete, the very works that I am doing, testify on my behalf that the Father has sent me.
The healing at the pool is one of those works. In John, the signs are a kind of speech: God is saying who Jesus is (CCC 548).
You search the scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify on my behalf.

A warning for every reader of the Bible, including those who love it most. One can study the words and miss the person. The Scriptures are good and they are God's word; their purpose is to lead us to meet him.
How can you believe when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the one who alone is God?
“The one who alone is God” recalls the great prayer of Israel, “The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Faith is hard when we are busy keeping up our standing with other people.
If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.

Christians have thought especially of Deuteronomy 18:15, the prophet like Moses, and of the whole Law as preparing for Christ. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord will begin “with Moses and all the prophets” (Luke 24:27).
ch: The Second Vatican Council says that God wisely arranged that the New Testament be hidden in the Old and the Old be made manifest in the New, using St Augustine's phrase (Dei Verbum 16; CCC 129). St Jerome's saying is close to this Gospel: “Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ” (Dei Verbum 25; CCC 133). The Church also teaches that God's covenant with the Jews has not been revoked (CCC 121), and the Pontifical Biblical Commission (2001) says that the Jewish reading of the Bible is a possible one, while Christians read the same pages in the light of Christ. So “your accuser is Moses” is no verdict on a people. It warns Christians too: the same Scriptures will accuse us if we hear them and do not follow.

qa: Can God change his mind?

God does not change as we do: “God is not a human being … that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). Exodus speaks in human terms, as Scripture often does, to tell us something true: God's mercy is real and prayer truly matters. St Augustine prays to God: you change your works, but you do not change your plan (Confessions 1,4). From all eternity God has willed to save through the prayer of those who plead with him. Moses' prayer is not an obstacle to God's will; it is part of how his mercy comes.
study: Moses refused the offer of a great name for himself in order to plead for sinners. For whom am I standing in the breach? Is there someone I have given up on, and for whom I should begin again to pray?
“You accept glory from one another.” Whose good opinion do I most fear losing? How does that affect what I say and do about my faith?

lead: From today the Passion comes clearly into view. The Book of Wisdom gives the reasoning of people who cannot bear a just man and decide to test his claim that God is his Father. John shows Jesus going up to Jerusalem quietly, teaching in the Temple while people argue about where he comes from, and no one able to touch him because “his hour had not yet come”. Psalm 34 answers both: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.” The plot is real, but the hour belongs to God.

r.h: Let us test him
set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek by a Jewish author, very probably at Alexandria in Egypt, in the first century BC or close to it. It speaks in the name of Solomon as a literary device. Its readers were Jews living among Greek thought and pagan religion, under pressure to give up their way of life. The Catholic Church counts it among the inspired books of the Old Testament (CCC 120), as the Council of Trent reaffirmed (1546). It came down in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Church; Protestant Bibles, following the shorter Hebrew canon, leave it out or print it apart. The difference can be stated without hostility.

The speakers are “the ungodly” (1:16). In vv. 1b–11, which the reading leaves out, they set out their creed: life is short, death is the end, so let us enjoy ourselves and let might be our right. Many scholars think that some of them are Jews who have abandoned the Law, since the just man accuses them of “sins against the law” (v. 12). This is a writer warning his own community, not a judgment on any people.
str: v. 1a: the verdict: they reasoned unsoundly.
vv. 12–16: why they hate the just man: he is a living reproach.
vv. 17–20: the plan: test his claim by torture and a shameful death.
vv. 21–22: the author's comment: they did not know God's secret purposes.
kw: Pais (v. 13) means both child and servant. The same word is used for the Servant in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, so the two ideas meet here: the just man is both God's servant and his child.

The word in v. 19, which also carries the sense of patience and fairness. Paul uses it of “the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:1). The persecutors mean to test it by cruelty, and in the Passion it stands the test.

Literally “the mysteries of God” (v. 22). Their logic is sharp, but it leaves out what God intends. The next verse says that God created us for incorruption, and 3:1 says that “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God”.
vv: because he is inconvenient to us and opposes our actions;
It is an honest confession. They do not say he is wrong, but that he is in the way. A good life can feel like an accusation to those around it.
the very sight of him is a burden to us,
He does not need to preach. His way of living is enough. The verse describes a hatred that many just people have met, in every age.
Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life; for if the righteous man is God’s child, he will help him,

These words come strikingly close to the mockery at the Cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). Matthew's words also recall Psalm 22:8, and the Church hears both as a preparation for the Passion.
Thus they reasoned, but they were led astray, for their wickedness blinded them,
The author does not say that God failed to help. He says that their calculation was wrong, because they could see only as far as death.
ch: St Augustine reads this passage as a prophecy of the Passion of Christ (City of God 17,20, in substance). Heard two weeks before Good Friday, it invites us to listen to the voice of those who plotted and to ask whether it is ever our own. The Church has always taught that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion (CCC 598), so the people of Wisdom 2 cannot be identified with any nation. And she has never drawn from this page the idea that God does not help the just: the answer to “he will help him” is Easter.

r.h: His hour had not yet come
set: The festival of Booths (Sukkot) is the great autumn pilgrim feast, when people lived in shelters of branches to remember the desert years (Leviticus 23:42–43). In Jesus' time it included rites of water and light in the Temple, and John will use these (7:37–39; 8:12). Since the sabbath healing in Jerusalem (chapter 5) Jesus has stayed in Galilee, because the authorities in Judea are seeking his death. In v. 1 the Greek Ioudaioi stands in contrast to Galilee: it refers to those in Judea who oppose him.
The reading passes over the conversation with his brothers (vv. 3–9) and his early teaching in the Temple (vv. 11–24), and picks up the dispute among the people of Jerusalem.
str: vv. 1–2: Jesus stays in Galilee; Booths is near.
v. 10: he goes up, not publicly.
vv. 25–27: the people of Jerusalem wonder, and raise an objection about his origin.
vv. 28–29: Jesus cries out in the Temple.
v. 30: they try to arrest him, and no one can.
kw: The word that governs John's Gospel. At Cana “My hour has not yet come” (2:4); here again; at 12:23 “The hour has come”. It means the Passion, death, Resurrection and return to the Father. Nobody can force it or stop it.
The verb in v. 28, used for a loud and solemn proclamation. Jesus is not secretive once he is in the Temple: he speaks so that all can hear.
vv: But after his brothers had gone to the festival, then he also went, not publicly but as it were in secret.
He goes up on his own terms and at the Father's timing. On “his brothers”, see the question below.
Yet we know where this man is from; but when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.

Some Jewish writings of the time speak of the Messiah as hidden until he appears; others expected him from Bethlehem, as tomorrow's Gospel shows (7:42). John's irony is gentle: they know that he comes from Nazareth, and they do not know that he comes from the Father.
I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.
The whole of Jesus' identity is in this short verse: he knows the Father, he comes from the Father, he is sent. He answers the question of where he is from at a level his hearers had not considered.
Then they tried to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.
Danger surrounds him, yet he is not a victim of chance. When the hour comes he will give himself: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (10:18).
ch: The Church teaches that Jesus' death did not happen by chance, but belongs to the mystery of God's plan (CCC 599), and that he accepted it willingly (CCC 609). The Catechism also notes that the religious authorities in Jerusalem were not unanimous about him (CCC 596), and today's Gospel shows the same mixed picture among the people: wondering, objecting, some drawn to him. The first reading gives us the plot, and the Gospel shows who is really in charge.

qa: Did Jesus have brothers?

The Church has always understood Jesus' “brothers” as close relations, not as other children of Mary (CCC 499–501). In Hebrew and Aramaic usage “brother” could cover close kinsmen: Abram says it of his nephew Lot (Genesis 13:8, where the NRSV says “kindred”). The Gospels themselves show that James and Joseph, named among the “brothers” (Matthew 13:55), are the sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56; CCC 500). Other Christians read these verses differently, and the Catholic understanding can be explained with respect.
study: “The very sight of him is a burden to us.” Whose goodness makes me uncomfortable? What might that discomfort be trying to teach me?
Jesus moved through real danger with trust in his Father's hour. What is in front of me that I am trying to control, instead of trusting God's timing?

lead: Tomorrow the Church turns to the Fifth Sunday of Lent, and today the shadow lengthens. Jeremiah discovers that the people of his own town have been plotting against him, and he calls himself “a gentle lamb led to the slaughter”. In John the crowd is split about Jesus, the Temple police come back with empty hands, and one quiet voice among the authorities asks for fairness. Psalm 7 prays, “O Lord, my God, in you I take refuge”. Both Jeremiah and Jesus are in danger because of the word they carry.

r.h: A gentle lamb
set: This is the first of the so-called Confessions of Jeremiah, personal prayers of the prophet scattered through chapters 11–20 (see also 15:10–21; 17:14–18; 18:18–23; 20:7–18). No other prophet lets us see so far into his own heart. Jeremiah preached in Judah from about 627 BC until after the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.

He came from a priestly family of Anathoth (1:1), a village a short distance north-east of Jerusalem. The verses just after today's reading explain the plot: the men of Anathoth are telling him to stop prophesying or he will die (11:21). The danger comes from his own neighbours, and soon also from his family (12:6).
str: v. 18: God shows Jeremiah what he did not know.
v. 19: the lamb who suspected nothing; the words of the plotters.
v. 20: he hands his case over to God.
kw: ’Allûp means tame or familiar, as a pet lamb raised close to the family, which follows trustingly and does not know where it is being led. This is exactly Jeremiah's case: he trusted those around him.

Literally “kidneys and heart”. In Hebrew thought the kidneys stand for the hidden feelings and the heart for the thinking and will. God sees all of the person, even what no one else can see, so he can be trusted as a judge.
vv: But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter.
Isaiah 53:7 uses a similar picture for the Servant. Christians cannot hear these words without thinking of the Lamb of God (John 1:29).
Let us destroy the tree with its fruit,

The Hebrew is obscure and may mean “the tree with its sap” (literally “its bread”). St Jerome's Latin rendering of it speaks of putting wood into his bread, and St Jerome and other Fathers read in this a hidden reference to the Cross and the Body of Christ (in substance). This is a spiritual reading of the text rather than the plain sense, but it shows how the early Church heard this prayer on the lips of Christ.
let me see your retribution upon them, for to you I have committed my cause.
It is a hard prayer, and an honest one. See the question below. Notice that he does not take up any weapon himself. He places the matter in God's hands.
ch: The Fathers saw Jeremiah, persecuted by his own people and gentle as a lamb, as a figure of Christ in his Passion, and the text suits these last days of Lent. The Catechism says of the prophets that their prayer is at times an argument or a complaint, yet always an intercession that awaits God's saving action (CCC 2584). Christians read such pages with their eyes on the Cross, where the true Lamb prays for those who put him to death (Luke 23:34).

r.h: Never has anyone spoken like this
set: We are still at the festival of Booths. On its last great day Jesus has cried out that rivers of living water will flow (7:37–38), and these are the reactions. The chief priests and Pharisees had sent the Temple police to arrest him (7:32). John's picture is not of a single block of enemies. The crowd is divided, the police are shaken, and Nicodemus, “one of them”, speaks up.

A note on the text. The last verse, “each of them went home”, really begins the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11). That passage is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts, but the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Today's Gospel simply ends with this line.
str: vv. 40–43: three opinions about Jesus, and a division.
v. 44: no one lays a hand on him.
vv. 45–46: the police report.
vv. 47–49: the scorn of the leaders.
vv. 50–51: Nicodemus asks for a hearing.
v. 52: they turn on him; v. 53: everyone goes home.
kw: The word gives us “schism”. It occurs here in v. 43 and again in 9:16 and 10:19. Jesus does not leave people where they are: everyone has to decide.
The promised prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). The crowd means someone specific, as in 1:21 and 6:14.
vv: Has not the scripture said that the Messiah is descended from David and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?

They have in mind passages like 2 Samuel 7:12 and Micah 5:2. John does not correct them, and leaves the irony for his readers: those who know the story know where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:4).
The police answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
Those who were sent to bind him come back bound by his word. They bring no theology to the discussion, only what they have heard.
“Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?”

Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), now speaks in the daylight, a little. He does not even defend Jesus; he defends the Law's own justice (Deuteronomy 1:16). He will appear once more, with spices for the burial (19:39). Faith can grow slowly in a person.
Search and you will see that no prophet is to arise from Galilee.
This is said in anger, and it overlooks Jonah son of Amittai, who came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25). One very early papyrus reads “the prophet”, which would fit the discussion well.
ch: The Catechism notes this very dissension. Among the religious authorities of Jerusalem, it says, Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples of Jesus, and there was long-standing disagreement about him (CCC 595–596). It also says that Jesus' relations with the Pharisees were not simply hostile (CCC 575). So the scorn in v. 49 is not the voice of all of them, or of Judaism. This page can be read as a warning to anyone in authority, Church leaders included, who has stopped listening.

qa: How can a holy prophet pray to see “retribution”?

The Bible records honest prayer, including anger. Jeremiah is a man wronged by his own people, and he asks God to do justice; he does not take revenge himself. That is itself a kind of restraint, and St Paul gives the same counsel (Romans 12:19). But this prayer is not the last word. Christ teaches us to love our enemies (Matthew 5:44), and he prays for his persecutors. The Christian may bring anger to God as Jeremiah did, and then ask for the grace to pray as Jesus did.
study: Jeremiah was betrayed by his neighbours, and Jesus was argued over by the crowd. When have I been hurt by those closest to me? Have I handed that hurt to God, or do I still carry it?
Nicodemus asked only for a fair hearing. Where in my family, parish or workplace is someone being judged without one? What small thing could I say?

lead: This Fifth Sunday of Lent, in the Year B readings, brings us to the threshold of the Passion, and the four readings tell of a new covenant and of what it costs. Jeremiah promises that God will write his law on the heart. The psalm asks for exactly that: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” Hebrews shows Jesus in prayer, “with loud cries and tears”, learning obedience through suffering. And John brings some Greeks to the door, and Jesus answers with the picture of a grain of wheat falling into the ground.

The readings move from promise to price. A new heart is what God offers, and the Cross is how he gives it. Next Sunday the Church will carry palms and read the Passion. The key words today are heart, obedience and hour.

r.h: I will write it on their hearts
set: Chapters 30–31 of Jeremiah are often called his Book of Consolation. They stand in a book mostly filled with warnings, and many scholars connect them with the years around the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The prophet had lived through King Josiah's reform (about 622 BC), yet Judah's sin is still “engraved on the tablet of their hearts” (17:1). Now he looks past the catastrophe.

“The house of Israel and the house of Judah” means the whole people, the northern kingdom that fell in 722/721 BC and the southern kingdom, whose ruin Jeremiah saw. This is the only place in the Old Testament that uses the words “new covenant”. The idea has close companions in Ezekiel 36:26 and Deuteronomy 30:6.
str: v. 31: the promise: a new covenant, with both houses.
v. 32: it will not be like the covenant of the Exodus, which they broke.
v. 33: its content: the law within, written on the heart; “I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”
v. 34a: everyone will know the Lord.
v. 34b: the foundation: forgiveness.
kw: Berît is a solemn bond that creates a relationship. What is new is not God's law or God's faithfulness but where it is written, and that it will not be broken. The old formula remains in v. 33: “I will be their God”.
More than a list of rules: instruction, the way of life God teaches. God does not cancel it here. He moves it from stone to the heart.
In the Bible the heart is less the seat of feelings than the centre of the person, where one thinks, decides and chooses. To write the law there is to make God's will one's own.
More than information. It is the knowledge of a relationship, used in Hebrew also of husband and wife. It fits the image of v. 32, and it is why knowing God brings a change of life.
vv: The days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.

God speaks these words to Israel. Jesus takes them up at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and the priest repeats them at every Mass over the chalice: “the Blood of the new and eternal covenant”.
It will not be like the covenant that I made with their ancestors when I took them by the hand … though I was their husband, says the Lord.

“By the hand” is the picture of a parent and a small child. “Their husband” translates bā‘altî, which can also mean “their master”; the POC reads “their Lord”. The Greek Old Testament, which Hebrews 8:9 follows, has a different sense here: “I had no concern for them.”
I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts;

At Sinai God wrote on stone (Exodus 31:18). Here the writing surface is a person. St Augustine, in his work On the Spirit and the Letter, says that what is written on the heart is the presence of the Holy Spirit himself, who pours out love (in substance).
for I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more.

This is the reason for everything before it, for the verse begins “for”. The new covenant starts with mercy. God's “not remembering” does not mean that he forgets; it means that he no longer holds the sin against us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law, the law of the Gospel, fulfils this promise: it is an interior law of charity (CCC 1965), and, in St Thomas Aquinas's words, “the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ” (CCC 1966). Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes the whole passage. The Church also insists that “the Old Covenant has never been revoked” (CCC 121), and that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). So we read Jeremiah's promise with gratitude to the people to whom it was first spoken.

r.h: Create in me a clean heart
set: The Miserere, as it is called from its first word in Latin, is the most famous of the penitential psalms. Its heading links it with David after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 12). Many scholars think that it reached its present form later, perhaps around the exile, which would explain its last verses on the rebuilding of Jerusalem. It is the prayer of anyone who has sinned and knows it.
The Lectionary takes the opening plea and the second half, skipping the confession of vv. 3–9, so that it answers Jeremiah directly.
str: vv. 1–2: the plea for mercy, with three words for sin and three for cleansing.
vv. 10–11: a new creation: heart and spirit.
v. 12: the joy of salvation.
v. 13: the forgiven person becomes a teacher of others.
kw: God's faithful, covenant love. The psalmist has nothing else to rely on: he appeals not to his own merits but to who God is.
The verb of Genesis 1:1 in v. 10, used in the Bible only of God. Forgiveness is not only a clean record. It is a new creation that only God can make.

It comes three times in vv. 10–12. In v. 11 “your holy spirit” is one of only a very few uses of that phrase in the Hebrew Bible (compare Isaiah 63:10–11). Christians hear in it a first hint of the Holy Spirit whom Christ sends.
vv: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love;
The first word is a plea, not a defence.
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and put a new and right spirit within me.
This is Jeremiah's promise turned into a prayer. What God said he would do, the sinner now asks him to do.
Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your holy spirit from me.
The worst thing the psalmist can imagine is not punishment but separation from God.
Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and sustain in me a willing spirit.
Repentance is meant to end in joy. Lent is not a season for a gloomy heart.
ch: The Catechism says that interior conversion is above all the work of God's grace, who gives us the strength to begin anew, and that the human heart needs God to give it a new heart (CCC 1431–1432). The Latin Church prays this psalm at Morning Prayer each Friday in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Psalm 51 has long been a prayer for those preparing to go to Confession.

r.h: He learned obedience
set: Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22), and it was addressed to Christians who were growing tired. The author is not named. Chapters 4–5 have just said that we have a high priest who can “sympathize with our weaknesses” and who was tested in every way, “yet without sin” (4:15). A high priest must be chosen from among mortals and able to deal gently with the weak (5:1–2). These three verses show that Jesus truly is one of us.
str: v. 7: Jesus' prayer in the days of his flesh, and the answer.
v. 8: obedience through suffering, though he was Son.
v. 9: made perfect, he becomes the source of salvation.
kw: A word that speaks of godly fear and reverence. The POC says “ദൈവഭയം”. This is what made his prayer pleasing: not his loud cries, but his surrender.
A play on words in Greek, also found in Greek proverbs: mathein, pathein. Here it is used of the Son, who did not need correction but entered our human way of obeying from the inside.

Not that he had been morally imperfect. The verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for the consecration of priests (Exodus 29:9). Through his suffering Jesus is fully established in his priestly role.
Cause or source. What he has passed through as our representative becomes the source of eternal salvation for us.
vv: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.

The scene recalls Gethsemane (Mark 14:33–36), and today's Gospel gives John's version of it (12:27). “He was heard”, and yet he died. The Greek for “from death” can mean “out of death”: the Father did not spare him the grave, but he brought him through it in the Resurrection. The Catechism says that all the troubles of humanity for all time are gathered up in this cry, and that the Father answers them by raising his Son (CCC 2606).
Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered;
The Catechism applies this to us: if the Son learned obedience in this way, how much more should we, who are sinners and creatures (CCC 2825). See the question below.
and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,
The obedience runs both ways: he obeyed the Father, and those who are saved obey him. Salvation is his gift, and we receive it by following him.
ch: The Church confesses that Christ has two wills, divine and human, and that his human will follows his divine will without resistance (Third Council of Constantinople; CCC 475). The horror of death that he felt in the garden (CCC 612) shows that his humanity is real. The Fathers defended this truth; St Gregory of Nazianzus gave the reason: what has not been assumed has not been healed (Letter 101). When we pray at Mass in our own distress, we are praying with one who has been there.

r.h: Unless a grain of wheat falls
set: This is the last Passover of Jesus' life (12:1). He has entered Jerusalem to the crowd's acclaim (12:12–19), and the Pharisees have just said, “Look, the world has gone after him!” (12:19). Immediately, in John's telling, some Greeks appear. They are probably Gentiles who worship the God of Israel, sometimes called “God-fearers”, and not Greek-speaking Jews, for John's word is Hellēnes.

Philip and Andrew are the only two of the Twelve with Greek names, and Philip comes from Bethsaida, a town near the Gentile territory (1:44). John does not say whether the Greeks ever reached Jesus. Their request simply sets off his answer: the hour has come, and through it the nations will come.
str: vv. 20–22: the Greeks; Philip and Andrew.
vv. 23–24: the hour and the grain.
vv. 25–26: the same law for the disciple.
vv. 27–28a: “Now my soul is troubled”: John's Gethsemane.
vv. 28b–30: the voice from heaven.
vv. 31–33: judgment on the world; the ruler driven out; the lifting up.
kw: “My hour has not yet come” (2:4); “his hour had not yet come” (7:30; 8:20). Now, for the first time: “The hour has come” (12:23). It is the hour of the Cross, and John calls it glory.
In John the Cross itself is where God's glory is seen, and the Son's love shines most clearly. Glory here is not an escape from suffering.
In v. 25 the word for one's natural life is psychē, and “eternal life” is zōē. To “hate” is a Semitic way of saying “to put second”.
It means both to raise physically and to exalt. On the Cross Jesus is literally raised up, and that is his enthronement (3:14; 8:28). John explains in v. 33 what he meant.
John's name for the devil (see 14:30; 16:11). At the moment he seems to win, he is cast out.
vv: They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and said to him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”
In John “to see” often means more than eyesight: to see is to come to believe. These words are the request of every seeker, and of every congregation before a preacher.
Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
They ask to see him, and he says, in effect: you will see me on the Cross. Whoever wants to know Jesus has to look there.
Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

A law of nature serves as a parable of Jesus' own death. In the granary a seed is safe, but it stays alone. St Augustine says that Christ himself was the grain that had to die and be multiplied (Tractates on John 51, in substance). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to the beasts in Rome, called himself God's wheat, to become the pure bread of Christ (To the Romans 4).
Those who love their life lose it, and those who hate their life in this world will keep it for eternal life.
The same law now applies to us. It is not contempt for God's gift of life, which is good; it means refusing to make our own life the highest thing. See the question below.
“Now my soul is troubled. And what should I say … ‘Father, save me from this hour’? No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour.

John does not describe the agony in the garden; it is here. The fear is real: the Greek verb speaks of deep inner disturbance, and the words recall the Greek form of Psalms 6:3 and 42:6. His decision is not an absence of fear, but obedience in the midst of it, which is just what Hebrews describes.
Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came from heaven, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
This is the only voice from heaven in John's Gospel. This prayer takes the place of “save me”, and it is John's counterpart to the first petition of the Our Father.
now the ruler of this world will be driven out.
At the moment when the world seems to be judging Jesus, the true judgment is taking place. Victory over the devil is won once for all at this hour (CCC 2853).
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”

A note on the text. Most copies read “all people”, as the NRSV and the POC do. Some early manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate read “all things”. The coming of the Greeks is the first fruit of this promise: the pull of the Cross has no borders.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ's being lifted up on the Cross signifies and begins his lifting up in the Ascension (CCC 662), and that the gathering of all people into the Kingdom is accomplished through it (CCC 542). St Leo the Great exclaims in a Passion sermon: you drew all things to yourself, Lord, when you were lifted up; the Cross is the source of all blessing (in substance). The grain of wheat also speaks of the Eucharist: the grain that dies becomes the bread of the altar and feeds the whole Church.

qa: How could the Son of God “learn obedience”? Was he ever disobedient?

No. Hebrews itself says that he was “without sin” (4:15). As God the Son he always shared the Father's will. As man he had a real human life, with a human will and a human way of learning (CCC 472, 475). Learning here does not mean moving from disobedience to obedience. It means living out obedience in a human life, in the conditions of suffering, all the way to death. So he knows from within what obedience costs us.
Does Jesus really tell us to hate our lives?

“Hate” is a Semitic way of saying “love less”, as Luke 14:26 and Matthew 10:37 show when placed together. Jesus does not teach contempt for life, for the body or for ourselves, since God made these good, and the Church defends every human life. He teaches that when our own survival or comfort becomes the highest good, we lose what we are trying to keep. Those who give themselves find life, and martyrs, parents and quiet servants of the poor all know this.
Does the “new covenant” mean that God has replaced Israel?

No. The Second Vatican Council said that the Jews remain very dear to God, who does not take back his gifts and his call (Nostra Aetate 4; compare Romans 11:29), and the Catechism says that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121). Jeremiah speaks of a new covenant with “the house of Israel and the house of Judah”, and Christians believe that in Jesus this promise is fulfilled and opened to the nations. So Christians confess Jesus as the Messiah of Israel and the mediator of the new covenant, and do so without contempt, gratefully and with hope.
rite: In the Latin Church this is the Sunday of the Third Scrutiny for adults preparing for Baptism at the Easter Vigil. In those parishes the Year A readings, with the raising of Lazarus, may be used, and the Church prays that the elect be delivered from the power of sin and death. Where the custom is kept, crosses and images in the church may be veiled from this Sunday, and on the weekdays of this week the Preface at Mass is of the Passion of the Lord. In the last days before Palm Sunday, a good Confession is the plainest way of asking for Jeremiah's new heart.
study: Jeremiah speaks of a law written on the heart. What part of God's will do I still carry as an outside rule, and what would it take for it to become my own desire?
Jesus prayed “with loud cries and tears”. Have I ever prayed to God that honestly? What would I say if I did so today?
What in my life is the grain that I have kept safe in the granary, refusing to let it fall into the ground?
“We wish to see Jesus.” When people look at me, my family or my parish, what would they see of him?

lead: Two women stand accused in public, and both face death. Susanna has done nothing, and God stirs up a young man to expose the lie told against her. The woman in John’s Gospel has been caught in sin, and Jesus turns the question back on those who accuse her. One story shows God defending the innocent; the other shows him raising up the guilty. As Lent draws toward the Passion, both ask who has the right to condemn. The key words are witness, condemn and sin.

r.h: The Lord heard her cry
set: The story of Susanna is not found in the Hebrew and Aramaic book of Daniel. It has come down to us in Greek, in two forms, and the Catholic Church receives it as inspired Scripture together with the other deuterocanonical parts of Daniel. The Latin Vulgate places it after the visions, as chapter 13. Some Greek manuscripts put it at the head of the book, since Daniel is still a youth here.

The scene is the Jewish community in exile in Babylon, where honored elders serve as judges. The story is told as a lesson: the fear of God is stronger than the fear of death, and a witness, however respected, must be examined.
str: vv. 1–9: the household, the garden, and two judges who turn their eyes away from Heaven.
vv. 15–30: the trap in the garden, Susanna’s choice, and the summons to the assembly.
vv. 33–41: the false testimony and the sentence.
vv. 42–46: her prayer; God stirs up Daniel.
vv. 47–62: the witnesses are separated, the lie falls apart, and the assembly blesses God.
¶ The shorter form begins at the sentence of death, in v. 41.
kw: The name comes from the Hebrew for a lily. Nothing in the story depends on it, but the contrast with the two judges is plain: she keeps faith in a closed garden, and they lose it in the seat of honor.
Usually explained as “God is my judge”. The name suits this chapter, in which human judges fail and God gives judgment through a boy.

In the Greek, Daniel’s sentences play on the name of each tree: schinos with schisei (he will cut you), prinos with prisai (to saw you). In the third century Julius Africanus and Origen already discussed what this wordplay says about the story’s origin.
vv: I choose not to do it; I will fall into your hands, rather than sin in the sight of the Lord.

She sees both roads clearly, and neither leads to safety. What decides it is not the danger but the presence of God: “in the sight of the Lord”. The two judges, by contrast, “turned away their eyes from looking to Heaven” (13:9).
O eternal God, you know what is secret and are aware of all things before they come to be;
No one in the assembly believes her, so she speaks to the one Judge who saw. The prayer is short and asks nothing for herself except what is true.
The Lord heard her cry.
A very short sentence, and the story turns on it. God’s answer comes in a human voice, through a young man who will not stay silent.
Are you such fools, O Israelites, as to condemn a daughter of Israel without examination and without learning the facts?
Daniel does not attack the law of Moses. He asks that it be kept. The law itself requires judges to make a careful inquiry into witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:18).
Thus innocent blood was spared that day.

The two judges receive what they planned for her, as Deuteronomy 19:19 lays down for a false witness. The story reflects the law of its time. The Church today teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that the death penalty is inadmissible (CCC 2267).
ch: St Hippolytus of Rome, in his commentary on Daniel, read Susanna as a figure of the Church, slandered yet kept by God (in substance). Her story is painted in the Roman catacombs, and the Church’s old prayers for the dying ask God to deliver the soul as he delivered Susanna from a false charge. The Catechism names false witness as a grave offense, because it leads to the condemnation of the innocent (CCC 2476). That teaching reaches every courtroom, and every conversation in which a reputation is at stake.

r.h: Neither do I condemn you
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple at dawn, soon after the festival of Booths (7:2), with the people gathered around him.

A note on the text. This passage is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts of John, and some later manuscripts place it elsewhere, even in Luke. Many scholars think it is an ancient memory of Jesus that entered the Gospel text later. St Jerome kept it in the Vulgate, and St Augustine suspected that some had removed it for fear that it would seem to excuse adultery (in substance). The Church receives it as inspired Scripture and as a true part of the Gospel.
str: vv. 1–2: dawn in the Temple; Jesus sits down to teach.
vv. 3–6a: the woman is set in the middle, and the test is put.
vv. 6b–8: he writes, speaks one sentence, and writes again.
v. 9: the accusers leave, beginning with the elders.
vv. 10–11: he and the woman, alone.
kw: The same verb is used of the tempter in the desert in the other Gospels (Mark 1:13). The question is not asked in order to learn what the law says but “so that they might have some charge to bring against him” (8:6).
This word occurs only here in the New Testament. Jesus does not ask who is innocent of this one act, but who is without sin at all.

To pass a sentence against someone. The word comes twice in vv. 10–11, in a question and in an answer. John has already said: “Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world” (3:17).
vv: Now in the law Moses commanded us to stone such women.

The law they cite names both partners: “both the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death” (Leviticus 20:10; compare Deuteronomy 22:22). Where the man has gone, the text does not say. Many scholars note that under Roman rule the death sentence was not in their hands (compare 18:31), and this would explain the trap: “stone her” sets Jesus against Rome, “let her go” sets him against Moses.
Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.

The Gospel does not say what he wrote, and we should not claim to know. St Jerome suggested that he wrote the sins of the accusers (in substance). Some connect it with Jeremiah 17:13, where the Hebrew speaks of those who turn from God as written in the earth (the NRSV has “recorded in the underworld”).
Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.
The law had the witnesses throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus does not set the law aside, nor does he call the woman innocent. He places the judges in the same light as the accused.
Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.
The two halves belong together. Mercy comes first and opens the way; the new life is what mercy is for. The one person there who was without sin is the one who does not throw.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this scene, says that only two remained, misera et misericordia, misery and mercy. Pope Francis took those words as the title of his apostolic letter at the close of the Year of Mercy in 2016. The Catechism calls the Gospel the revelation in Jesus Christ of God’s mercy to sinners (CCC 1846). The passage is a good one to pray before going to confession.

qa: Does Jesus make light of adultery?

No. He calls it sin (“do not sin again”), and the Church teaches that it does grave injury to the marriage bond and to justice (CCC 2380–2381). What he refuses is to let a sin be used as a weapon by those who ignore their own.
study: Susanna looks to the God who knows what is secret. When have I been misjudged, and where did I turn?
Am I more ready to pick up a stone or to examine my own heart? Whose reputation can I protect this week?

lead: Today’s readings are joined by one verb: to lift up. Moses lifts a bronze serpent on a pole, and those who look at it live. Jesus says that when the Son of Man is lifted up, people will know who he is. As the Cross comes nearer, the Church sets beside it an old story about complaint, poison and healing. The key words are look, lifted up and I am.

r.h: Look at it and live
set: Israel is near the end of the desert years. Edom has refused them passage (20:14–21), so they must go the long way around it. Aaron has just died on Mount Hor (20:22–29). The people have been through this complaint before, but here they reject the food God himself has given. “This miserable food” is the manna.
str: vv. 4–5: impatience, and the complaint against God and Moses.
v. 6: the serpents.
v. 7: the people admit their sin and ask Moses to pray.
vv. 8–9: the remedy: look and live.
¶ Notice that God does not take the serpents away. He gives a way to live though bitten.
kw: The Hebrew calls these “fiery” serpents, perhaps from the burning of the bite, and the NRSV translates “poisonous”. The word has the same root as the seraphim of Isaiah 6.
A play on sound: Moses makes a nĕḥaš nĕḥōšet, a “serpent of bronze”.
Also a banner or signal raised for all to see. The remedy is put where anyone can find it.
vv: and we detest this miserable food.
The bread from heaven has become, for them, something to despise. Complaint can blind us to the gift in our hands.
We have sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you; pray to the Lord to take away the serpents from us.
The first honest word in the passage. Those who spoke against Moses now ask for his prayer, and “Moses prayed for the people” without a word of reproach.
and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.
What had brought death is now the shape of healing. Those who were bitten must look at the very thing they fear.
ch: The Book of Wisdom already guards against any magical reading: the one who looked “was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all” (Wisdom 16:7). And when people later burned incense to the serpent, King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). The Catechism cites it among the images God allowed that pointed toward salvation through the incarnate Word (CCC 2130). St Justin Martyr makes a similar point in his Dialogue with Trypho, reading it as a sign of the Cross (in substance). Jesus himself draws the line: “just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14), and the Church reads Numbers 21 at Mass on the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross.

r.h: When you have lifted up the Son of Man
set: The setting is still the Temple, at the festival of Booths; Jesus has been teaching “in the treasury of the temple” (8:20). He speaks of going away, and the listeners cannot follow his meaning. They wonder if he plans to take his own life, when in fact others are planning his death.
In John, “the Jews” often means the authorities who oppose Jesus, not a whole people; Jesus, his mother and his first disciples were Jews, and many in this very scene believe in him (8:30).
str: vv. 21–22: “I am going away”, and the misunderstanding.
vv. 23–24: from below, from above; “unless you believe”.
vv. 25–27: “Who are you?”
vv. 28–29: the Cross will show who he is.
v. 30: many believe.
kw: The Greek has no “he”. The words can be an ordinary “It is I”, but in these verses they echo God’s own speech in the Greek Old Testament: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (Isaiah 43:10; compare Exodus 3:14).
John uses it three times of the Cross (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). It means both raising on a cross and exalting in honor. In this Gospel the two happen together.
vv: for you will die in your sins unless you believe that I am he.
This is a warning, not a verdict. Faith is held out as the way of escape from the very thing he warns of.
Why do I speak to you at all?

A note on the text. The Greek of this reply is famously hard, and translators differ. The NRSV hears a sigh. The Malayalam POC, like the Latin tradition, takes it as “what I have told you from the beginning”. Either way, Jesus does not give them a new title; he points them back to what they have already heard.
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he,
The Cross will not hide who Jesus is. It will show it. What looks like his defeat is the place where he is known (compare 12:32).
for I always do what is pleasing to him.
He is not alone, even at the hour when all will leave him. Compare 16:32.
ch: The Catechism quotes John 8:28 to teach that the Resurrection confirms the truth of Jesus’ divinity (CCC 653). The Church teaches that Jesus’ death cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, or against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Every sinner has a part in it (CCC 598). We read “you have lifted up” as spoken to ourselves.

study: What do I complain about that was first given to me as a gift? What would it mean to give thanks for it today?
When I look at a crucifix, what do I see? What wound of mine can I bring to that look?

lead: Today both readings ask what it means to be truly free. Three young men in Babylon are bound and thrown into a furnace, and they walk about unbound in the fire, for no king owns their worship. Jesus says to those who are proud of never having been slaves that sin has its own slavery, and that the Son sets people loose from it. The key words are but if not, continue and make free.

r.h: But if not
set: The stories in Daniel 1–6 are set in the court of Babylon. Many scholars think the book reached its final form in the second century BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV, when Jews were being forced to give up their faith. Whatever the date, it was read as a word for people in that very danger. The dying Mattathias recalled these three to his sons: “Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael believed and were saved from the flame” (1 Maccabees 2:59).

Between vv. 23 and 91 the Greek Bible has the prayer of Azariah and the song of the three young men, from which today’s psalm is taken. The Lectionary passes over the prayer and goes on to the king’s astonishment.
str: vv. 14–15: the king’s demand and his challenge: “who is the god that will deliver you?”
vv. 16–18: their answer.
vv. 19–20: rage, and the furnace heated seven times over.
vv. 91–92: four men walking in the fire.
v. 95: the king blesses their God.
kw: Aramaic for the two words on which the story rests (3:18). The three men believe that God can save them, but they do not make their fidelity depend on it.
Literally “a son of gods”, the king’s pagan way of speaking of a heavenly being. The NRSV has “a god”, and the POC ദേവകുമാരൻ. In v. 95 the king himself calls him God’s angel.
vv: If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and out of your hand, O king, let him deliver us.
The “if” does not doubt God’s power. It refuses to tell God what he must do. The Malayalam POC states it more firmly: he is able, and he will deliver.
But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods and we will not worship the golden statue that you have set up.
Here is mature faith. They do not serve God for the rescue. Many who have died for the faith, and whom no angel brought out of the fire, have lived by these words.
But I see four men unbound, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are not hurt;
They went in bound (3:21), and now they walk unbound. And they are not alone there. God’s help comes not around the furnace but inside it.
who has sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him.
A pagan king ends up as a witness to the God he had challenged. His question in v. 15 has been answered.
ch: Many early Christian writers saw a figure of the Son of God in the fourth man, while the text itself speaks of an angel. The three young men in the furnace are a frequent scene in catacomb art, and St Cyprian set them before Christians facing persecution (in substance). The Catechism warns that idolatry is not only a matter of pagan statues: we commit it whenever we honor a creature in place of God, such as power, pleasure, race, the state or money (CCC 2113). For those who suffer for the faith in many lands today, this reading is a companion, and a call to pray for them and for those who wrong them.

r.h: The truth will make you free
set: Jesus now speaks to people who “had believed in him” (8:31), and the talk becomes a dispute within one family of faith, about who are the true children of Abraham. The language in this chapter is sharp, as arguments among close kin can be. John’s Gospel was written at a time when, many scholars think, relations between Christians and the synagogue were painful. These words may never be used against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: vv. 31–32: continue, know, be made free.
vv. 33–36: “never been slaves”; the slave and the son.
vv. 37–41a: whose children? What did Abraham do?
vv. 41b–42: “one father”; he came from God.
kw: One of John’s favorite words. To be a disciple is not a single moment of belief but a staying, as a branch stays on the vine (15:4).
In the ancient world, the act that releases a slave. Freedom here is not doing whatever one likes, but being released from what holds us back from God.
A slave has no lasting place in the house; a son belongs there. Jesus uses this household picture to speak of himself, the Son, who can give others a place in the Father’s house.
vv: If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples;
The verse sets out the order: staying with his word, then knowing, then being made free. Freedom is at the end of a road of discipleship.
and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.
Often quoted without its first half. In John the truth is not only an idea but a person: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (14:6).
everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin.
They appeal to their descent, but Jesus speaks of something any person can know from within. Paul describes the same slavery (Romans 6:17–18; 7:15).
So if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
Only the Son of the house has the standing to release a slave. Grace is what sets us free.
ch: St Augustine says that the beginning of freedom is to be free from crimes (in substance), and St John Paul II quotes him in Veritatis Splendor 13. The same pope wrote that Christ meets people of every age with these same words about truth and freedom (Redemptor Hominis 12). The Catechism draws the lesson: the more one does what is good, the freer one becomes, and a choice for evil leads to “the slavery of sin” (CCC 1733; see also 2466).

qa: Why does Jesus speak so harshly to people who had believed?

He is warning people he has not given up on, as the prophets warned Israel. They rightly honor Abraham, and Jesus says so (8:37). His point is that being a child of Abraham shows in doing what Abraham did: welcoming God’s word. The warning applies first to us: being baptized and belonging to a Catholic family does not excuse us from it.
study: “But if not.” Where do I need to go on trusting God even if he does not do what I ask?
What habit has a hold on me that I call by a softer name? What would it be to ask the Son to set me loose from it?

lead: Abraham stands at the center of both readings. In Genesis, God gives him a new name and an everlasting covenant. In John, Jesus claims that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and then says the words that bring stones into people’s hands: “before Abraham was, I am.” The covenant with Abraham leads to the one Abraham longed to see. The key words are covenant, name and I am.

r.h: An everlasting covenant
set: Abram is ninety-nine years old (17:1), and he and Sarai have no son together. God has made him promises (Genesis 12; 15), and he now confirms them with a covenant and a new name, under the title “God Almighty”. The chapter goes on to give circumcision as the sign of the covenant and to promise Isaac (17:10–21).
str: v. 3: Abram falls on his face.
vv. 4–6: “As for me”: God’s side: many nations, a new name, kings.
vv. 7–8: the everlasting covenant and the land.
v. 9: “As for you”: Abraham’s side: keep the covenant.
kw: A solemn bond that makes two parties belong to one another. The word comes over and over in this chapter. God is the one who starts it and who holds it in being.
ancestor of a multitude of nations
The new name Abraham sounds like these words. Abram means something like “exalted father”, and for an old man with no son by Sarai, each use of the new name was a promise not yet seen.
‘Ôlām points to a long, unbounded time. God does not take back what he has given here.
vv: As for me, this is my covenant with you: You shall be the ancestor of a multitude of nations.
God speaks first, and he speaks of what he will do. The obligation (v. 9) comes after the gift.
No longer shall your name be Abram, but your name shall be Abraham;
In the Bible a new name means a new calling (compare Genesis 32:28; Matthew 16:18). Abraham is named for what he cannot yet see.
to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
This is the heart of every covenant in Scripture: “I will be your God”. Everything else, even the land, serves this.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God called Abraham to gather together scattered humanity, and made his descendants the trustees of the promise (CCC 59–60). The Jewish people remain the first to hear the word of God, to whom the covenant belongs, “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4). In the Roman Canon the Church calls Abraham “our father in faith”.

r.h: Before Abraham was, I am
set: This is the close of the long dispute in the Temple at the festival of Booths. The argument has been about Abraham, and it now reaches its peak. As before, “the Jews” in this Gospel refers to those of his hearers who are in dispute with him, not to a whole people. To them, Jesus’ words sounded like blasphemy, and they respond as they believe the law requires (Leviticus 24:16).
str: v. 51: keep my word and never see death.
vv. 52–53: “Abraham died.” “Who do you claim to be?”
vv. 54–55: the Father glorifies him.
v. 56: Abraham’s joy.
vv. 57–59: “before Abraham was, I am”; the stones.
kw: A word for exultant joy, used often in the Greek psalms. Some Jewish writings speak of God showing Abraham the ages to come. John says that what Abraham longed for was this day.
The contrast is in the verbs. Genesthai means “to come to be”, and Abraham did. Eimi simply means “I am”. Jesus does not say “I was”.
vv: Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.
They think he means the end of bodily life, and so they point to Abraham’s grave. He means the life that death cannot end (compare 11:25–26).
Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.
Jesus does not set Abraham aside. He calls him their ancestor and makes him a witness to his coming.
Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.

Here the “I am” of this chapter is plain. St Augustine says that Jesus does not say “I was” because the words belong to the Godhead, for whom there is no past or future (in substance). The Catechism lists this saying among those that only his divine identity can justify (CCC 590).
So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
His hour has not yet come (compare 8:20). He goes out of the Temple. When the hour does come, he will lay down his life of his own accord (10:18).
ch: The Church’s faith in the Son, “God from God, Light from Light”, rests on sayings like this one. The Catechism also explains that such a claim was a real stumbling block for many in Israel, and it treats those who rejected him with care (CCC 589–591). The Passion is not to be charged against the Jewish people (CCC 597).

study: God gave Abram a new name before he had a son. What new thing has God begun in me that I cannot yet see?
Who do I say Jesus is when I pray? Does “I am” change how I bring him my fear of death?

lead: Today the Church sets aside the purple of Lent for white and keeps the solemnity of St Joseph, the husband of Mary. All the readings follow one promise on its way. God tells David through Nathan that an heir of his will have a throne forever. St Paul recalls Abraham, who believed a promise when all appearances were against it. Matthew shows both promises reaching their goal through a man of David’s line who says nothing and does what he is told. Today’s psalm sings of the same promise to David.
The Gospel may be either Matthew or Luke 2:41–51a; a note on Luke is among the questions below. The key words are house, hoping against hope and righteous.

r.h: I will establish his kingdom
set: David is king in Jerusalem and has brought the ark there (2 Samuel 6). Settled in his house of cedar, he wants to build a house for God, since “the ark of God stays in a tent” (7:2). The prophet Nathan approves at first, but that night the word of the Lord comes to him.

This oracle is the foundation of Israel’s hope for a son of David. The word “covenant” does not appear in this chapter, but Psalm 89, today’s psalm, uses it: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one” (89:3).
str: vv. 4–5a: God’s word comes to Nathan: are you the one to build me a house?
vv. 12–13: David’s heir: his kingdom and his throne.
v. 14a: father and son.
v. 16: David’s house, kingdom and throne, forever.
¶ The Lectionary omits vv. 5b–11, where God recalls what he has done for David, and vv. 14b–15, where he promises that even if the heir sins, his steadfast love will not depart.
kw: The whole chapter plays on this one word. It can mean a palace (David’s), a temple (the one he plans) and a dynasty (what God promises). David offers God a house; God says “the Lord will make you a house” (7:11).
Literally “seed”. It first points to Solomon, who will build the Temple (1 Kings 6), and it opens out toward a son beyond him.
From the same root as our word Amen: firm, reliable. The future of David’s house rests on God’s fidelity, not on the conduct of its kings.
vv: Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
David’s idea is generous, but God will not be housed by a king’s plan. The first move in this story, as in every story of grace, is God’s.
I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.
The promise looks beyond David’s death. He will not live to see what is promised, a thing he shares with Abraham.
I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me.
A king of Israel was called God’s son by adoption. Hebrews 1:5 applies this verse to Christ, in whom it is true in a way no king of Judah could have dreamed.
Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.
Solomon’s kingdom split, and the last king of Judah went into exile. Israel went on hoping because this word still stood. Psalm 89 itself shows the pain of that waiting.
ch: The angel says to Mary: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David” (Luke 1:32). The Catechism says that God called Joseph to take Mary as his wife so that Jesus should be born into the messianic lineage of David (CCC 437), and that many recognized in Jesus the promised son of David (CCC 439). Joseph holds no throne. He is a workman in a small town, and through him the line is handed on. Jesus also speaks of the true house of God, “the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

r.h: Hoping against hope
set: St Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, probably around AD 57, before going to Jerusalem and hoping to reach them. In chapters 1–4 he argues that Jews and Gentiles alike are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ. Abraham is his great witness, since Genesis says he believed and God “reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), before circumcision and long before the law given at Sinai.
Paul does not despise the law: “we uphold the law” (3:31). His point is about where the promise comes from.
str: v. 13: the promise came through the righteousness of faith.
vv. 16–17: it rests on grace, for all Abraham’s descendants, in the presence of the God who gives life.
v. 18: hoping against hope.
v. 22: reckoned as righteousness.
kw: What God binds himself to do. A promise can only be received and trusted. This is Paul’s key word in the chapter.
Literally “beyond hope, in hope”. All human reasons for hoping have gone, and Abraham hopes because of God.

A word from accounting: to enter to someone’s account. Paul is quoting Genesis 15:6. For the Catholic understanding, God’s reckoning is not merely a legal entry: justification truly makes us just and renews us within (CCC 1987–1989).
vv: For the promise that he would inherit the world did not come to Abraham or to his descendants through the law but through the righteousness of faith.
Genesis promised Abraham a land and many nations. Paul widens it to “the world”: all peoples are to share in the blessing.
in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his descendants,
If it rested on our record, it would never be secure. Because it rests on grace, it holds.
who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.
The God of Abraham’s faith is the Creator and the God of resurrection. This is what makes hope possible when things look finished.
Hoping against hope, he believed that he would become “the father of many nations,”
The verse fits Joseph as well. In the dark, with no explanation that anyone could check, he trusted what God said.
Therefore his faith “was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
The Lectionary ends here, and Matthew’s Gospel then calls Joseph righteous (Matthew 1:19). The word links the two.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham shows what faith is (CCC 146), and that Christian hope has its origin and model in his (CCC 1819). St John Paul II wrote in Redemptoris Custos that Joseph was the first to share in the faith of the Mother of God (5). Faith, as Paul says elsewhere, works “through love” (Galatians 5:6), and by grace our deeds truly bear fruit (CCC 2008–2010). Joseph’s faith, like Abraham’s, lives in what he does.

r.h: He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him
set: Matthew’s Gospel opens with the genealogy of Jesus, “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (1:1), and each line runs “the father of”. At v. 16 the pattern breaks: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”. In Greek “of whom” is feminine. So the genealogy leaves a question: how does Jesus belong to David’s line if Joseph is not his natural father? Vv. 18–25 give the answer.

Background. Betrothal in that time was a binding bond. The couple were already called husband and wife, and it could be ended only by a formal divorce, but the woman often stayed in her family home for a time before moving to her husband’s house. It is in this interval that Mary is found to be with child.
str: v. 16: the end of the genealogy.
v. 18: Mary is with child “from the Holy Spirit”.
v. 19: Joseph’s decision.
vv. 20–21: the angel in a dream: do not be afraid; name him.
v. 24a: he wakes and obeys.
¶ This is the first of four dreams in which God directs Joseph (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22). The Gospels do not record a single word he said.
kw: In Matthew, one who lives by God’s will as the law teaches it. His righteousness shows here in his care both for God’s law and for Mary’s name.
The usual word for ending a marriage or a betrothal by divorce. “Quietly” probably means with the fewest possible witnesses, without a public charge.

The Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, from the name Yehoshua, “the Lord saves” (CCC 430). The father gave the name. By naming the child, Joseph takes him legally as his son, and so Jesus becomes, in law, a son of David.
vv: and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
Matthew chooses his words with care: Jesus is born of Mary, and Joseph’s place is that of her husband.
Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.

The Fathers read this in more than one way. St Jerome says that Joseph, knowing Mary’s purity, kept silent about a mystery he did not understand (in substance). St Bernard says that in reverence he felt unworthy to stay near so great a mystery (in substance). Others think he believed that she had sinned and yet would not shame her. On every reading he is merciful.
Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

Elsewhere in Matthew “son of David” is said of Jesus alone. The title reminds Joseph who he is and why he is needed. The Catechism says that the angel’s words teach the virginal conception, a divine work beyond all human understanding (CCC 497).
She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.
Joseph is given a task, not an explanation of everything. The name says what the child will do.
he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him;
This is Joseph’s whole answer: he gets up and does it. St John Paul II calls this the “obedience of faith” in Joseph (Redemptoris Custos 4, in substance).
ch: St Augustine defended the marriage of Mary and Joseph as a true marriage, and Joseph as truly a father to Jesus, though not by the flesh (in substance). Pius IX declared him patron of the universal Church in 1870, and Pope Francis marked the 150th anniversary with the letter Patris Corde (2020), which speaks of him as a father in the shadows, working, accepting and creatively courageous. The Catechism commends us to St Joseph as patron of a happy death (CCC 1014).

qa: Did Mary and Joseph have other children? Verse 25 says “until”.

The Greek word for “until” says what happened up to a point, not what happened afterward. The Church confesses Mary’s perpetual virginity (CCC 499). The “brothers” of Jesus in the Gospels are understood as close relatives; the word could have that wider sense in Semitic usage (CCC 500).
What does Joseph teach us if he never speaks?

That holiness does not depend on being heard. His whole witness is doing what God asks, at once and in the dark, for the sake of those in his care. Countless fathers and workers, whose lives no one will ever write about, can see themselves in him.
What of the other Gospel, Luke 2:41–51a?

There Jesus, aged twelve, stays behind in the Temple. Mary says, “your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety” (2:48), and Jesus speaks of his Father’s house. Then “he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them” (2:51). So the Son of God learned as a boy to obey this man, in the home he provided (CCC 532, 534).
rite: In the Roman calendar this is a solemnity: the Gloria and the Creed are said at Mass even in Lent. This year it falls on a Friday, and the Church’s law does not bind us to Friday abstinence when a solemnity falls on that day (Code of Canon Law, canon 1251). St Joseph’s name has stood in the Roman Canon since St John XXIII added it in 1962, and it was added to the other Eucharistic Prayers in 2013. Many Catholics keep March as St Joseph’s month. Two days from now Holy Week begins, and we can ask him, who protected the child from those who sought his life, to stay with us as we walk beside the Son at the Passion.
study: David wanted to do something great for God, and God said he would do it himself. What am I trying to build by myself that I should let God build?
Joseph acted without having the full picture. What is the next plain thing God is asking of me, even if I do not see where it leads?
Paul says the promise rests on grace. Where do I still act as if it rests on my record?
Who are the people in my care whom I protect, as Joseph did, without being noticed? How can I honor those who do this for me?

lead: On the eve of Palm Sunday the theme is one word: gather. Ezekiel promises that God will bring his scattered people home, make them one and dwell among them. In John, the high priest says more than he knows: Jesus will die “to gather into one the dispersed children of God”. The response today, from Jeremiah, sings of the God who gathers his flock like a shepherd. The plot is now set, and the Passover is near. The key words are one, gather and dwelling.

r.h: I will make them one nation
set: Ezekiel is a priest among the exiles in Babylon, and this oracle comes after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. Just before our reading come the vision of the dry bones (37:1–14) and the sign of two sticks joined into one, Judah and Joseph (37:15–20). The northern and southern kingdoms had been divided since the time after Solomon (1 Kings 12), and the north had fallen long before. Our reading gives the meaning of the sign: there will be one people, one king and one sanctuary.
str: vv. 21–22: gathered from the nations, one nation, one king.
v. 23: cleansed, and God’s own people once more.
vv. 24–25: David, the one shepherd, in the land.
vv. 26–28: an everlasting covenant of peace, and God’s sanctuary among them.
kw: The word keeps sounding through this passage: one nation, one king, one shepherd. Division was a wound in Israel’s history, and the promise is that God will heal it.
Šālôm is more than the absence of war. It is wholeness, everything being as it should be between God and his people.
The word for the tent in the desert, from the verb “to dwell”. God’s plan from the start is to live among his people.
vv: I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel;
A God who keeps his word to scattered exiles can be trusted when there seems to be no people left.
I will save them from all the apostasies into which they have fallen, and will cleanse them.

A note on the text. The NRSV’s “apostasies” follows a small correction of the Hebrew, supported by some ancient Greek witnesses. The Hebrew as we have it reads “dwellings”, which the Malayalam POC follows (വസതികൾ). In either case, the return is not only a journey home, but a cleansing.
My servant David shall be king over them; and they shall all have one shepherd.
David had long been dead. Ezekiel is speaking of a king to come, in his line. Compare Ezekiel 34:23 and Jesus’ words in John 10:16.
My dwelling place shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
The formula of the covenant once more. The last book of the Bible uses the same picture for the end of all things (Revelation 21:3).
ch: This promise was made to Israel, and it stands, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839). Christians hear in it also the work of Christ, the shepherd in David’s line, who “lived among us” (John 1:14), and they see the Church as a people gathered by God (CCC 762, 781). Here the Lenten call to reconciliation meets the prayer for Christian unity.

r.h: To gather into one
