set: Jesus has just raised Lazarus (11:1–44). John shows the result: many believe, and some report to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees call a meeting of the council. Their fear is real: the Romans, who rule Judea, might see a popular movement as a threat and crush it. John’s first readers know that the Romans did destroy the Temple in AD 70.

Caiaphas was high priest for many years, from about AD 18 to 36. “That year” means that fateful year. The Catechism notes that the authorities were not all of one mind about Jesus (CCC 596), and many here believe in him (11:45).
str: vv. 45–46: two responses to the sign.
vv. 47–48: the council’s fear.
vv. 49–50: Caiaphas’s reasoning.
vv. 51–52: John’s comment: he prophesied.
vv. 53–54: the plan; Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.
vv. 55–56: Passover is near; will he come to the festival?
kw: “Our holy place” (11:48) means the Temple, the place of God’s presence. The irony is that John has already told us that Jesus’ body is the true temple (2:21).
The verb is related to the word synagogue. The phrase is John’s own comment, and it gives the Cross a purpose as wide as the world.
vv: If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and destroy both our holy place and our nation.
They are thinking of their people’s survival, and that is no small thing. But a good aim does not make it right to take an innocent life.
it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed.

The cold logic of power in every age: one person may be sacrificed for the sake of the rest. The Catechism answers this very case: the end does not justify the means, and the condemnation of an innocent person cannot be justified as a way of saving the nation (CCC 1753).
He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation,
John says that God can use even a word spoken for an evil purpose. Caiaphas meant “instead of the nation”, and God meant “for the sake of the nation”.
and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
The heart of the reading. Compare 10:16 and 12:32. The Cross is where the scattered are brought home.
ch: The Catechism quotes this scene and speaks of the division among the authorities (CCC 596), and it takes up 11:52 when it says that Christ, the offspring promised to Abraham, gathers into one the scattered children of God in the Spirit (CCC 706). St Augustine notes that the Spirit of prophecy can use even a wicked man, because of the office he holds, not because of his merit (in substance). In this way the passage prepares us for Holy Week: human plans go ahead, and God’s plan goes through them, without excusing them.

qa: How could God speak through a man plotting a death?

The gift of prophecy here belongs to his office, and it says nothing of his holiness. John does not excuse Caiaphas’s plan. Nor is he a picture of a whole people: the Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged to all the Jews of that time or of ours (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
study: Where is there a division around me, in my family, parish or town, that I can help to heal this Holy Week?
Have I ever accepted that someone else should pay for “the greater good”? What would Jesus’ way be in that case?

lead: Palm Sunday holds two moods in one Mass. It begins outside, with branches and Hosanna, as Jesus comes to Jerusalem on a colt. It goes on with the Servant who does not hide his face from insult, the hymn of the one who emptied himself, and the whole Passion according to Mark. The shouts of welcome give way to other shouts, and the disciples run away.

The Philippians hymn gives the shape of it all: down to the Cross, and then raised above every name. Holy Week opens on the road that goes through the first half of that hymn on the way to the second. The key words are Hosanna, emptied and handed over.

r.h: Blessed is the one who comes
set: Jesus has come up from Jericho (10:46), and this is the first time in Mark that he reaches Jerusalem. He has told the disciples three times what awaits him there (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). Bethphage and Bethany lie on the Mount of Olives, across from the city, where Zechariah pictures the Lord standing on his great day (Zechariah 14:4). Pilgrims were going up for the Passover, the feast of liberation.
The Lectionary also offers John 12:12–16. John alone mentions palm trees, and he adds, “His disciples did not understand these things at first” (12:16).
str: vv. 1–3: Jesus sends two disciples with exact instructions.
vv. 4–6: it happens as he said.
v. 7: the colt, the cloaks, and Jesus seated.
v. 8: the cloaks and branches on the road.
vv. 9–10: the shout.
kw: Mark does not quote Zechariah 9:9, but readers who know it hear it: “your king comes to you … humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey”. It is the mount of a king of peace, not a warhorse.
From the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25, “Save us, we beseech you”. By this time it had also become a shout of praise.
Mark’s word is general: leaves or rushes cut in the fields. Cloaks on the road greet a king (2 Kings 9:13).
vv: just say this, ‘The Lord needs it and will send it back here immediately.’
He owns nothing and borrows a young animal, and yet he speaks with authority. God can ask for what is ours.
Then they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it; and he sat on it.
Earlier he refused to be publicized (8:30). Now he acts out in public who he is, but in a way that does not fit what people expected.
Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
Psalm 118 is a song of entry into the Temple (118:19–26). The Church has kept these words, and they ring out at every Mass in the Sanctus.
Blessed is the coming kingdom of our ancestor David!
The promise to David stands in the air. But the throne is to be a cross, and the inscription over it will say “The King of the Jews” (15:26).
ch: The pilgrim Egeria described the people of Jerusalem in the fourth century going down from the Mount of Olives on this day with branches, the children too (in substance). The Catechism says that the Church takes up the Hosanna in the Sanctus to introduce the memorial of the Lord’s Passover (CCC 559), and that with this celebration the liturgy solemnly opens Holy Week (CCC 560). St Andrew of Crete, in a sermon the Church reads in her Office on this day, says that we should spread ourselves under Christ’s feet, rather than cloaks or branches (in substance).

r.h: I did not hide my face
set: This is the third of the four “Songs of the Servant” in the second part of Isaiah (42:1–9; 49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). These chapters speak to Jews in exile in Babylon. Who the Servant was in the first place is much discussed: Israel, or a faithful figure within Israel, or the prophet himself. The Servant here does not yet die, but he is already suffering, and he does not run away.
str: v. 4: a tongue that has first learned to listen.
v. 5: an open ear, and no turning back.
v. 6: the blows and the insults.
v. 7: God’s help, and a face set like flint.
kw: A disciple or pupil. It comes twice in v. 4. A teacher who can comfort is one who has stayed a pupil.
A very hard rock. He is not hard toward people, but he is firm toward his task. Luke says of Jesus that “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51).
vv: that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word. Morning by morning he wakens
The gift of a comforting word comes from a morning habit: listening to God before speaking to anyone.
The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious, I did not turn backward.
Obedience (from the Latin “to listen”) is what makes the suffering a gift and not only a misfortune.
I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.
“I gave”: he is not merely overcome. Pulling the beard was a deep insult in that world. Mark tells of the spitting at Jesus’ trial (14:65; 15:19).
The Lord God helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced;
The verse does not say that the pain has stopped. All the confidence is in who stands beside him. The same note sounds at the end of the Passion psalm (Psalm 22:22–23).
ch: The Catechism says that the Servant Songs proclaim the meaning of Jesus’ Passion (CCC 713), and that Jesus himself explained his life and death in the light of the Suffering Servant (CCC 601). The Church reads Isaiah 50 on this day so that we hear the Passion as willing obedience, from one who has listened to the Father every morning of his life.

r.h: He emptied himself
set: St Paul writes from prison (1:13) to a community he loves, which has its own rivalries. In 2:1–5 he asks them to have “the same mind” that was in Christ Jesus, and then come these verses. Many scholars think that this is an early Christian hymn that Paul is quoting or shaping; if so, it shows how very early believers already worshipped Christ.
str: vv. 6–8: the descent: form of God, form of a slave, death on a cross.
v. 9: “Therefore”: the turn, with God now the one acting.
vv. 10–11: the ascent: every knee, every tongue, “Jesus Christ is Lord”.
kw: He was “in the form of God” and took “the form of a slave”. The hymn means something real on both sides: true God and true man.

A rare word, and its exact meaning is debated: something to seize, or something to hold on to for one’s own gain. Whichever is right, the sense is that he did not use his equality with God for his own advantage.
The basis of the term kenosis. He did not stop being God. He emptied himself by taking on what he had not been: our human condition, as a servant.
vv: who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited,
Adam grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5). Many readers have seen Christ here as the new Adam, who does the opposite.
but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness.
St Leo the Great says in his Tome that this emptying was a stooping down of compassion, not a loss of power (in substance).
he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death…even death on a cross.
The last phrase breaks the rhythm. Crucifixion was a death of shame, given to slaves and rebels. No one in Paul’s world would have put it in a hymn to a god, and that is the point.
Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,
Many take this name to be “Lord” (v. 11), the title that the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name.
so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend,
This takes up Isaiah 45:23, “To me every knee shall bow”, words spoken by the Lord himself. Paul applies them to Jesus.
and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
The honor given to the Son does not take from the Father. It is “to the glory of God the Father”.
ch: The Catechism quotes the hymn as the Church’s song of the Incarnation (CCC 461), and teaches that calling Jesus “Lord” confesses his divinity (CCC 449). The Church prays it every Saturday evening in the Liturgy of the Hours, at the start of the Sunday. Today’s verse before the Passion also takes up vv. 8–9 of this hymn.

r.h: Truly this man was God’s Son
set: Many scholars think that Mark is the earliest of the four Gospels, and it gives the Passion a very large part of its pages. Ancient tradition, reported by Papias, links Mark with the preaching of St Peter, and Peter’s failure is told here without any softening.

Background. Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36. Only he could order a crucifixion, a Roman punishment. Passover recalled Israel’s release from Egypt, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. In Mark the Last Supper is a Passover meal (14:12).

Mark’s account is bare. Jesus speaks less and less: he answers the high priest and says little to Pilate, then falls silent until the cry from the Cross. Everyone leaves him, one group after another. The first human being in this Gospel to call him God’s Son is a Roman soldier, at the moment of his death.
str: 14:1–11: the plot, the anointing at Bethany, Judas.
14:12–26: the Passover and the bread and the cup.
14:27–52: the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, the arrest, the flight.
14:53–72: Jesus before the council; Peter in the courtyard.
15:1–15: Pilate and Barabbas.
15:16–32: the mockery, the road, the Cross.
15:33–39: darkness, the cry, the death, the curtain, the centurion.
15:40–47: the women who watched; the burial by Joseph of Arimathea.

¶ The shorter form is 15:1–39. A note on the text: the NRSV has no verse 15:28, because the sentence some later manuscripts have there is missing from the best Greek witnesses. The POC divides these verses differently, so its verse 28 is not that sentence.
kw: The word runs through the Passion like a thread. Judas hands him over (14:10), the council hands him to Pilate (15:1), and Pilate hands him to be crucified (15:15). Jesus had foretold it (9:31; 10:33). Paul uses the same word both for that night and for the handing on of the Eucharist (1 Corinthians 11:23).

Aramaic, the word a child or grown son used to his father. Mark alone of the Gospels keeps it, in the hour of greatest fear (14:36). Paul says that Christians pray with this word in the Spirit (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).

Used in Mark at only two moments: the heavens are “torn apart” at the baptism (1:10), and the curtain of the Temple is “torn in two” at the death (15:38). At both, a voice names him God’s Son (1:11; 15:39).
vv: Take; this is my body.
The words come in the middle of a Passover meal, on the night of betrayal. He gives what they are about to take from him.
This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

“Blood of the covenant” repeats Moses’ words at Sinai (Exodus 24:8), and “for many” recalls the Servant who “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). The Catechism says that in the Eucharist the sacrifice of the Cross is made present (CCC 1365–1366).
Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want.
He really asks, and he truly fears. Here is a true human will, which accepts the cup from the Father’s hands (CCC 612). Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.
All of them deserted him and fled.
Just a little before, “all of them said the same”: they would die with him (14:31). From here on, he is alone.
Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?…I am;

After long silence comes his first open public claim in Mark, and he joins to it Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1. The secret comes out only when no one can mistake him for a conqueror, as he stands bound before his judges.
And he broke down and wept.
Only Mark says the cock crows twice. Peter’s story does not end here (16:7). St Ambrose says that he reads of Peter’s tears, but not of what he said (in substance).
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
The first line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. The psalm begins in abandonment and ends in praise. Whoever prays its opening line is still calling God “my God”.
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
“From top to bottom”: the act comes from above. Mark gives no explanation, and readers have seen in it both a sign of grief and a way opened to God (compare Hebrews 10:19–20).
Truly this man was God’s Son!

This looks back to the first verse of the Gospel (1:1). No miracle moves him: only “that in this way he breathed his last”. A Gentile soldier is the first human being in this Gospel to say what we have come here to say.
ch: The Catechism follows the Passion step by step. It speaks of the Supper as the anticipation of Jesus’ willing offering (CCC 610), and of his acceptance of the cup at Gethsemane (CCC 612). On the cry from the Cross, it says that he did not experience reprobation as if he himself had sinned, but in redeeming love he took us on, in our state of sin, and could say it in our name (CCC 603). Quoting the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent, it says that sinners were the authors and ministers of all the Redeemer’s sufferings (CCC 598).

qa: Who is responsible for the death of Jesus?

Mark names particular people: Judas, some of the temple leaders, Pilate, the soldiers, and a crowd stirred up on one morning. The Church teaches firmly that the Passion “cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today” (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). She adds that all sinners were its authors, and that we Christians bear the greater guilt when we sin knowingly against him (CCC 598). Jesus’ own consent stands behind it all (CCC 609).
Did the Father really abandon Jesus on the Cross?

The Father and the Son were never divided: Jesus’ redeeming love always united him to the Father (CCC 603). The cry is real anguish, and it is also prayer: he is praying Psalm 22, which ends with trust. Those who feel abandoned by God today can pray with the same words, knowing that he has been there before them.
Mark does not mention palms. Why do we carry them?

Mark speaks of “leafy branches” cut in the fields (11:8). John’s Gospel has “branches of palm trees” (12:13), and palms were a sign of victory. In Kerala people commonly carry tender coconut fronds. The point lies in what is shouted, and in who is welcomed.
rite: The Roman liturgy opens today with the blessing of branches and the Gospel of the entry, followed by a procession or a solemn entrance. Red vestments are worn. The Passion is read without candles, incense or the signing of the book, and when it reaches the death of Jesus, all kneel and pause. Today begins Holy Week, the week when the Church walks with the Lord through his Passover. Keep the blessed branch at home, near a crucifix: it is the sign of a promise made in public, and traditionally the following year’s ashes are made from such branches.
study: The crowd shouted “Hosanna” and soon people were shouting something else. When has my own praise turned so easily?
Isaiah’s Servant listens every morning. How can I make time in Holy Week to listen before I speak?
Philippians says that he emptied himself. What is one advantage I could let go of this week for someone else’s sake?
Where do I find myself in Mark’s Passion: asleep, running away, warming myself by the fire, carrying the cross with Simon, or watching from a distance with the women?

lead: Holy Week’s first weekday sets two figures side by side, and both are quiet. In Isaiah a chosen servant will not break even a bruised reed. In John a woman says nothing at all, pours out a pound of perfume on the feet of Jesus, and is defended by him. On the first three weekdays of this week and again on Good Friday the Church reads the four Servant Songs of Isaiah, so that we walk toward the cross with the Servant before our eyes. Psalm 27 gives the answer of trust: “The Lord is my light and my salvation”.

r.h: A servant who will not break the bruised reed
set: Isaiah 40–55 speaks to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Many scholars speak of a prophet in the school of Isaiah, often called Second Isaiah, who announces that God will bring them home. Within these chapters are four poems about a mysterious Servant of the Lord (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), named the Servant Songs by scholars since the late nineteenth century. Today’s reading is the first, with the verses that follow it.
str: vv. 1–4: God presents his servant: chosen, filled with the spirit, gentle, unwearied.
vv. 5–7: God the Creator speaks to the servant and gives him his mission: covenant, light, release.
kw: A servant in Israel could be a slave, but “servant of the Lord” is also a title of honour, given to Moses and David. Here the honour lies in belonging wholly to God.
It comes three times in vv. 1–4. It means more than a court’s verdict: it is the right order that God wants in the world. The servant establishes it without force.
A striking phrase: the servant does not only announce a covenant, he is himself given as a covenant (v. 6). Christians hear in this the Lord who says “the new covenant in my blood”.
vv: Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights;
The voice from heaven at the Baptism of Jesus echoes these words (Matthew 3:17), and CCC 536 sees there the beginning of his mission as the suffering Servant.
a bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench;
A reed and a lamp’s wick are the weakest things in a house. Most conquerors break what is already cracked. This one protects it. Anyone who feels nearly finished can take heart from this verse.
to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon,
For the exiles this meant release from Babylon. In the Gospels the blind see, and the Passion is the price of a wider release, from sin and death.
ch: Matthew 12:18–21 quotes the song directly and applies it to the gentle ministry of Jesus. The Catechism teaches that the Messiah’s characteristics are revealed above all in the Servant Songs, which proclaim the meaning of his Passion (CCC 713). The first song does not yet speak of suffering. It shows the manner of the one who will suffer: he wins without shouting, and he does not grow faint (v. 4) until his work is done.

r.h: The house filled with fragrance
set: John dates the scene “six days before the Passover”, so the countdown to the cross has begun. Bethany lies close to Jerusalem (11:18), and Lazarus, just raised from the dead, sits at the table. That raising has led the authorities to resolve on the death of Jesus (11:47–53). So life and death share this supper.

Matthew 26:6–13 and Mark 14:3–9 tell of an anointing at Bethany in which an unnamed woman pours the ointment on his head. Luke 7:36–50 tells of a sinful woman in Galilee. John alone names Mary, the sister of Martha.
str: vv. 1–3: the dinner and the anointing.
vv. 4–6: Judas objects.
vv. 7–8: Jesus defends her.
vv. 9–11: the crowd comes, and the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too.
kw: A costly perfumed oil made from a plant of the Himalayan region, brought a very long way to the Mediterranean. The Greek word beside it, pistikēs, is uncertain, though it is usually taken as “pure”.

The money box of the group (12:6; 13:29). The verb translated “steal” (ebastazen) can also simply mean “carry”; here the two meanings meet, and John’s bitter point is that he carried it and also carried it off.
A rare word, used only here and in the parallel in Mark 14:8. Its related verb comes in John 19:40, when Joseph and Nicodemus wrap his body with spices. Mary’s act looks ahead to that tomb.
vv: Mary took a pound of costly perfume made of pure nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

A Roman pound was about 325 grams, a great quantity. It was more usual to anoint a guest’s head, so to anoint the feet is an act of deep lowliness. In the next chapter Jesus himself will wash and wipe feet. St Augustine says that as the house was filled with the scent, so the world is filled with the good report of what she did (in substance).
“Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?”
A denarius was a labourer’s day wage (Matthew 20:2), so this is the wage of most of a year. The question sounds right, which is why John adds what lay behind it (12:6).
“Leave her alone. She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial.
The Greek is hard to render exactly, and translations differ. The sense is clear: she has done something fitting for what is about to happen.
ch: The Church has seen in Mary of Bethany the love that does not count the cost. Her name stands in the Roman calendar: since 2021, Mary and Lazarus are honoured with Martha on 29 July, and the calendar keeps her distinct from Mary Magdalene, with whom she was long identified in the West. The chief priests’ plan (v. 10) is John’s dark irony: they would kill a man who had been raised from the dead. Verse 9’s “crowd of the Jews” is an ordinary crowd in Judea, many of whom came to believe (v. 11). The plot belongs to some of the authorities, not to a people (CCC 597).

qa: Was Jesus saying the poor do not matter?

No. “You always have the poor with you” echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which goes on to command open-handed giving. The Catechism says that Jesus does not soften the older demands here but invites us to recognise his own presence in the poor, who are his brethren (CCC 2449). Mary’s moment was unique: he was about to die.
study: Who is the “bruised reed” near me, and how can I avoid breaking it this week?
What is my “pound of nard”, the thing I would give to the Lord without counting the cost?

lead: Today’s two readings are both about a calling that seems to have failed. The Servant cries, “I have labored in vain”, and God answers by making his mission wider. At the supper Jesus is troubled, Judas goes out into the night, and Peter promises more than he can give. Yet at that very moment Jesus says, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”. Psalm 71 prays from the womb onward, as the Servant does: “Upon you I have leaned from my birth”.

r.h: A light to the nations
set: This is the second Servant Song. In the first, God spoke about the Servant. Now the Servant speaks for himself, and he addresses the coastlands and peoples far away. In Babylon the exiles felt forgotten (49:14). The song answers that weariness from within: even God’s chosen one has felt he has achieved nothing.
str: vv. 1–3: the call from the womb; mouth like a sword; “You are my servant”.
v. 4: the Servant’s discouragement and his trust.
vv. 5–6: God’s answer: the mission grows to the end of the earth.
kw: A polished arrow is kept hidden in the quiver until the moment it is needed. Long hiddenness is part of the Servant’s preparation, as it was in the thirty years at Nazareth.

In v. 4 the Servant says he has spent his strength for tōhû, the word used for the formless earth in Genesis 1:2. The word beside it, hebel, is the “vanity” of Ecclesiastes. He holds nothing back from God about how it feels.
See also 42:6. The Latin form of this phrase gives the Second Vatican Council’s Constitution on the Church its opening words, Lumen gentium, and the Council says at once that the light is Christ.
vv: The Lord called me before I was born, while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
St Paul describes his own call in these words (Galatians 1:15; compare Jeremiah 1:5). A vocation begins earlier than any human decision.
“You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”

“Israel” stands in nearly all manuscripts, yet in vv. 5–6 this servant has a mission to Israel. Here is the song’s riddle: the Servant both embodies the people and serves them. Christians see it resolved in Jesus, the faithful Israelite who gathers Israel and the nations. The people of Israel remain God’s own, whose gifts and calling are not withdrawn (Romans 11:29).
I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
God answers a complaint of failure not by making the work smaller but by making it larger.
ch: Old Simeon, holding the child, calls him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). Paul and Barnabas take 49:6 as their own charter in Antioch of Pisidia (Acts 13:47). So the song belongs first to Christ, and then to those who share his mission. The Catechism lists it among the Songs that proclaim the meaning of the Passion (CCC 713). Those who feel their work has come to nothing can pray v. 4 honestly, including its second half: “yet surely my cause is with the Lord”.

r.h: And it was night
set: We are at the supper, after the washing of the feet (13:1–20). John’s reader already knows the devil’s work in Judas (13:2). The Mass reading passes over vv. 34–35, the new commandment. The verses left in show three disciples around Jesus: the one who betrays, the one who rests close to him, and the one who boasts and will fall.
str: vv. 21–26: “One of you will betray me”; the disciple Jesus loved asks who; the piece of bread.
vv. 27–30: Satan enters; Judas goes out; night.
vv. 31–33: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”; “Little children”.
vv. 36–38: Peter’s promise and the warning about the cock.
kw: The same verb is used at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33) and when his hour comes near (12:27). The Jesus who goes so firmly to death in John is not untouched by what is coming. Betrayal by a friend hurts him.
A morsel dipped in the shared dish. Many commentators think that to be offered it by the host was a mark of friendship. If so, the last thing Jesus does for Judas is to hold out his hand to him.
In John the glory of Jesus is not reached after the cross as though it were a mere reward. The cross is itself the place where God’s love is shown in full, and so where he is glorified.
vv: the one whom Jesus loved…was reclining next to him;

Greek has “on the bosom of Jesus”, the word used of the Son who is “close to the Father’s heart” (1:18). As the Son rests in the Father, so this disciple rests in the Son. The Gospel does not name him; ancient tradition sees him as John the son of Zebedee, while some modern scholars keep the question open.
So, after receiving the piece of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.

A time of day and a state of soul. Jesus has said that whoever walks at night stumbles (11:10). St Augustine remarks that Judas was not harmed by something evil in the bread: he took a good thing badly (in substance).
“Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”

Peter uses the very words of the Good Shepherd (10:11). He means them sincerely, but he has the order reversed: Jesus lays down his life for Peter first. After the Resurrection Peter will be called three times to love and will truly follow (21:15–19).
ch: The Church reads the two failures of this night together. Judas and Peter both fail their Lord. The difference shows itself after the fall, in Peter’s return. No one should say of any person that he is beyond mercy. The words “It was night” are followed at once by “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”: the darkest deed of the week is taken up into the plan of love.

qa: If Jesus foretold the betrayal, did Judas have any choice?

Yes. To know beforehand is not to force. The Catechism says that God sees all moments of time in his eternal present, so his plan includes each person’s response, and he permits the acts that flow from human blindness in order to bring about his plan of salvation (CCC 600). Judas acted, and answered for it.
study: Where have I felt, like the Servant, that I “labored in vain”? Can I also say the second half of his verse?
Where am I closest to Peter this week, promising much out of love but relying on my own strength?

lead: In English tradition this day has long been called Spy Wednesday, for the Gospel in which Judas goes to the chief priests. Isaiah’s Servant and Matthew’s Judas stand as opposites. The Servant’s ear is opened every morning, and he turns neither back nor aside. Judas hears the same Teacher every day, and looks for his opportunity. Psalm 69, which the New Testament often quotes of the Passion, prays between them: “Insults have broken my heart”.

r.h: Morning by morning
set: This is the third Servant Song. The word “servant” does not appear in the song itself but in the verse just after it (50:10). Here for the first time we hear plainly of suffering. The speaker is a disciple who is beaten for what he has been given to say, yet he remains sure of God’s help. Part of this reading was also heard on Palm Sunday, as the first reading before the Passion. Today we hear it as far as the question “who will declare me guilty?”
str: vv. 4–5a: the disciple’s tongue and ear.
vv. 5b–6: he does not resist: back, cheeks, face.
vv. 7–9a: God helps him; he faces his accusers as if in court.
kw: The Hebrew word comes twice in v. 4. A teacher is first of all one who is taught: the word that comforts comes from an ear that has listened.
The Hebrew repeats the word. This is not one great vision but a daily schooling, the prayer of an ordinary morning repeated.

One of the hardest stones of the region. “I have set my face like flint” is not hardness toward others, but a firmness that does not turn back. Luke says that Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51).
vv: The Lord God has given me the tongue of a teacher, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word.
The purpose of this gift is the tired person in front of us.
I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.

To pull out a man’s beard was a deep humiliation in that world. The Gospels recall the blows and the spitting at the trial of Jesus (Matthew 26:67; 27:30). The verbs are active: he gave his back. Suffering is not simply something that befalls him.
he who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?
St Paul takes up the language of this courtroom in Romans 8:33–34: “It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?”
ch: The Church reads this song of Christ, of whom Peter writes, “When he was abused, he did not return abuse” (1 Peter 2:23), and the Catechism counts it among the Songs that proclaim the meaning of his Passion (CCC 713). Anyone who teaches the faith can make v. 4 a morning prayer. It gives the order of a Christian day: first to listen, then to speak.

r.h: Surely not I?
set: Matthew has just told of the woman who anointed Jesus at Bethany (26:6–13), and now he sets another disciple’s act beside it. She gives away something costly for him. Judas asks what he can get for him. The scene then moves to the preparation for the Passover and the meal itself.
str: vv. 14–16: Judas and the chief priests.
vv. 17–19: the Passover is prepared.
vv. 20–25: at table: “one of you will betray me”.
kw: The key verb of the Passion, here in vv. 15, 16, 21, 23, 24 and 25. It can also mean simply to hand over. People hand Jesus over; yet behind them, as Paul says, God “gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32, the same verb).

Only Matthew gives the sum. It recalls the price for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the shepherd’s insulting wage in Zechariah 11:12–13, which Matthew takes up in 27:9–10. A small price for such a man.

The word means a set, decisive time. The disciples are told to say it to a stranger in the city. Judas is watching for an opportunity (v. 16, eukairia, from the same root), but the true time belongs to Jesus.
vv: “What will you give me if I betray him to you?”

Only Matthew has Judas ask this, which fits the charge of greed in John 12:6. Why he really did it the Gospels do not fully explain. This passage names some of the chief priests, not the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
And they became greatly distressed and began to say to him one after another, “Surely not I, Lord?”
The Greek form expects the answer “no”, yet they ask, and none is sure of himself. It is a healthy fear.
Judas, who betrayed him, said, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” He replied, “You have said so.”
The others say “Lord”; Judas says “Rabbi”, a title Jesus had told his disciples not to claim (23:8). The answer leaves the responsibility with the one who asks. Even now, there is still time.
ch: The Church has never taught that God made Judas betray: God “predestines no one to go to hell” (CCC 1037). Verse 24 joins two truths: “as it is written” means that God’s plan is not defeated, and “woe” means that the human act remains guilty. The Mass, too, is set in this story: Paul begins his account of it with “on the night when he was betrayed” (1 Corinthians 11:23). We approach the table knowing that we might be the one who asks, “Surely not I?”

qa: Does “better not to have been born” mean that Judas is in hell?

The words are a grave warning, and Christian writers have often been severe about Judas. But the Church has never declared of any named person that he is lost, and she leaves the judgment to God. What we must take from the verse is the seriousness of sin, and our own need of mercy.
study: What is my “morning by morning”? When and how does God open my ear each day?
Judas asked, “What will you give me?” Where in my life am I tempted to set a price on my fidelity?

lead: With this evening Mass Lent ends and the Paschal Triduum begins. The Church hears three readings about one night. In Exodus a family eats a lamb with sandals on, and the blood on the door is its protection. In Corinthians, the oldest written account of the Eucharist, Jesus takes bread and a cup on the night of his betrayal. In John he takes a towel and a basin, and John’s account of the supper does not describe the bread and the cup at all, for he has placed the meaning of the night in the washing of feet.
Psalm 116 joins them: “I will lift up the cup of salvation”. Passover, Eucharist and service are one mystery. The key words are memorial, covenant and to the end.

r.h: This day shall be a day of remembrance
set: Nine plagues have not moved Pharaoh. Before the last and most terrible, God gives Israel not a battle plan but a meal. The law of Passover is set into the story itself, so that every later generation that keeps it will find itself inside that night. The reading leaves out vv. 9–10, on how the lamb is cooked and what is done with any that remains.

Many scholars think that behind this feast lie an older shepherds’ spring rite and a farmers’ feast of unleavened bread, which Israel joined and filled with the memory of the Exodus. Whatever its earlier history, the text’s own claim is clear: this meal belongs to what God did.
str: vv. 1–2: a new beginning for the calendar.
vv. 3–8: the lamb: chosen, kept, slaughtered; blood on the door; the meal.
v. 11: how to eat it: dressed to leave.
vv. 12–13: what God will do that night.
v. 14: the command to keep it forever.
kw: The verb pāsaḥ is usually understood as “pass over”. In Isaiah 31:5 the same verb stands beside “protect” and “deliver”, and so it may also carry the sense of standing guard over. The exact origin of the word is debated. God does not simply avoid these houses: he shields them.

More than a mental recollection. In the Bible, to keep a memorial is to bring the saving act before God and before the people, so that it touches those who celebrate it. A later Jewish teaching in the Mishnah (Pesahim 10:5) says that in every generation each person must regard himself as having come out of Egypt.
Śeh covers both sheep and goats (v. 5). Tāmîm means whole, complete. The New Testament applies this language to Christ: “like that of a lamb without defect or blemish” (1 Peter 1:19).
vv: they are to take a lamb for each family, a lamb for each household.
The first Passover is celebrated at home. Salvation comes to Israel as a people, and to each household within it.
They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel
Blood is life in biblical thought (Leviticus 17:11). Here it marks a house as belonging to God. The Church has heard in these verses the protection of the blood of Christ.
your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly.

People who eat like this are travellers. The word for “hurriedly” (ḥippāzôn) comes to mark the Exodus itself. The Eucharist too is food for those on the way, and we call the last Communion of a dying person Viaticum, food for the journey.
when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you
Note who sees: God does. The sign is for them, as the verse says, and God keeps his word to those who trust it.
This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.
The feast is still kept by the Jewish people today, for whom it remains a living gift from God.
ch: St Paul writes: “our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). St Melito of Sardis, in a second-century Paschal homily, reads the whole night as a figure of Christ, the true lamb (in substance). The Catechism teaches that by celebrating the Last Supper in the course of the Passover meal, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340). It also takes the biblical idea of memorial as the key to the Mass: the saving event is made present (CCC 1363–1364). God’s covenant with Israel has not been revoked (CCC 121), and the Christian reading of this night honours it as the root from which we draw.

r.h: I received from the Lord what I also handed on
set: Paul writes to Corinth from Ephesus (16:8), around the middle of the fifties. So this is the oldest written account of the Lord’s Supper that we have, earlier than any of the Gospels. And Paul was not the first to say it, because he is passing on a tradition he had already handed on when he founded the church there.

He quotes it to correct a scandal. In Corinth, the rich were eating well at the assembly while the poor went hungry (11:17–22). A Eucharist that despises the poor, he says, is not really the Lord’s Supper (11:20). The warning to those who eat unworthily follows straight after our reading (11:27–29).
str: v. 23a: Paul’s claim: received and handed on.
vv. 23b–24: the bread.
v. 25: the cup.
v. 26: what the celebration does: it proclaims until he comes.
kw: to hand on, to hand over

The same verb is used twice in v. 23: Paul “handed on” the tradition, and Jesus “was betrayed” (handed over). In the night when one disciple handed him over, Jesus handed himself over, and so the Church hands on this gift.
The participle from which the word “Eucharist” comes. At the centre of the Mass stands a great thanksgiving to the Father, on the pattern of the Jewish blessing at table.

It comes twice (vv. 24–25). The Greek of the Old Testament also uses it for memorials offered before God. Linked to Exodus 12:14, it does not mean “think about me sometimes”. The Church understands it as a memorial in which Christ’s sacrifice is made present (CCC 1362–1366).
A word used for announcing the gospel. The rite itself preaches. Every Mass announces the Lord’s death, as an event that gives life and looks to his coming.
vv: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you,
Paul uses the terms of Jewish teaching for handing on a tradition. He means that this comes from Jesus, and that he has not invented it.
“This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

A note on the text. Some later manuscripts add “broken” to “for you”; the oldest do not. The Council of Trent teaches that with “Do this” Christ made the apostles priests of the New Covenant (Session 22, canon 2; CCC 611).
“This cup is the new covenant in my blood.
“Covenant in blood” recalls Sinai (Exodus 24:8). “New covenant” is the promise of Jeremiah 31:31. Before his death Jesus interprets it as the sealing of God’s covenant.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

The Mass faces two ways: back to the cross and forward to the return. In the Roman Mass the people answer in similar words after the consecration: “We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again.”
ch: St John Paul II opened his last encyclical with the words “The Church draws her life from the Eucharist” (Ecclesia de Eucharistia 1), and he dated it on a Holy Thursday. The Second Vatican Council describes the Mass as the memorial of Christ’s death and resurrection, a sacrament of love, a sign of unity, a bond of charity (Sacrosanctum Concilium 47). The Catechism gathers this teaching: the Eucharist is a sacrifice because it makes present the sacrifice of the cross (CCC 1366), and the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1367).

r.h: He loved them to the end
set: With 13:1 the Gospel of John turns. Up to now, his “hour” has been coming. Now it has come. John tells of the last evening at great length (chapters 13–17), and in that account there is no word over bread and cup. The Bread of Life discourse (chapter 6) has already given the teaching. What he gives us here is the same love, shown with a basin.
Washing feet was a service of hospitality on dusty roads, usually done by a servant, and a disciple might do it for a teacher. It was not the custom for a teacher to do it for his disciples.
str: vv. 1–3: the solemn opening: what Jesus knows.
vv. 4–5: the action, told verb by verb.
vv. 6–11: Peter’s objection, and “Not all of you are clean”.
vv. 12–15: the explanation: “an example”.
kw: This means both “to the last moment” and “to the uttermost”. The verb from the same root comes from the cross in 19:30: “It is finished”. The whole Passion is contained in this phrase.

In v. 4 Jesus “takes off” his robe with the verb he used for laying down his life in 10:17–18. In v. 12 he “puts on” with the verb used for taking it up again. Many commentators think John means us to see the whole mystery of death and resurrection in the action.
“You have no share with me” (v. 8). The word can be used of a share in an inheritance. Being washed is not a minor courtesy: it is how one comes to belong to him.
More than a good illustration. In 2 Maccabees 6:28 the same word describes the noble death of the old man Eleazar, and so here it may include the death to which the washing points.
vv: Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
John has used the verb “to love” sparingly up to now; in chapters 13–17 it comes far more often. CCC 1337 and 616 begin from this verse: it is love that gives the sacrifice its worth.
got up from the table, took off his outer robe, and tied a towel around himself.

Compare Philippians 2:6–8: “emptied himself, taking the form of a slave”. John shows in an action what that hymn sings. Note v. 3: he does this knowing the Father has given all things into his hands. His humility does not forget who he is.
“Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.”
Peter’s refusal seems humble, but in fact he wants to decide how he will be loved. Receiving is the first thing a disciple must learn.
“One who has bathed does not need to wash, except for the feet, but is entirely clean.

A note on the text. “Except for the feet” is lacking in some important witnesses, and scholars disagree about whether it is original. St Augustine reads it as baptism, which is once, and the daily need for forgiveness of sins (in substance).
So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

Judas too has had his feet washed: see v. 11. Whatever “one another” means, it does not exclude the one who will wound us. St Augustine says that Christians wash one another’s feet whenever they forgive and bear with each other (in substance).
ch: The Church has kept this command in the most literal way in the rite called the Mandatum. The word comes from “a new commandment” (mandatum novum, 13:34). The Catechism places it beside the institution of the Eucharist: he washed their feet and gave them the commandment of love, then left a pledge of that love (CCC 1337). The altar and the basin belong together. To share in the Mass and refuse to serve would contradict what we celebrate, as Paul told the Corinthians. Christian priesthood takes its form from this night: the one who stands at the altar in the person of Christ is one who has been told to kneel.

qa: Did Jesus really mean “This is my body”, or only a symbol?

The Church believes he meant what he said. Paul, in the same chapter, says that one who eats unworthily “will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord” (11:27), which would make no sense if it were a mere sign. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ is truly, really and substantially present, and that the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into his Body and Blood, which is named transubstantiation (Council of Trent; CCC 1374, 1376).
Is every Mass a new sacrifice of Christ?

No. Christ died once for all (Hebrews 9:26–28). The Mass does not repeat the cross or add to it. It makes that one sacrifice present, offered now in an unbloody manner, with the same priest and the same victim (CCC 1366–1367).
Did Jesus wash the feet of Judas?

The text does not make an exception. Verses 10–11 say that “not all of you are clean” and that he knew who would betray him, and Judas leaves only later (13:30). So John’s account implies that Judas’s feet were washed too, in the same way.
rite: In the Roman Rite this Mass is the door of the Triduum: the Universal Norms on the Liturgical Year say that the Triduum begins with it, and that Lent ends before it. Priests in many places have already gathered around their bishop at the Chrism Mass, which may be held in the morning or on an earlier day. The Gloria is sung with bells, which then fall silent until the Vigil. After the homily there may be the washing of feet; since 2016, those chosen may be drawn from all the people of God. During the procession of gifts, gifts for the poor may be brought, and Ubi caritas may be sung, which says that where true charity is, God is there. After Communion the Blessed Sacrament is carried to a place of repose, with the Pange lingua traditionally ascribed to St Thomas Aquinas, and the faithful stay in adoration. The altar is then stripped. There is no dismissal: the liturgy continues tomorrow.
This year 25 March falls on Holy Thursday. The Solemnity of the Annunciation therefore gives way, and is kept after the Octave of Easter.
study: In Exodus the people eat ready to leave. What am I still too settled in to leave behind, as I come to the Lord’s table?
Paul says the Corinthians’ divisions made their supper “not really” the Lord’s Supper. What does this say of my parish’s care for its poor?
Peter finds it hard to let Jesus wash him. Where do I find it hard to receive, from God or from others?
Whose feet, in practice, is the Lord asking me to wash this Easter?

lead: On this day, when no Mass is celebrated, the Church simply listens, and then kneels before the cross. Isaiah’s fourth Servant Song speaks centuries in advance of one who bears the sins of many, and it is told by people who are astonished to find that he suffered for them. Hebrews looks inside that suffering, and sees a high priest with loud cries and tears, who can feel our weakness. John tells the Passion itself, and in his telling the prisoner is a king, who goes to his death knowing what he does and hands over his spirit at the end.

Psalm 31 gives us the words from the cross recorded by Luke: “Into your hand I commit my spirit”. The readings together answer the question of the day: what is this death? The key words are bore, obedience and finished.

r.h: He bore the sin of many
set: This is the fourth and greatest Servant Song, from the exile in Babylon, in the sixth century before Christ. Its form is unusual. God speaks at the start and at the end. In between, a shocked “we” confesses: we thought he was being punished by God, and we were wrong. The Servant himself never speaks a word, and the song says so twice (53:7).

Who was he? The text does not say, and the Ethiopian official asks the same in Acts 8:34. Jewish interpreters have often understood the Servant as the people of Israel, who suffered so much among the nations, and others have looked to a prophet or a righteous figure. Christians confess that the song finds its full meaning in Jesus. The Church can respect the Jewish reading while proclaiming her own faith.
str: 52:13–15: God speaks: the Servant will be lifted up; nations and kings are astonished.
53:1–3: “we” confess: no beauty, despised, rejected.
53:4–6: the turning point: it was our sins he bore.
53:7–9: silent like a lamb; unjust death and burial.
53:10–12: God’s plan: the offering, the offspring, the victory.
kw: The verb comes in v. 4 (“borne our infirmities”) and v. 12 (“he bore the sin of many”). The same verb is used of the scapegoat, which bears the people’s iniquities (Leviticus 16:22). Here a person takes this on, willingly.
The word in v. 10 is the name of a sacrifice of reparation, for wrongs that must be put right (Leviticus 5). What is offered here is the Servant’s own life, which is a striking thought.
“By his bruises we are healed” (v. 5). It is the mark left by a blow. 1 Peter 2:24 takes the phrase up and applies it to Christ.

The word occurs throughout the song (52:14, 15; 53:11, 12). In biblical speech “many” can have the sense of a great multitude, not of a limit set on God’s will to save. Jesus takes it up: “a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
vv: See, my servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
The song begins from the end. Before we hear of the wounds, God tells us the outcome. John’s “lifted up” (3:14; 12:32) uses this language: the cross is already an exaltation.
He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity;
Nothing in him drew the eye. This lets anyone rejected or disfigured know that God has been there before them.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.

The verse at the centre of the poem. “Made us whole” renders shālôm. The Church teaches that Christ’s death is a true expiation for sin, and that its source is love: in giving up his Son for our sins, God “manifests that his plan for us is one of benevolent love” (CCC 604).
like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.

These are the very words the Ethiopian was reading when Philip met him, and Philip began from them to tell him about Jesus (Acts 8:32–35). The silence of Jesus before Pilate (John 19:9) fits this verse.
Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him with pain.

A hard verse, and the Hebrew in vv. 10–11 is difficult. It does not say that God took pleasure in cruelty. It says that even this was not outside his plan, which is to bring life out of it, as the rest of the verse shows: “he shall see his offspring”. See CCC 599–600.
Out of his anguish he shall see light;

A note on the text. “Light” is missing from the traditional Hebrew text, but is found in the Greek and in the Isaiah scrolls from Qumran, and the NRSV follows these. It is one of the places where the Dead Sea Scrolls have helped translators. The song’s hope reaches beyond death.
yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
Compare Luke 23:34: “Father, forgive them”. At the Last Supper Jesus applies this verse to himself (Luke 22:37).
ch: No Old Testament passage is more present in the New Testament’s account of the Passion: see Matthew 8:17, Luke 22:37, Acts 8:32–35, Romans 4:25 and 1 Peter 2:22–25. St Jerome says that Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet (in substance). The Catechism teaches that the Scriptures foretold this plan through the death of “the righteous one, my Servant” (CCC 601), and that by his obedience unto death Jesus accomplished the substitution of the suffering Servant (CCC 615). It adds that this was a mystery of universal redemption, and that there is not, never has been and never will be a single human being for whom Christ did not suffer (CCC 605).

r.h: Loud cries and tears
set: The author of Hebrews is not named. Origen’s remark that God alone knows who wrote it has often been repeated, and the letter’s elegant Greek is unlike Paul’s. It seems to address Christians tempted to tire and drift away. Its great theme is that Jesus is the high priest. The two pieces chosen today show how he is qualified: he has come all the way down to us, and he has passed through to the Father.
str: 4:14: we have a great high priest: so hold fast.
4:15: he can feel with us: tested, without sin.
4:16: so approach with boldness.
5:7–9: his prayer, his obedience, his being made perfect, our salvation.
kw: Literally “to suffer with”. This is no distant pity. The priest who stands for us has felt what we feel.

The right of a citizen to speak openly. Hebrews recalls that only the high priest entered the inner sanctuary, once a year (9:7). Now all are told: come close to the throne, since it is a throne of grace.
he learned through what he suffered

A play on words in Greek, and an old Greek saying said much the same of human experience. Here it does not mean he was first disobedient. The eternal Son, in his human nature, entered into obedience from within, at its most costly.

Not moral improvement, as if he had been lacking. In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used for the consecration of priests (Exodus 29:9), so it includes his being installed as our high priest, through his death and exaltation.
vv: but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin.
He is one with us in everything except sin (Council of Chalcedon; CCC 467, 540). Sinlessness does not make his testing lighter. One who never gives way feels the full weight of the pull.
Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness,
On this day the Church does this literally, walking up to kiss the wood of the cross.
with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.

Hebrews may be thinking of Gethsemane, though it does not name it. He prayed to be saved from death, and he died. How then “was he heard”? He was brought out of death, in the Resurrection. The Catechism says that all the troubles of humanity are summed up in this cry, and that the Father answers it beyond all hope by raising his Son (CCC 2606).
Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered;
“How much more reason have we sinful creatures to learn obedience”, the Catechism says on this verse (CCC 2825).
ch: This reading guards the Church against two errors: a Christ who did not really suffer, and a Christ who is only a suffering man. Here he is the Son and he is in tears. Hebrews’ later teaching that he offered himself once for all (9:26–28) is why there is no other priesthood apart from his. The priests of the Church share in it, and his one sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist (CCC 1545). Today the Church does what this text encourages, and asks for mercy, and for grace in time of need.

r.h: It is finished
set: In the Roman Rite the Passion according to John is read every Good Friday. John knows the same events as the other evangelists, but he tells them from another height. He does not tell of the prayer of agony or the cry of being forsaken. Jesus comes forward to meet his captors, he carries the cross by himself (19:17), and he bows his head only when all is finished. This does not deny the pain. It shows the love that goes through it with open eyes.

Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea (about AD 26–36), and crucifixion was a Roman punishment. Caiaphas was high priest at this time, and Annas was his father-in-law, a former high priest of great influence. John says “the Jews” often in this Passion. Most of the time he plainly means the Temple authorities and those around them. Many scholars think that the word also carries the pain of later quarrels between John’s community and the synagogue. It must never be heard as a charge against the Jewish people, then or now (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Jesus, his mother and his first disciples were Jews, and John himself quotes Jesus: “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22).
str: 18:1–11: the garden: “I am he”.
18:12–27: Annas questions Jesus; Peter denies him at the fire.
18:28–19:16: before Pilate, in scenes that alternate outside and inside: seven movements, with the crowning at the centre (19:1–3).
19:17–30: Golgotha: the title, the tunic, the mother, the thirst, “It is finished”.
19:31–42: the pierced side and the burial in a garden.
kw: A simple “It is I”, but in Greek also the words God uses of himself (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10). That is why those who come to arrest him step back and fall. He is arrested only because he lets it happen (10:18).

The word runs through the trial before Pilate: “Are you the King?”, the purple, “Hail, King”, “Here is your King”, the title on the cross. John’s irony: everyone mocks a truth they do not know they are saying. The hundred pounds of spices at the burial also suit a king.
From telos, the end or goal: not “it is over”, but “it has been brought to completion”. It answers 13:1, “he loved them to the end”, and the Father’s work given to him (4:34; 17:4).

An unusual way to say “he died”. It can simply mean his last breath. Some commentators hear more: the Spirit promised for the hour of his glory (7:39) is given over from the cross, to his mother and the disciple standing below.
vv: When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they stepped back and fell to the ground.
They came with lanterns and torches to find the light of the world (8:12).
“Am I not to drink the cup that the Father has given me?”
Here John’s Passion echoes the prayer in the garden told by the other Gospels. The cup comes from the Father’s hand, and so he takes it (CCC 607).
Now the slaves and the police had made a charcoal fire because it was cold,

The Greek word for charcoal fire is found in only one other place in the New Testament: at the lakeside, where the Risen Lord will ask Peter three times, “Do you love me?” (21:9). Three denials at one such fire; three professions of love at another.
“You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.”

The prisoner has become the judge. The next verse has Pilate’s question, “What is truth?”, spoken to the Truth himself (14:6). The Creed names “Pontius Pilate” so that we remember this happened at one real place and time.
Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!”

Ecce homo in the Latin. Pilate perhaps means, “Look at this poor figure.” John means more: this is what humanity looks like when it loves to the end. The verse also recalls the “man of suffering” of Isaiah 53:3.
The chief priests answered, “We have no king but the emperor.”

These are the words of the chief priests at a moment of pressure, and they are the dramatic high point of the trial. They do not speak for the Jewish people, whose prayers have always called God their King.
It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”
In Latin this gives the letters INRI on our crucifixes. Written in three languages (19:20), it announces more than Pilate intends: in a sense, the first proclamation of the king to that whole world.
now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top.
St Cyprian sees in this undivided robe the unity of the Church, which must not be torn (in substance). Some also recall the high priest’s seamless robe described by Josephus.
“Woman, here is your son.”

He called her “Woman” at Cana too (2:4), when his hour had not yet come. It has come now. The Church sees more here than a son’s care for his mother: the Second Vatican Council and St John Paul II read this as the gift of Mary as mother to the disciple, and so to the Church (Lumen Gentium 58; Redemptoris Mater 23; CCC 964).
“It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
He bows his head first, and then dies. In a Gospel where no one takes his life from him (10:18), even this is an action.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

John insists that an eyewitness saw it (19:35). St John Chrysostom sees water for Baptism and blood for the Eucharist, and the Church formed from Christ’s side as Eve from the side of Adam (in substance; the Liturgy of the Hours gives this passage on Good Friday). The Second Vatican Council and the Catechism make the same reading their own (Sacrosanctum Concilium 5; CCC 766, 1225).
Now there was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden there was a new tomb in which no one had ever been laid.

The Passion begins and ends in a garden. Only John tells us so. Many readers recall Eden, and the Risen Lord will be taken for a gardener (20:15). Joseph, a secret disciple, and Nicodemus, who first came by night, step into the open when it can gain them nothing.
ch: The Catechism draws together the meaning of this death: it is love “to the end” that gives Christ’s sacrifice its value as redemption and reparation (CCC 616); this is the one sacrifice that completes and surpasses all others (CCC 613–614); and the Council of Trent teaches that by his most holy Passion on the wood of the cross he merited justification for us (CCC 617). Jesus knew and loved each of us in his Passion (CCC 478). St Augustine says that the cross became a teacher’s chair, from which he taught us how to love (in substance). So Good Friday is not a funeral, for those who kneel before the cross already know how the story continues. It is the hour of the victory of love, even if today we keep silent before the price.

qa: Who was responsible for the death of Jesus?

The personal guilt of those involved is known to God alone. Pilate condemned him, Roman soldiers crucified him, and some of the authorities pressed for it. “The one who handed me over” (19:11) may mean Judas or Caiaphas; interpreters differ. The Church teaches firmly that neither all Jews of that time nor Jews today can be charged with what was done in his Passion (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). She teaches something harder for us: sinners were the authors of his sufferings, and so Christians must not lay on others what belongs to their own sins (CCC 598).
Did the Father want his Son to suffer?

The Father does not take delight in pain. He sent his Son in love (John 3:16), and the Son went in love and obedience (John 10:17–18). In a world of sin, love that goes to the end meets the cross. His death is a true sacrifice of expiation for our sins. Human beings did what they did, and God permitted it and brought salvation from it (CCC 599–600, 604–606).
Did he die on Passover day or the day before?

Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), which puts his death on the feast. John places his death on the Day of Preparation (18:28; 19:14, 31), around the time the lambs were killed for the feast, and so links him to the Lamb of God (1:29). Scholars have proposed several solutions, and none is agreed. Pope Benedict XVI, in his book Jesus of Nazareth, inclined to John’s dating. All the Gospels agree that he died on a Friday, on the eve of a Sabbath, at Passover time, and all see his death in the light of Passover.
rite: There is no Mass in the Roman Rite today. The Church keeps the Celebration of the Passion of the Lord, usually about three in the afternoon. The priest, in red, enters in silence and prostrates himself or kneels before the bare altar. Then come the Liturgy of the Word, the Solemn Intercessions, the Adoration of the Cross and Holy Communion from the hosts consecrated yesterday. In the Intercessions the Church prays for the whole world, and also for the Jewish people, to whom God spoke first, that they may grow in love of his name and faithfulness to his covenant. At the Adoration the cross is shown with the words “Behold the wood of the Cross”, and the people come forward to venerate it. It is a day of fasting and abstinence (Code of Canon Law, canon 1251). In many places, the day’s collection helps the Christians of the Holy Land, and the Way of the Cross is prayed. Everyone leaves in silence, for there is no dismissal.
study: Read Isaiah 53:4–6 with “I” and “my” in place of “we” and “our”. What changes?
Hebrews says he can “sympathize with our weaknesses”. What weakness of mine have I not yet brought to the throne of grace?
In John, the disciple takes the Mother of Jesus into his home. What would that mean for my home?
The Passion moves from Peter’s denial to Joseph’s and Nicodemus’s courage. Where is the Lord calling me out of being a secret disciple?

lead: This is the longest Liturgy of the Word in the Roman year, and it is built as one story told in the dark, by the light of the paschal candle. Seven readings from the Old Testament walk through the history of salvation: creation, Abraham and Isaac, the crossing of the sea, then the promises of the prophets. At least three are read (in serious circumstances at least two), and the reading from Exodus 14 is never left out. After each one the people answer with a psalm or canticle: Psalm 104 or 33 on creation, Psalm 16 on trust beyond death, the Song of the Sea, Psalm 30, the song of Isaiah 12, Psalm 19 on the law, and Psalms 42 and 43 (or Isaiah 12, or Psalm 51) on thirst for God.

Then the Gloria is sung and the bells ring. Paul tells us what all this has to do with us: in baptism we went down into Christ's death and came up into his life. The priest intones the Alleluia, unheard since before Lent, and Psalm 118 answers it. Finally Mark sends the women to an open tomb. The key words of the night are light, water and new. Everything God did in the Scriptures is now seen from the morning of the Resurrection, and those to be baptized tonight step into the same story.

r.h: God saw everything, and it was very good
set: The Vigil begins where the Bible begins. Many scholars think that this first account of creation reached its final form among the priests of Israel around the time of the exile in Babylon, when people lived among temples to the sun, moon and stars. Its language is calm and solemn. It does not argue with those gods. It simply says that the great lights are lamps which God has hung in the sky, and it does not even give them the names of sun and moon.
str: 1:1–2: the beginning: a formless void, darkness, and the wind from God over the waters.
1:3–13: days one to three: God separates light from dark, waters from sky, sea from land.
1:14–31: days four to six: God fills these spaces with lights, fish and birds, animals and, last, human beings.
2:1–2: the seventh day: God finishes his work and rests.
¶ The two halves match: what is made in the first three days is filled in the next three. The refrain “and God saw that it was good” builds up to “very good” at the end.
kw: In the Old Testament the subject of this verb is always God. It is the word for what only God can do. The clear teaching of creation out of nothing comes later (2 Maccabees 7:28), and the Church finds it in harmony with this chapter.

Rûaḥ means both wind and spirit, so the NRSV has “a wind from God”, while the Malayalam POC speaks of God's spirit. The Church's blessing of baptismal water tonight recalls this Spirit moving over the waters.
In the ancient world a king set up his image to show who ruled the land. Here every human being, man and woman, is God's image in the world, and this is said of all people, not only of a king.
vv: Then God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light.

God creates by speaking. The Vigil has just begun with the new fire and the candle, and the deacon has sung “The Light of Christ” in a dark church. The first word of God and the first sign of Easter meet.
So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
This is the root of the dignity of every person. Nobody earns it and nobody can take it away.
God saw everything that he had made, and indeed, it was very good.
Sin has not yet appeared, and the world is good from God's own hand. Easter does not rescue us out of creation. It heals creation and begins it again.
And on the seventh day God finished the work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done.
Christ rested in the tomb on the seventh day, and on the day after the Sabbath he rose. So the Fathers call Sunday the eighth day.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture presents the Creator's work symbolically as a succession of six days (CCC 337), and that the seventh day completes the first creation while the eighth day, the day of the Resurrection, begins the new creation (CCC 349). Its treatment of baptism begins with this water over which the Spirit moved (CCC 1218). The prayer of the Roman Missal after this reading says, in substance, that nothing is more marvellous than the creation of the world except that, at the end of the ages, Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Creation is great. Redemption is greater.

r.h: God himself will provide the lamb
set: God had promised Abraham countless descendants through Isaac, the son of his old age. Now God seems to ask for that promise back. The chapter is one of the most carefully told stories in Genesis. Jewish tradition calls it the Aqedah, the Binding of Isaac, and holds it in deep honour. The second book of Chronicles (3:1) identifies Mount Moriah with the hill on which Solomon built the Temple.
str: vv. 1–2: God's test: “Here I am”, and the command.
vv. 3–8: three days of silent journey; Isaac's one question.
vv. 9–12: the altar, the knife, and the angel's call.
vv. 13–14: the ram, and the name of the place.
vv. 15–18: God swears by himself: blessing for all the nations.
kw: The narrator tells us at the start that this is a test. It is a test of Abraham's trust, and the reader is told so that the story will not be misread as God's wish for a child's death.
The word is repeated (vv. 2, 12, 16). The Greek Old Testament renders it agapētos, “beloved”, the very word the Father uses of Jesus at his baptism (Mark 1:11).
Literally “the Lord will see”. To see to a need is to provide for it. The Malayalam POC keeps the Hebrew name of the place.
vv: He said, “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,
The phrases come slowly, one after another, and each is heavier than the one before. The story knows what it is asking.
“The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
The only question Isaac asks. It is the question of the whole Old Testament, and John the Baptist answers it: “Here is the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).
Abraham said, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So the two of them walked on together.
Abraham does not explain, and he does not lie. His answer is pure hope. The phrase “the two of them walked on together” occurs twice (vv. 6, 8), and it is one of the most moving lines in the Bible.
“Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him;
The story ends with God stopping the knife. The law and the prophets will later condemn child sacrifice outright (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31).
ch: Hebrews 11:17–19 says that Abraham trusted that God could raise even the dead, and that “figuratively speaking” he received Isaac back. St Paul seems to echo this chapter when he speaks of God “who did not withhold his own Son” (Romans 8:32). The Catechism sees here the final purification of Abraham's faith, and links it with the Father who did not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). Origen, preaching on Genesis, sees in Isaac carrying the wood a figure of Christ carrying his Cross (in substance). What Abraham was spared, the Father gave. The Roman Canon still names “the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith”.

r.h: The Israelites walked on dry ground through the sea
set: This is the one reading that may never be omitted, because it is the Passover itself. Israel has left Egypt and is trapped between Pharaoh's chariots and the water. The people have just cried out in fear (14:10–12). The place cannot be fixed with certainty. Elsewhere the Hebrew calls it yam sûp (13:18; 15:4), which may mean “Sea of Reeds”, and the Greek Old Testament made it the Red Sea.
str: vv. 15–18: God's command: go forward, stretch out your hand.
vv. 19–20: the angel and the cloud move behind Israel.
vv. 21–25: the night of wind, the dry ground, the confusion of the chariots.
vv. 26–29: at dawn the waters return.
vv. 30–31: Israel saw, feared and believed.
15:1: the song begins.
kw: The same word as “dry land” in Genesis 1:9. God brings dry land out of the water a second time. The Exodus is told as a new creation.
The strong east wind that drives back the sea (14:21) is the same Hebrew word as the wind over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2).
From the root that also gives us “Amen”: to stand firm on something, to rely on it. The story ends with a people who have learned to trust (14:31).
vv: Then the Lord said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.
The time for standing still is over. Faith here is a step taken toward the water, before the water parts.
The Israelites went into the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.
Death stands on both sides, and a road runs through it. So it is with the Christian: the way to life goes through the waters of death.
So the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses.
The goal of the whole event is not only escape but faith.
“I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
Israel's first song. Its praise is for God who broke the power of an oppressor; it is a slave people's cry that God is stronger than Pharaoh.
ch: St Paul says that our ancestors “were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2). The Catechism names the crossing of the Red Sea as a figure of baptism, the true liberation from slavery (CCC 1221), and St Ambrose teaches the newly baptized the same in his work on the sacraments (in substance). The Exsultet has already sung of it tonight: this is the night when you led our forebears through the sea dry-shod. And the prayer after this reading asks, in substance, that the whole world may become children of Abraham and receive the dignity of Israel. The Church does not take the Exodus away from Israel. She asks to be brought in.

r.h: With everlasting love I will have compassion on you
set: These words belong to the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–55), addressed to the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem lies in ruins and is pictured as a wife who has been sent away and left childless. The chapter follows straight after the song of the suffering servant (52:13–53:12), and it shows what that suffering has opened: a future for the people.
str: vv. 5–6: your Maker is your husband; he calls you back.
vv. 7–8: a brief moment of anger, everlasting love.
vv. 9–10: the oath, as in the days of Noah.
vv. 11–14: the afflicted city rebuilt in precious stones, her children taught by the Lord.
kw: God's faithful, covenant love, which does not stop when the other fails. Verse 8 calls it ḥesed ‘ôlām, everlasting love.
Related to reḥem, the womb. It is the tender feeling a mother has for her child.
The next of kin, whose duty was to buy back a relative from debt or slavery. God takes on himself the duty of family.
vv: For your Maker is your husband, the Lord of hosts is his name;
The image goes back to Hosea and is used by Jeremiah and Ezekiel. God's covenant is not a contract. It is a marriage.
For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.
The prophet does not pretend that the exile did not hurt. But he puts the anger and the love on two different scales: a moment against forever.
This is like the days of Noah to me:
Water appears here too. The flood ended with a promise, and God now makes the same kind of promise to Jerusalem.
For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed,
To the ancient mind nothing was more lasting than the mountains. God's love is more lasting still.
ch: These words were spoken first to Israel, and they remain true for her, for God's gifts and call are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).
