The Catechism teaches that this prophetic image of married love prepared the way for the fuller understanding of marriage in Christ (CCC 1611). The New Testament also speaks of the Church as the bride for whom Christ gave himself (Ephesians 5:25–27; CCC 796). At the Vigil, those who feel abandoned hear that God's anger is the moment and his love the forever.

r.h: Come to the waters
set: This is the closing chapter of the Book of Consolation. The exiles are being invited home. The opening sounds like a street seller in a market, but what is on sale costs nothing, and the invitation also recalls Lady Wisdom calling people to her table (Proverbs 9:5). At the Vigil it is heard above all by those about to be baptized.
str: vv. 1–3: the invitation: water, bread, wine and milk without price; an everlasting covenant.
vv. 4–5: David's role passes to the people, a witness to the nations.
vv. 6–7: seek the Lord; he will abundantly pardon.
vv. 8–9: God's thoughts and ways are higher.
vv. 10–11: the rain and the word.
kw: The covenant love promised to David's house (2 Samuel 7) is here opened out to the whole people. Paul quotes this verse of the Resurrection, in its Greek form (Acts 13:34).
Often the word for going to a holy place to consult God. To seek the Lord is to go to him with one's whole life.
In Hebrew a word is also a deed. God's word does what it says, as it did on the first day of creation.
vv: Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and you that have no money, come, buy and eat!
There is only one condition: to be thirsty. Grace is a gift that cannot be paid for.
let the wicked forsake their way, and the unrighteous their thoughts; let them return to the Lord, that he may have mercy on them, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
Forgiveness is not cheap, for it means turning around. Yet what we meet when we turn is a mercy larger than our sins.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord.
In this setting, the verse is about mercy. God forgives in a way that human beings would not.
so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and succeed in the thing for which I sent it.
The word comes down like rain, does its work and goes back. Christians also hear in this movement the Word who came from the Father and returned to him (John 16:28).
ch: Jesus takes up this call on the last day of the feast of Tabernacles: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (John 7:37), and John adds that he spoke of the Spirit. The Bible closes with the same invitation (Revelation 22:17). The Catechism teaches that water signifies the Holy Spirit's action in baptism (CCC 694). Bread and wine and water without price: the Church hears in this reading the sacraments about to be given tonight.

r.h: Walk toward the shining of her light
set: The Book of Baruch bears the name of the scribe of Jeremiah and is set among the exiles in Babylon. Many scholars think that it was put together later from several pieces. It is one of the deuterocanonical books, preserved in Greek and received by the Catholic Church in her canon (CCC 120). This passage is a poem on wisdom, in the spirit of Job 28 and Sirach 24, written to a people asking why they are in a foreign land.
str: 3:9–13: why are you in exile? You forsook the fountain of wisdom.
3:14–15: learn where wisdom is.
3:32–36: only God knows the way to her, and he gave her to Israel.
3:37: she appeared on earth and lived with humankind.
4:1–4: she is the law; walk in her light; happy are we.
kw: Not cleverness, but knowing how to live in God's world. In the poem she is pictured as a woman whom no one can catch or buy.
The law is not a burden laid on life but the way that leads to it (compare Deuteronomy 30:15–20).
vv: Hear the commandments of life, O Israel; give ear, and learn wisdom!
The opening echoes the great prayer of Israel, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom.
A short verse with the whole diagnosis. The exile did not begin with Babylon's armies. It began when the people left the source.
Afterward she appeared on earth and lived with humankind.

Wisdom came near in the law given to Israel, which is what the poem goes on to say. Many of the Fathers heard in this line also the Word who became flesh and lived among us. Some scholars think the verse is a later addition; the Church's reading is the same either way.
She is the book of the commandments of God, the law that endures forever.
The same step is taken in Sirach 24:23: wisdom is found in the Torah. Israel's love of the law is honoured here, and it is a love Jesus shared (Matthew 5:17–18).
Happy are we, O Israel, for we know what is pleasing to God.
The poem ends in gratitude: the gift of knowing God's will is the people's happiness.
ch: St Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and John's Gospel says that the Word “lived among us” (John 1:14). Christ says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). So the Church reads this poem by the paschal candle and hears it as a call to walk toward the one who is the light. The Church does not read it against the law of Israel. She reads it as one who has received wisdom from Israel's hand.

r.h: A new heart I will give you
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in the deportation of 597 BC. He speaks after the fall of Jerusalem in 587, to people who have lost their land and Temple and who feel that their God has lost too. The oracle looks back on the causes of the disaster and then forward to what only God can do. The next chapter is the valley of dry bones.
str: vv. 16–21: the people's sin and exile; God's name is dishonoured among the nations.
vv. 22–23: God will act for the sake of his holy name.
vv. 24–28: gathering, clean water, new heart, God's spirit, and the covenant formula.
kw: God will “sanctify” his name, that is, show who he truly is. The Our Father asks for this very thing.
In Hebrew the heart is not chiefly the seat of feeling but of thought, decision and will. A new heart means a new centre of the person.
heart of stone / heart of flesh
A stone cannot respond. Flesh is alive and can feel and answer. Here “flesh” is a good word, unlike its use in some other texts.
vv: It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name,
This sounds harsh, but it is the strongest kind of comfort. Salvation does not depend on our having deserved it. It depends on who God is.
I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you.
Priestly language from the rites of purification (compare Numbers 19). Later tonight the priest will bless the water and sprinkle the people after they renew their baptismal promises.
A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
Like Jeremiah 31:31–34, Ezekiel sees that the people's problem is deeper than behaviour, and that the cure must come from God.
I will put my spirit within you, and make you follow my statutes and be careful to observe my ordinances.
The Spirit does not abolish obedience. He makes it possible from within.
and you shall be my people, and I will be your God.
The words of the covenant. The promise is first of all to Israel, and God does not take it back.
ch: Jesus says to Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom “without being born of water and Spirit” (John 3:5), and he expects a teacher of Israel to have understood this. The Catechism sees in Ezekiel the conviction that conversion is first a work of grace: God must give us a new heart (CCC 1432). It also places these prophecies among the promises of the Spirit fulfilled at Pentecost (CCC 715). All seven readings have now brought us to this point: water and a new heart. Next comes the Gloria.

r.h: Christ, raised from the dead, will never die again
set: Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome around AD 57, before he had ever visited them. He has just said that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (5:20). Someone might then ask: should we go on sinning so that grace may grow? His answer is to remind them what happened at their baptism. This is the first reading of the New Testament on this night, and it is the key to all the Old Testament readings that came before.
str: vv. 3–4: baptized into his death, buried with him, to walk in newness of life.
vv. 5–7: united with him; the old self crucified; the slave released.
vv. 8–11: Christ will never die again; therefore consider yourselves alive to God.
kw: It means to plunge or immerse (CCC 1214). Paul has in mind a person going down into the water and coming up. The picture of burial and rising is natural to it.
Kainos means new in kind and not only recent. The life given is the life of the risen Christ.
Literally “the old man”, the person ruled by sin, the self in Adam (5:12–21). The “body of sin” in v. 6 is that self under the power of sin. Paul does not mean that the body itself is evil.
Christ's death is unique and never repeated. The Letter to the Hebrews also uses this word.
vv: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
“Do you not know?” Paul assumes that this is common teaching, and something the Roman Christians already understand.
Therefore we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.
The point of the sentence lies at its end. The goal of baptism is a way of walking, a daily life. Israel walked through the sea; the baptized walk in newness of life.
We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.
The Resurrection is more than the return of a dead man to this life, as with Lazarus, who died again. Christ has passed beyond death's reach (CCC 646).
So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
This is the first moral command in the chapter, and it rests on a fact. Become what you already are, by grace.
ch: The Catechism teaches, with this very passage, that the believer enters through baptism into communion with Christ's death, is buried with him and rises with him (CCC 1227). The instructions to the newly baptized at Jerusalem, traditionally linked with St Cyril, explain that we did not really die or get buried, but that while the imitation was in figure, the salvation is real (in substance). That is why the Easter Vigil is the Church's great night for baptism, and why all present renew their promises after the homily.

r.h: He has been raised; he is not here
set: In this year's cycle (Year B) the Vigil Gospel is from Mark. These women had watched from a distance at the Cross (15:40) and had seen where the body was laid (15:47). They could not anoint him before the Sabbath, so they bought spices when it ended, on the Saturday evening, and came at sunrise. The Church reads to v. 7. The oldest complete manuscripts of Mark stop at v. 8, with the women in fear; the verses that follow (16:9–20) are also received by the Church as inspired Scripture.
str: vv. 1–2: the women come with spices to the tomb.
vv. 3–4: their worry about the stone, and the stone already rolled back.
v. 5: the young man in white, and their alarm.
v. 6: the message: he has been raised; here is the place.
v. 7: the mission: tell his disciples and Peter; go to Galilee.
kw: The form is passive: God has raised him. Peter will preach the same in Acts. It is also the word for waking from sleep.

Mark does not say “angel”, although his white robe shows that he comes from God (compare 9:3). Mark used the same word of the young man who fled naked at the arrest (14:51–52), and some scholars see a link; others do not.
A strong word found only in Mark in the New Testament (also 9:15; 14:33). It is the awe of people who find themselves before the work of God.
vv: They had been saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance to the tomb?”
They came to care for a dead body, and they were worried about the wrong problem. God had already dealt with it.
“Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here.
The Greek form of “crucified” suggests a lasting state. The risen one is still the Crucified, and his wounds are not erased. The sentence is the shortest statement of the faith.
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.”
“And Peter”: he has denied Jesus three times (14:66–72), and he is named now. Galilee is where it all began. Jesus had promised this at the Last Supper (14:28). The call to follow can start again.
ch: The Catechism says that the empty tomb is not in itself a direct proof of the Resurrection, but an essential sign, and the first step toward recognizing it (CCC 640). It also notes that the women were the first to encounter the mystery and the first messengers of the Resurrection, even to the apostles (CCC 641). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, says that we too come to the tomb with spices when we seek the Lord with the fragrance of good works and virtues (in substance). Those newly baptized tonight are sent out with the same message.

qa: Must we believe that God made the world in six days of twenty-four hours?

No. The Catechism says that Scripture presents the work of creation symbolically as a succession of six days (CCC 337). What the chapter teaches is that God alone is the Creator, that all he made is good, and that human beings bear his image. The Church welcomes the sciences, which study how the world has developed, and sees no conflict between them and faith in the Creator (CCC 283–284).
Did God really want Abraham to kill his son?

The narrator says from the first line that this is a test, and the story ends with God stopping the knife. Later Scripture firmly forbids child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31). The chapter teaches that nothing we love, even God's own gift, comes before God, and that God provides. The Church does not read it as an example for anyone to copy.
Does God rejoice at the death of the Egyptians?

The song celebrates the end of slavery and of an oppressor's power. It is an ancient song and it speaks in the language of its time. A well-known story in the Jewish Talmud says that when the angels wished to sing that night, God stopped them, because the Egyptians too were the work of his hands. Christians, too, sing of the victory over the deeper slavery of sin and death, and pray for all who suffer and for those who wronged them.
rite: The Roman Missal calls this “the mother of all holy Vigils”, a phrase from St Augustine. It has four parts: the service of light with the paschal candle and the Exsultet; the Liturgy of the Word; baptism and the renewal of promises; and the Eucharist. The rubrics ask that it begin after nightfall and end before daybreak. If you have only attended the shorter Masses of Easter, try to come to the Vigil once, and bring your children. In catechesis, the seven readings may be taught as seven steps in the one story of God who saves through water and word.
study: Which of the seven Old Testament readings is closest to my own life this year, and why?
Isaac asks, “Where is the lamb?” How has God provided in a situation where I could not see a way forward?
Isaiah says that we can come without money. What do I still try to pay for or earn before God, rather than receiving by grace?
Paul says that we walk in newness of life. Which part of my daily walk needs to change after my baptismal promises are renewed tonight?

lead: The Gospel of this morning does not show the risen Lord at all. It shows a stone moved, two men running, cloths lying in a tomb, and one disciple who “saw and believed”. Around that quiet scene the other readings tell us what it means. Peter, in a Roman officer's house, gives the first summary of the Christian message: we ate and drank with him. Psalm 118 sings of the rejected stone and of “the day that the Lord has made”. Colossians says that our own life is now hidden with Christ. The alternative second reading from First Corinthians calls Christ our paschal lamb and tells us to keep the feast.

Before the Gospel the Church sings the Sequence, Victimae paschali laudes, an eleventh-century hymn usually attributed to Wipo of Burgundy. It is a small drama: death and life have fought a wondrous duel, and Mary is asked, “Tell us, what did you see on the way?” The key words today are witness, raised and above.

r.h: We ate and drank with him
set: Peter has come to Caesarea, the Roman capital of the province, to the house of Cornelius, a centurion who feared God. Through a vision on a rooftop Peter has learned not to call anyone unclean (10:9–16, 28). This is a turning point in Acts: the first preaching of the Gospel to a Gentile household. Many scholars see in the speech a summary of the early Church's preaching, in the same order as the Gospels themselves: John, Galilee, Jerusalem, the Cross, the Resurrection.
str: v. 34a: Peter begins (his words about God's impartiality are not read today).
vv. 37–38: the ministry of Jesus, anointed with the Spirit.
vv. 39–41: the death and Resurrection, and the chosen witnesses.
vv. 42–43: the command to preach; judge of all and forgiveness for all who believe.
kw: The verb behind the title Christos. Peter is explaining to a Gentile what “Christ” means: the one anointed with the Holy Spirit and power (CCC 453).
Someone who speaks of what he has seen and is ready to answer for it. The word occurs twice in these few verses. It later came to mean one who witnesses with his blood.
A word for wood or a tree, recalling Deuteronomy 21:22–23, about one hanged on a tree. Peter calls the Cross by the most shameful name, and then says that God has overturned the shame.
vv: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power; how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
The whole public life in one line. God is the first actor in the sentence, and the Trinity is quietly present: God, Jesus and the Spirit.
They put him to death by hanging him on a tree; but God raised him on the third day and allowed him to appear,

“They” here are those in Jerusalem who were involved in that day's events. The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The weight of the sentence is on “but God”.
not to all the people but to us who were chosen by God as witnesses, and who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
This is the detail that a witness would remember. A ghost does not eat. The risen Jesus shared meals and showed that he was truly alive (CCC 645).
All the prophets testify about him that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”
“Everyone” is the word Cornelius needed to hear. As Peter speaks, the Holy Spirit falls on the listeners (10:44).
ch: This speech shows the Church's faith in its first form: a story with witnesses, not a theory. The Catechism speaks of the appearances to witnesses as the basis of the Resurrection faith, and calls the apostles and Peter above all “the foundation stones” of the Church (CCC 642). The sacrament of Easter joy is also a meal: we too eat and drink with him, at every Mass.

r.h: This is the day that the Lord has made
set: Psalm 118 closes the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), the psalms Jewish families have long sung at Passover. So it is very likely the hymn that Jesus and his disciples sang before going out to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26). It is the song of someone who has come through mortal danger and goes up with a procession to give thanks at the Temple. The Church sings it on the morning of Easter, and its verse “This is the day” is the refrain today and an antiphon throughout the Octave.
str: vv. 1–2: the call to give thanks: his steadfast love endures forever.
vv. 16–17: the right hand of the Lord; “I shall not die, but I shall live”.
vv. 22–23: the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.
kw: The refrain of the psalm: God's covenant love does not run out.
the right hand of the Lord
An image of God's power in action. It was used in the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:6). On Easter morning the Church hears it of the God who raised Jesus.
Literally “head of the corner”, the stone that holds two walls together or crowns the building. The stone first thrown away is now the most important one.
vv: I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the Lord.
The psalmist spoke of rescue from danger. In the mouth of the Church this line goes further, because the risen Christ can say it for good.
The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This is the Lord’s doing; it is marvelous in our eyes.

Jesus applies this to himself at the end of the parable of the vineyard (Mark 12:10–11). Peter quotes it before the council (Acts 4:11), and it appears again in 1 Peter 2:7. Notice who does the reversal: “the Lord’s doing”.
This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
This refrain is not among the numbered verses of today's psalm, but it is what the people sing. For the Church “the day” is Easter itself, and so also every Sunday.
ch: The Roman liturgy has used this psalm at Easter from early times. Its verse “This is the day” is sung throughout the Octave as if the whole week were one single day. Today's psalm therefore teaches us to read Easter as the Lord's doing, and to answer with thanks before anything else. The Church gives thanks, and joins the song of Israel; she does not take it away from Israel.

r.h: Your life is hidden with Christ in God
set: The letter comes to us under Paul's name. Many scholars think that it was written by a disciple of his in his spirit, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself, and the Church receives it as inspired in either case. It answers teachers at Colossae who urged special rules and visions (2:16–23). These four verses turn from the doctrine of the first two chapters to the moral teaching of the rest: because you are raised, live so.
str: vv. 1–2: raised with Christ, seek and set your minds on what is above.
v. 3: you have died; your life is hidden.
v. 4: when Christ is revealed, you will be revealed with him.
kw: A past event. Paul says “you have been raised”, not only “you will be”. Baptism has already joined us to the Resurrection (2:12).
Not the sky, and not a flight from this world. It means the realm where Christ reigns, as the next verses show, for they deal with honest speech, forgiveness and home life (3:5–21).
A perfect tense: it has been hidden and remains so. No one can see the new life from outside, yet it is safe.
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
“If” here means “since”. “Seated at the right hand” is from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
The strongest sentence of the reading. The newly baptized know that they have died in the water, and their true life is kept where nothing can touch it.
When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.
Not “he gives you life”, but “who is your life”. The hiddenness will end. What is secret now will be seen.
ch: The Catechism uses these words directly: united with Christ by baptism, believers already truly participate in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, but this life remains “hidden with Christ in God” (CCC 1003). The risen Christ is the source of our own future resurrection (CCC 655). So Easter is both a fact and a hope.

r.h: Our paschal lamb has been sacrificed
set: This is the alternative second reading. Paul is writing to Corinth around AD 54 about a case of grave sin that the community has tolerated (5:1–2). He answers with a picture from the Passover: before the feast every Jewish house had to be cleared of yeast (Exodus 12:15). The passage shows that Christians already spoke of Christ's death as the Passover, little more than twenty years after the event.
str: v. 6b: a little yeast leavens the whole batch.
v. 7: clean out the old yeast; Christ our paschal lamb has been sacrificed.
v. 8: let us celebrate the festival with sincerity and truth.
kw: In this image a little of the old dough, carried into the new, spreads through all of it. It stands for what corrupts.
Pascha means the Passover and also its lamb. Paul's sentence is very short in Greek, and very bold.
A continuing action. The whole Christian life is to be kept as a feast.
vv: Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, as you really are unleavened. For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.
Once more the same logic: become what you are. The cleansing does not win the feast; the lamb has already been slain, and the house is put in order because of that.
Therefore, let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
Easter joy has a moral shape. Yeast and bread have become ways of speaking of the heart.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse: as often as the sacrifice of the Cross by which “Christ our Pasch has been sacrificed” is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is carried out (Lumen Gentium 3; CCC 1364). The first Easter Preface of the Roman Missal takes up the same words.

r.h: He saw and believed
set: John's account of Easter opens “while it was still dark”, in a Gospel where light and darkness matter from the first page (1:5). Mary Magdalene stood at the Cross (19:25). The burial was hurried by the coming of the Sabbath (19:42). The “other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved” is the witness behind this Gospel (21:24), whom tradition identifies with St John the Apostle.
str: vv. 1–2: Mary finds the stone removed and runs to tell Peter and the other disciple.
vv. 3–5: the two run; the other disciple arrives first and looks in.
vv. 6–7: Peter goes in and sees the wrappings and the head cloth.
vv. 8–9: the other disciple goes in, sees and believes; they did not yet understand the Scripture.
kw: When Lazarus came out of his tomb he was still bound with strips of cloth, with a cloth around his face (11:44); he would need them again. Here they are left behind.
The cloth is folded or rolled and placed apart. Whatever happened in that tomb, it was not a hurried theft.

John uses three different verbs for seeing in this passage (vv. 5, 6, 8). The last one goes with “believed”. John's vocabulary should not be pressed too far, but the story moves from looking to faith.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.
“The first day of the week” marks a new creation, and Christians will soon gather on this day. It is why we keep Sunday.
“They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”
Her first thought is theft. Nobody in this scene expected the Resurrection. The disciples did not invent a hope they did not have.
and the cloth that had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen wrappings but rolled up in a place by itself.
St John Chrysostom points out that thieves would not have stripped the body and taken time over the cloths, which were stuck with myrrh (in substance).
Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

He has not yet seen the risen Lord, only signs of absence. Love reads the signs first. Yet he waits and lets Peter go in first (v. 5), and many readers see in this the respect of love for Peter's office.
for as yet they did not understand the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
Understanding of the Scripture will come only afterward. That is the task of the Emmaus road and of the whole Easter season.
ch: The Catechism explains that the empty tomb is not a direct proof, but it was the first step to recognizing the Resurrection, as with the beloved disciple who “saw and believed” (CCC 640). It teaches that the Resurrection is a real, historical event, attested by witnesses, and also one that transcends history (CCC 639, 647). Christ's risen body is the true body, now in a new state (CCC 645–646).

qa: Could the disciples have stolen the body or simply imagined all this?

The Gospels themselves show that nobody expected it: Mary thinks the body has been taken, and the disciples “did not understand the scripture”. The Catechism notes that their faith did not produce the Resurrection; the Resurrection produced their faith, for they were downcast and frightened, and at first took the women's report as an idle tale (CCC 643–644). People do not give their lives for what they know they made up.
Is the Resurrection like the raising of Lazarus?

No. Lazarus came back to this life and later died. Christ passed through death to a glorious life, with a true body no longer subject to time and space, and he will never die again (Romans 6:9; CCC 646).
Why do Christians gather on Sunday rather than the Sabbath?

Because the Lord rose on “the first day of the week” (John 20:1). The Church honours the Sabbath as God's gift to Israel and sees Sunday as the fulfilment of its meaning for Christians (CCC 2174–2175).
rite: Today the Sequence must be sung or recited, and the renewal of baptismal promises with the sprinkling of water may take the place of the Creed. The double Alleluia is added at the dismissal through the Octave, and the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. The Vigil's Gospel of Mark may also be read today, and Luke's Emmaus account may be read at an afternoon or evening Mass. The Code of Canon Law asks every Catholic to receive Holy Communion at least once a year, in the Easter season if possible (can. 920). In your family, let the day begin with the simple greeting: Christ is risen!
study: Peter's speech is a summary of the Gospel in a few lines. How would I tell the good news of Jesus to a neighbour in five sentences?
Psalm 118 says, “This is the Lord’s doing.” What rejected or broken stone in my life has God used?
Colossians says that my life is “hidden with Christ”. What difference does this make to how I face failure or praise?
Mary ran, Peter ran, the other disciple ran. What makes me run toward Christ, and what slows me down?

lead: For eight days the Church lives one long Easter, and each day's readings show a further witness. Today Peter stands up at Pentecost and proclaims in Jerusalem what he had once denied. He reads Psalm 16, today's psalm, as a prophecy of the Resurrection: David died, and his tomb is still there, so he must have been speaking of another. In Matthew, the women running from the tomb are met by Jesus himself, while the guards are given money to tell a different story. The key words are witness, joy and go. Truth is spreading, and a false report is spreading too.

r.h: This Jesus God raised up
set: It is the day of Pentecost, the Jewish feast of Weeks, and pilgrims from many lands are in Jerusalem. The disciples have just received the Holy Spirit, and the crowd is astonished. Peter, who a few weeks earlier denied Jesus to a servant girl (Luke 22:56–57), now speaks in public. This is the first Christian sermon in Acts. Peter speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews, and he reads their own Scripture with them.
str: v. 14: Peter stands with the eleven and raises his voice.
vv. 22–24: Jesus' works, his death by God's plan and human hands, and God's raising him.
vv. 25–28: Psalm 16 quoted.
vv. 29–31: the argument: David died, and his tomb is here, so he spoke of the Messiah.
vv. 32–33: we are witnesses; the exalted Christ has poured out the Spirit.
kw: The Cross took no one by surprise in heaven. God's plan and human guilt stand side by side in the verse, and Scripture does not resolve the tension.

The Greek of v. 24 speaks of God loosening the “birth pangs” of death, which the NRSV renders “having freed him from death”. The picture is that the grave has been in labour, and has brought forth life.
The Greek Old Testament's reading of Psalm 16:10, where the Hebrew has “the Pit”. Peter's argument turns on this word: David's body decayed, and Jesus' body did not.
vv: But God raised him up, having freed him from death, because it was impossible for him to be held in its power.
The heart of the sermon. Death could not hold the author of life. The Catechism cites this verse in explaining that Christ's body did not see corruption (CCC 627).
“Fellow Israelites, I may say to you confidently of our ancestor David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.

Peter speaks with respect: “Fellow Israelites”, “our ancestor”. A tomb of David was known in Jerusalem in that time, and the Jewish historian Josephus also mentions one. The contrast is between a tomb with a body and a tomb without one.
This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.
The verse the whole week could be built on. The witnesses are the proof that Peter offers. Nothing explains the change in him except what he says here.
Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear.
The Father, the Son and the Spirit in one sentence. The sound and the speech that astonished the crowd are the sign that Jesus is alive and reigning.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' violent death was no accident but part of the mystery of God's plan, as Peter says here (CCC 599), and that God's foreknowledge did not take away human freedom (CCC 600). It adds that personal guilt cannot be placed on the Jews as a people (CCC 597), for all sinners were the authors of the Passion (CCC 598). When we hear “you crucified” in this reading we should hear it addressed to ourselves too.

r.h: Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers
set: In the verses just before (28:1–7), an angel has rolled back the stone and told the women to go to the disciples. Only Matthew tells of the guard at the tomb, set there at the request of the chief priests and the Pharisees (27:62–66). He places the two scenes side by side: the women go off to tell the truth while soldiers go off to report what happened. Many scholars think that Matthew wrote for a community with Jewish roots, in the decades when the two communities were debating these things.
str: v. 8: the women run, with fear and great joy.
vv. 9–10: Jesus meets them; they worship; “go and tell my brothers”.
vv. 11–15: the guards, the money and the story.
kw: An ordinary greeting, but its literal meaning is “rejoice”. It is the risen Lord's first word in Matthew.
To bow low in homage. Matthew uses this word from the Magi (2:11) to the last scene of the Gospel (28:17). These women are doing what is due to God.
Jesus had said that those who do the Father's will are his brothers (12:49). Now, after the disciples have fled, he still calls them that.
vv: So they left the tomb quickly with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
Fear and joy together: this is honest. A believer may have both at once, and that does not stop anyone from running with the news.
Suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came to him, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.
He comes to them on the road as they obey. They take hold of his feet, so he is no ghost. They worship, so he is more than a man who has come back.
Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.”
Not a word of reproach about their flight. He calls them brothers and sends them a message by the women.
So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story is still told among the Jews to this day.

Matthew is reporting a dispute of his own time about a particular rumour. It must not be read as a charge against the Jewish people, then or now (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The story itself admits one thing: the tomb was empty.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on the Psalms, mocks the soldiers' story gently: you bring sleeping witnesses? If you were asleep, how do you know what happened (in substance)? St Justin Martyr, in the second century, also knew of this rumour. The Catechism sees the women as the first messengers of the Resurrection (CCC 641), and it notes that by “my brothers” the risen Jesus shows the new relationship of adoption that his Resurrection has opened to us (CCC 654).

qa: Why does the Church keep repeating Easter for eight days?

An octave treats eight days as one great day, a very old custom, and the Octave of Easter keeps the rank of a solemnity. In the early Church the newly baptized wore white and received further instruction during this week. In the Liturgy of the Hours, each day of the Octave sings “This is the day”.
“You crucified him”: does the Bible blame the Jews for the death of Jesus?

No. Peter speaks to a particular crowd in Jerusalem, as one of them, calling them to repent and offering them forgiveness. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism says that we sinners ourselves bear the graver responsibility (CCC 598).
rite: In Italy and in some other places this day is called the Monday of the Angel, because of the angel at the tomb. The Regina Caeli is said in place of the Angelus. The Sequence may be sung again before the Gospel acclamation, and the double Alleluia is added at the dismissal. A household custom worth keeping is to pray the Regina Caeli together this week.
study: What in my life has changed because of the Resurrection, as Peter was changed?
The women had fear and great joy at once. How do I live with both?
Jesus calls those who fled “my brothers”. Whom have I written off that Christ has not?
Some people today prefer another account of Jesus. How can I answer them gently and with clear reasons?

lead: Yesterday's sermon reaches its end, and the crowd asks the right question: “What should we do?” Peter answers with repentance and baptism, and three thousand are baptized. In the Gospel one woman, in tears at a tomb, hears her name. These are two ways of meeting the risen Lord: in a crowd cut to the heart, and alone in a garden. Psalm 33 sings that the earth is full of God's steadfast love. The key words today are turn, name and send.

r.h: What should we do?
set: This is the conclusion of Peter's sermon at Pentecost. He has argued from Scripture that Jesus is the Messiah raised by God. Now he draws the conclusion, and the crowd responds. Acts is showing the beginning of the Church: the first converts are Jews and those who have joined them, from many lands, and God's promise is held out first to them.
str: v. 36: the conclusion: God has made him both Lord and Messiah.
v. 37: the crowd's response and question.
vv. 38–39: repent, be baptized; the promise is for you and for all who are far away.
vv. 40–41: Peter's urging; about three thousand are added.
kw: they were cut to the heart
A word for a sharp stab of pain. The word of God does what no argument can do, and sorrow here is the beginning of grace.
Literally “change your mind”. It reaches the whole direction of life, and it echoes the first preaching of John and of Jesus (Matthew 3:2; 4:17).
Kyrios is the title the Greek Old Testament uses for God. Peter does not mean that Jesus only then began to be who he is. The Resurrection shows and establishes publicly what he always was (CCC 445).
vv: Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and to the other apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”
They do not answer with anger. It is a good question to ask of every homily.
Peter said to them, “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
There are two steps and two gifts: turning and baptism, then forgiveness and the Spirit. “Every one of you” means that baptism is personal, and no one is too far gone for it.
For the promise is for you, for your children, and for all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to him.”
The words “far away” recall Isaiah 57:19, and the last words echo Joel 2:32. Peter's horizon is already wider than his listeners know, as Cornelius will show (Acts 10).
So those who welcomed his message were baptized, and that day about three thousand persons were added.
“Added” implies a passive: it is the Lord who adds (2:47). The Church grows by God's action, and the numbers are the fruit of one frightened fisherman's courage.
ch: The Catechism says that from the very day of Pentecost the Church has celebrated and administered holy baptism, and it cites Peter's words to the crowd (CCC 1226). The two main effects of baptism are purification from sins and new birth in the Holy Spirit (CCC 1262). The Church is not a club that one joins but a people whom the Lord gathers, and the Spirit first came on her for that mission.

r.h: I have seen the Lord
set: The disciples have gone home (20:10), and Mary stays. The scene takes place in a garden, for John alone has told us that the tomb was in a garden (19:41). Jesus' question “Whom are you looking for?” repeats his first words in this Gospel (“What are you looking for?” 1:38). The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name (10:3), and now he does it.
str: vv. 11–13: Mary weeps; two angels; “Woman, why are you weeping?”
vv. 14–15: Jesus stands behind her; she takes him for the gardener.
v. 16: “Mary!” “Rabbouni!”
v. 17: “Do not hold on to me”; “go to my brothers”.
v. 18: “I have seen the Lord.”
kw: Her mistake is natural, and many readers have also found it true in a deeper way: the new creation begins in a garden, as the first did.
An Aramaic form of “Rabbi”, warmer than the plain title. John calls the language “Hebrew” as he does elsewhere, and he adds a translation.
do not hold on to me

The Greek means “stop clinging to me” more than the Latin Noli me tangere, “do not touch me”, might suggest. Thomas will be invited to touch him (20:27). The point here is that the relationship has changed: she cannot keep him as he was.
vv: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb. As she wept, she bent over to look into the tomb;

She has nothing left to do, and she stays. St Gregory the Great says in his homily on this Gospel that holy desires grow by delay, and that she who stayed to seek was the one who found (in substance).
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!” (which means Teacher).
A single word opens her eyes, and it is her own name. She has already turned toward him once (v. 14). Now she turns in her heart.
Jesus said to her, “Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father.
Jesus will not stay as he was before. His presence from now on is of another kind: in the Spirit, in the word, in the sacraments.
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”; and she told them that he had said these things to her.
She is the first to say this sentence, which will be the apostles' own (20:25). Hence the old title “apostle of the apostles”.
ch: St Thomas Aquinas, among others, calls Mary Magdalene the apostle to the apostles. In 2016, at the wish of Pope Francis, her memorial of 22 July was raised to a feast with that title in mind. The Catechism sees in “my Father and your Father” the new relationship of adoption that the Resurrection opens up: we become Christ's brothers and sisters by grace, though he is Son by nature in a way that we are not (CCC 654). In the Sequence, the Church asks her: “Tell us, Mary, what did you see on the way?”

qa: Was Mary Magdalene the sinful woman of Luke 7?

The Gospels do not say so. Luke 8:2 says only that seven demons had gone out of her. In the West, from the time of St Gregory the Great, she was often identified with the sinful woman and with Mary of Bethany, and this shaped much of Western art and preaching. The Roman calendar since 1969 no longer makes that identification, and many scholars today treat them as different women. What the Gospel does say is greater: she stayed, she was called by name, and she was sent.
Why did Jesus send a woman first, when courts in the ancient world generally gave women's testimony less weight?

The Gospels record it without embarrassment because it happened. Inventors of such a story would hardly have made women the first witnesses, as many scholars point out. The Catechism notes that the women were the first messengers, even to the apostles (CCC 641).
Does “Lord and Messiah” mean that Jesus only became divine at the Resurrection?

No. Peter is proclaiming what God has publicly shown by raising him. The Church confesses that the Son is one in being with the Father from all eternity, and that the Resurrection reveals and glorifies him also in his humanity (CCC 445, 653).
rite: This week's Gospels are heard together with the Church's newly baptized. In the Latin tradition they are the white-robed company of the Octave. If your parish has had new baptisms, greet them and pray for them. In families, Tuesday is a good day to recall your own baptism date, to light the candle if you still have it, and to thank God by name.
study: When did a word of God last “cut me to the heart”, and what did I do about it?
Peter says the promise is “for your children”. How do I pass on the faith at home?
Mary stayed when others left. Where am I being asked to stay and wait?
Christ called Mary by name. In what way has he called me by mine?

lead: Two journeys today. Peter and John go up to the Temple for prayer, and a man who has never walked goes in with them, leaping. Two disciples walk away from Jerusalem in sorrow, and a stranger joins them on the road. In both, a person is raised up by the name or the presence of the risen Lord, and in both something is given that money could not give. Psalm 105 calls us to remember God's wonderful works. The key words are name, opened and bread.

r.h: What I have I give you
set: Luke has just described the first community, which was often in the Temple (2:46). The first Christians were still praying there, as faithful Jews. The hour of prayer at three in the afternoon was the time of the evening sacrifice. The Beautiful Gate cannot be identified with certainty today. People who could not work often asked for alms at the entrances to the Temple, because giving alms was a work of piety for those going in to pray.
str: vv. 1–3: Peter and John, the man, the request.
vv. 4–5: “Look at us”.
vv. 6–7: “in the name of Jesus Christ”; the right hand; the man is raised up.
v. 8: walking and leaping and praising God.
vv. 9–10: the people recognize him and are amazed.
kw: In the Bible a name stands for the person and his power. To act in Jesus' name is to act with his authority, and it is this name, not Peter's power, that heals (3:12, 16; CCC 434).
The same verb used for the Resurrection of Jesus. Luke's readers would hear it. What God did for Jesus is now reaching this man.
Isaiah had promised that in the day of God's coming “the lame shall leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). Luke lets us see that the promised time has begun.
vv: Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
Before the healing, a look. Those who gave alms might drop a coin and walk on, but the apostles stop and see him as a person.
But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.”
This does not mean that alms are unimportant, for the early Church cared greatly for the poor (Acts 2:45; 4:34). But it shows what the Church has above all to give. What she has is Christ.
And he took him by the right hand and raised him up; and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
Luke, by tradition a physician (Colossians 4:14), is exact about the feet and ankles. At this moment Peter's hand and Christ's name do the work; Peter will speak later of faith in that name (3:16).
Jumping up, he stood and began to walk, and he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
He had been carried to the gate each day but had stayed outside it. Now he goes in with them. Three words of movement end in one word of prayer.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Resurrection glorifies the name of Jesus, and that in his name the disciples perform miracles (CCC 434). The Church also teaches that she must have a preferential love for the poor (CCC 2448), and that love reaches the whole person: a coin is good, and being able to stand and enter the house of God is better. The Church is sent with this double care.

r.h: They recognized him in the breaking of the bread
set: This is one of the best-loved stories in the New Testament, and only Luke tells it. It takes place on Easter Sunday afternoon. Seven miles (sixty stadia; some manuscripts read a hundred and sixty) from Jerusalem lies Emmaus, a place that several later sites claim and that cannot be identified for certain. One traveller is named Cleopas; the other is unnamed. Many scholars note the shape of the story, which moves away from Jerusalem and back again, and which has the structure of the Mass itself: the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken.
str: vv. 13–16: the two walk; Jesus joins them; their eyes are kept from recognizing him.
vv. 17–24: “We had hoped”: their account.
vv. 25–27: he opens the Scriptures.
vv. 28–29: “Stay with us.”
vv. 30–32: the bread; eyes opened; hearts burning.
vv. 33–35: back to Jerusalem; “The Lord has risen indeed”.
kw: A key word in Luke (compare 9:22; 24:7, 44). The Cross was no failure of God's plan, as they had thought, but its road.
From the same family as our word “hermeneutics”. Jesus himself is the first Christian interpreter of the Old Testament, and he reads it as being about himself.
Luke uses this phrase in Acts for the gathering of the first Christians (Acts 2:42). It is one of the oldest names for the Eucharist (CCC 1329).
vv: While they were talking and discussing, Jesus himself came near and went with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He comes to them while they are walking the wrong way. “Were kept” suggests that seeing the risen Lord is a gift, not a matter of good eyesight.
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.
Perhaps the saddest line in the Gospel. They knew all the facts, including the women's report, and still they could not see. Theirs is a hope in the past tense.
Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.
The readings of the Vigil took this very road. The Church reads the Old Testament in the light of the Risen Christ, while knowing it first as the living word given to Israel (CCC 129).
When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.

The same four actions as at the feeding of the crowd (9:16) and at the Last Supper (22:19). The guest has become the host. He vanishes at the very moment he is known, as if to say: you now know where to find me.
They said to each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?”
Only now do they understand what they felt. Often we recognize God's presence only looking back.
ch: The Catechism says that the Mass has the same movement as this meal: the liturgy of the word and of the Eucharist form one act of worship (CCC 1346–1347). The Second Vatican Council says that the Church receives the bread of life from the one table of God's word and Christ's body (Dei Verbum 21). St Augustine asks where the Lord chose to be recognized, and he answers: in the breaking of bread (in substance). St John Paul II took the title of his 2004 apostolic letter on the Eucharist, Mane Nobiscum Domine, from their words: Stay with us, Lord.

qa: Why did they not recognize him?

Luke says that “their eyes were kept from recognizing him”, and he does not explain further. Elsewhere too the risen Jesus is not recognized at first (John 20:14; 21:4). His risen body is real but transformed (CCC 645), and to recognize him requires faith, which comes through the word and the bread.
Is the meal at Emmaus actually the Eucharist?

Luke does not say that in so many words. But he uses the same verbs as at the Last Supper, and he calls it “the breaking of the bread”, which is his term for the Eucharist in Acts. The Church reads it in that light (CCC 1329, 1347).
Does “I have no silver or gold” mean that the Church should not have any property or give alms?

No. The same book of Acts shows the community pooling goods to care for the poor (Acts 4:32–35). The verse teaches that the Church's first treasure is Christ. Whatever goods she has are for worship, for her mission and for the poor (CCC 2444–2448).
rite: At an afternoon or evening Mass on Easter Sunday the Emmaus Gospel may be read, and it returns today, in the Octave. Every Mass has this same shape: we walk in with our disappointments, the Scriptures are opened, and the bread is broken, and we are sent back to the others to say that the Lord has risen. After Communion this week, try saying simply, “Stay with us, Lord.”
study: Peter says, “What I have I give you.” What do I really have to give, apart from money?
Where in my life do I say, “We had hoped”? Have I told this to Jesus on the road?
When have I felt my heart burn as the Scriptures were opened? How can I hear them that way again?
The two disciples went straight back to Jerusalem at night. To whom should I go with news of the Lord?
